questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify the correct trend of acidic strength for the given alcohols.
questions.solution:
Primary alcohols are more acidic than secondary alcohols which are more acidic than tertiary alcohols. This is because the strength of alcohol as an acid is dependent on corresponding strength of its conjugate base, alkoxide ion. A more stabilised alkoxide is the weaker conjugate base and hence alcohol is more acidic.


Order of acidic strength is (I) > (II) > (III)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Identify $( Z )$ in the following reaction:

${CH}_{3}COOH\overset{{LiAlH}_{4}}{⟶} ( X ) \overset{Cu}{573K} ( Y ) \overset{dil . NaOH}{⟶}$$( Z )$
questions.solution:
${LiAlH}_{4}$ can reduce the carboxylic acid into the alcohol. So, the acetic acid is converted into the ethanol by ${LiAlH}_{4}$ in reaction $X$. Copper is an oxidising agent. It can oxidise the alcohol to the aldehyde. So, it oxidises the ethanol to the ethanal in reaction $Y$.

The ethanal has the alpha hydrogen. So, the weak base will take the acidic hydrogen. It will form the carbanion. After that the carbanion will give the nucleophilic addition reaction with another mole of ethanal. The $\beta$-hydroxylcarbonyl compound is formed as a product.

Reaction :-

${CH}_{3}COOH\overset{{LiAlH}_{4}}{⟶}{CH}_{3}{CH}_{2}OH\mathop{\to}_{573K}^{Cu}{CH}_{3}CHO\overset{dil . NaOH}{⟶}{CH}_{3} - CH ( OH ) - {CH}_{2} - CHO ( Aldol )$

Hence the $Z$ in this reaction is aldol.
questions.question:

${CH}_{3}COOH\overset{{LiAlH}_{4}}{⟶} ( X ) \overset{Cu}{573K} ( Y ) \overset{dil . NaOH}{⟶}$$( Z )$
questions.explanation:
${LiAlH}_{4}$ can reduce the carboxylic acid into the alcohol. So, the acetic acid is converted into the ethanol by ${LiAlH}_{4}$ in reaction $X$. Copper is an oxidising agent. It can oxidise the alcohol to the aldehyde. So, it oxidises the ethanol to the ethanal in reaction $Y$.

The ethanal has the alpha hydrogen. So, the weak base will take the acidic hydrogen. It will form the carbanion. After that the carbanion will give the nucleophilic addition reaction with another mole of ethanal. The $\beta$-hydroxylcarbonyl compound is formed as a product.

Reaction :-

${CH}_{3}COOH\overset{{LiAlH}_{4}}{⟶}{CH}_{3}{CH}_{2}OH\mathop{\to}_{573K}^{Cu}{CH}_{3}CHO\overset{dil . NaOH}{⟶}{CH}_{3} - CH ( OH ) - {CH}_{2} - CHO ( Aldol )$

Hence the $Z$ in this reaction is aldol.

questions.q: Which of the following metals is used as a catalyst in Haber's process of ammonia synthesis?
questions.solution:
Iron is used as a catalyst in Haber's process.

The Haber process, also called the Haber Bosch process, is the industrial implementation of the reaction of nitrogen gas and hydrogen gas. It is the main industrial procedure to produce ammonia and the& catalyst used is iron with a suitable promoter like ${K}_{2}O, CaO, {SiO}_{2}, and{Al}_{2}{O}_{3}.$

Hence, Iron is used in the Haber cycle as a cheap catalyst because it allows in acceptable time to reach a reasonable yield

${\left({CH}_{3}\right)}_{2}Cd$ is less nucleophilic than carbon. It can convert the acetic chloride into the acetone. The compound P is acetone. After that, acetone and acetaldehyde both have the alpha hydrogen. So, they give the cross-aldol and self aldol condensation reaction with sodium hydroxide and heat. The alkene can show the geometrical isomerism if there are different groups along the double bond.

Reaction :-

${CH}_{3}COCl\overset{i ) {\left({CH}_{3}\right)}_{2}Cd}{\to}\mathop{{CH}_{3}{COCH}_{3}}_{( P )}\mathop{{CH}_{3}{COCH}_{3}}_{( P )} + {CH}_{3}CHO\overset{ii ) NaOH ( aq . ) ∆}{\to}{( {CH}_{3} )}_{2}C = CH - CHO + {( {CH}_{3} )}_{2}C = CH - CO - {CH}_{3} + {CH}_{3}CH = CH - CHO + {CH}_{3}CH = CH - CO - {CH}_{3}$

Hence, the total number of products formed in the given reaction sequence is $4$.

A. The reactivity of aromatic aldehydes and ketones is less than that of aliphatic carbonyl compounds towards nucleophilic addition reactions.
B. Benzaldehyde does not give Fehling's test.
C. The \(\mathrm{H}\)-atoms in ethanal are acidic in nature.
D. \(p\)-nitro benzaldehyde is less reactive than benzaldehyde towards nucleophilic addition reactions.
questions.solution:
(A) Because of the attachments of bulkier groups (aryl), the attack of nucleophile to the \(s p^2\) carbon of \( > \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}\) group will face steric repulsion. So, rate of the reaction will decrease. (B) Fehling's solution is being a very mild oxidising agent, benzaldehyde does not respond to it. (C) Ethanol on tautomerisation produces its enol form. It atom attacked with \(\mathrm{OH}\) group of the enol is acidic.
(D) Because of the presence of \(-\mathrm{NO}_2\) group of para position ( \(-R\) effect), the carbon atom \(\left(s p^2\right)\) of
group becomes more susceptible for nucleophilic attack as the \(s p^2\) carbon gains more partial positive charge.
So, this statement is not correct.

questions.q: The relative basic strength of the compounds is correctly shown in the option.
questions.solution:
The correct order of relative basic strength will be
$\ddot{\mathrm{NH}_3 > \ddot{\mathrm{NH}_2-\ddot{\mathrm{NH}_2 > \ddot{\mathrm{NH}_2-\mathrm{OH}$
In $\mathrm{NH}_3$, the lone pair is completely available for donation, hence is most basic whereas $\mathrm{NH}_2-\mathrm{NH}_2$ and $\mathrm{NH}_2-\mathrm{OH}$ can be considered as derivatives of $\mathrm{NH}_3$. Here, $\mathrm{H}$ is replaced by $-\mathrm{NH}_2$ forming $\mathrm{NH}_2-\mathrm{NH}_2$ and $-\mathrm{OH}$ forming $\mathrm{NH}_2-\mathrm{OH}$ being highly electron withdrawing due to $-\mathrm{O}$ will decrease the election density most on $-\mathrm{N}$.
$\therefore$ Least basic elect;on withdrawing $-I$-effect of
$-\mathrm{NH}_2$ is less as compared to - $\mathrm{OH}$.
Hence correct order of basic strength is
$\mathrm{NH}_3 > \mathrm{NH}_2-\mathrm{NH}_2 > \mathrm{NH}_2-\mathrm{OH}$

questions.q:
Arrange the following bases in decreasing order of basicity is
(i) Aniline
(ii) O - nitroaniline
(iii) m-& nitroaniline
(iv) p& - nitroaniline
questions.solution:
Basicity is directly proportional to the $+ M, + I$ effect, but it is inversely proportional to the $- M, - I$ effect. Aniline is the highest basic because it does not have any group. But the nitro group can show the $- I$and $- M$ effect. The nitro group at meta position show only the $- I$ effect. But at ortho and para position, it will show the $- M, - I$ effect both. So, the $m -$nitroaniline is more basic than the $p -$nitroaniline and $o -$nitroaniline.

So, the basicity order is :-

Hence, the decreasing order of basicity is $( i ) >( iii )>( iv )>( ii )$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following vitamins cannot be stored in the body?
questions.solution:
Vitamins are classified into two groups depending upon their solubility in water or fat.

Fat soluble vitamins: Vitamins which are soluble in fat and oils but insoluble in water are kept in this group. These are vitamins $A, D, E$ and $K$. They are stored in liver and adipose (fat storing) tissues.

Water soluble vitamins: $B$ group vitamins and vitamin $C$ are soluble in water. Water soluble vitamins must be supplied regularly in diet because they are readily excreted in urine and cannot be stored (except vitamin ${B}_{12}$) in our body.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: How many tripeptides can be prepared by linking the amino acids glycine, alanine and phenyl alanine?
questions.solution:
Tripeptides are amino acids polymers in which three individual amino acid units, called residues, are linked together by amide bonds. In these, an amine group from one residue forms an amide bond with the carboxyl group of a second residue, the amino group of the second forms an amide bond with the carboxyl group of the third. Therefore, glycine $\left(\mathrm{NH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{COOH}\right)$,alanine
and phenyl alanine
can be linked in six different ways.

questions.q: Wurtz reaction of bromoethane gives \(n\)-butane. Sodium salt of \(X\) on heating with sodalime also results in \(n\)-butane. Compound \(X\) is
questions.solution:
In Wurtz reaction, two molecules of bromoethane react with 2 molecules of sodium to form \(n\)-butane.
\begin{aligned}$\mathrm{CH}_{3}- \mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{Br}+2 \mathrm{Na}+\mathrm{Br}$-$\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}_{3}$ \\
-2 $\mathrm{NaBr}$ \longrightarrow $\mathrm{CH}_{3}- \mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}_{3}$\end{aligned} \)
\(n\)-butane can also be obtain when sodium salt$ of $pentanoic acid \((X)\) gets heated with sodalime. The reaction is given as under :
\(\underset{(X)}{\mathrm{CH}_{3}\left(\mathrm{CH}_{2}\right)_3 \mathrm{COOH}}$\xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH}}\)
\(\underset{\text{ Sodium salt }}{\mathrm{CH}_{3}  \mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{CH}_{2}  \mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{COONa}} $\xrightarrow{$\mathrm{NaOH}$+\mathrm{CaO} \text{ (Sodalime) }} \underset{\text{n-butane}}{\mathrm{CH}_{3}  \mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{CH}_{2}  \mathrm{CH}_{3}}+\mathrm{Na}_{2}  \mathrm{CO}_{3}\)
Hence, \(X\) is \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}  \mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{CH}_{2}  \mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{COOH}\).

questions.solution:
According to Fajan rule, for covalent character, cation should be small in size and should have high positive charge and anion should be large in size and contain high negative charge.
(i) Iodine have more size than $\mathrmF^{-}$ so, $\mathrm{KI}>\mathrm{KF}$
(ii) $\mathrmK^{+}$ have more size the $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ so, $\mathrm{LiF}>\mathrm{KF}$
(iii) $\mathrm{Sn}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Sn}^{4+}\mathrm{Sn}^{4+}$ carry more charge than $\mathrm{Sn}^{2+}\text{ so, } \mathrm{SnCl}_4>\mathrm{SnCl}_2$
(iv) $\mathrm{Cu}^{+}$ have pseudo configuration so it has more covalent character than NaCl.
$\mathrm{CuCl}>\mathrm{NaCl}\therefore$ (i), (iii) and (iv) are correct

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Which of the following are not in accordance with the property mentioned against them?
I. $\mathrm{F}_2 > \mathrm{Cl}_2 > \mathrm{Br}_2 > \mathrm{I}_2$ : Oxidising power
II. $\mathrm{MI} > \mathrm{MBr} > \mathrm{MCl} > \mathrm{MF}$ : Ionic character of metal halide
III. $\mathrm{F}_2 > \mathrm{Cl}_2 > \mathrm{Br}_2 > \mathrm{I}_2$ : Bond dissociation enthalpy
IV. $\mathrm{HI} < \mathrm{HBr} < \mathrm{HCl} < \mathrm{HF}$ : Hydrogen-halogen bond strength
questions.solution:
Ionic character of metal halide :-
$\mathrm{M}-\mathrm{F} > \mathrm{M}-\mathrm{Cl} > \mathrm{M}-\mathrm{Br} > \mathrm{M}-\mathrm{I}$
This is due to low polarizability of fluorine due to very small size which gives more ionic character.
Thus, II is incorrect.
Order of bond dissociation enthalpy :-
$\mathrm{Cl}_2 > \mathrm{Br}_2 > \mathrm{F}_2 > \mathrm{I}_2$
This is due to very small size and $\mathrm{F}-\mathrm{F}$ bond length that causes repulsion between the atoms and possible multiple bonds between $\mathrm{Cl}_2, \mathrm{Br}_2$ and $\mathrm{I}_2$ due to availability of $\mathrm{d}$ orbitals.
Thus, III is incorrect.

Dipole moment of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ and $\mathrm{NH}_3$ They both have dipole moment because they do not have regular geometries. Dipole moment of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ is more than $\mathrm{NH}_3$ because $\mathrm{O}$ is more electronegative than $\mathrm{N}$.
Dipole moment of $\mathbf{B F}_3$ It is zero because it has symmetrical (triangular planar) structure.
Therefore, the correct order of dipole moments of molecules is $\mathrm{H}}_{2} \mathrm{O} \text{ (III) }> \mathrm{NH}$}_{3} $\text{ (I) }$>$\mathrm{NF}}_{3} \text{ (IV) }> \mathrm{BF}$}_{3} $\text{ (II) }$

questions.q: A covalent molecule $X - Y$ is found to have a dipole moment of $1. 5 \times {10}^{- 29}C. m$ and $a$ bond length of $150$ pm. The percent ionic character of the bond will be
questions.solution:
Dipole moment=& $q \times d$

Bond length $d = 150pm = 150 \times {10}^{- 12}m$

Charge $q = 1 . 6 \times {10}^{- 19}$

Dipole moment = $150 \times {10}^{- 12} \times 1 . 6 \times {10}^{- 19} = 2 . 4 \times {10}^{- 29}$

Percentage ionic character =$\dfrac{Dipoleobserved}{Dipolecalculated} \times 100$

Dipole observed =& $1 . 5 \times {10}^{- 29}$

Percentage ionic character = $\dfrac{1 . 5 \times {10}^{- 29}}{2 . 4 \times {10}^{- 29}} \times 100 = 62 . 5$

Hence, the percent ionic character of the bond will be $62 . 5 %$.

questions.solution:
The dipole moment depends on the charge and distance between the central atom and side atoms. But the charge is more prominent than distance. It is determined as polar and non-polar molecules.& It can be determined by the geometry of the molecule.

In case of& ${NCl}_{3} & {NH}_{3}$~the electronegativity difference between& $N - H$~is higher& than the& electronegativity difference between& $N - Cl$~bond so the shared pair of electrons shifted towards chlorine in case of ${NCl}_{3}$~and in case of& ${NH}_{3}$~it will be towards& Nitrogen.& So, for& ${NH}_{3}$~the net dipole moment will be towards& the direction of lone pair and will be added up into the dipole moment of lone pair while in case of& ${NCl}_{3}$~the moment due to three bond pairs will be in opposite direction to the dipole moment of the lone pair, and it will be subtracted results in lower value of net dipole moment.

In case of& ${CS}_{2}$, it has~the linear shape and so their& moment is balanced and so net dipole moment is zero.

In case of ethane& $\left({C}_{2}{H}_{6}\right)$, the electronegativity difference between carbon and hydrogen is minimal so unbranched alkanes have zero dipole moment.~

Hence,& ${NH}_{3}$& has maximum dipole moment among the given options.

questions.q:
The increasing order of acidic strength among the following compounds is

$I$. Benzoic acid
$II$. $4 -$nitrobenzoic acid
$III$. $3, 4 -$dinitrobenzoic acid
$IV$. $4 -$methoxybenzoic acid
questions.solution:
Since electron-donating groups decrease the acid strength, $4 -$methoxy benzoic acid is a weaker acid than benzoic acid. Further, since electron-withdrawing groups increase the acid strength, both $4 -$nitrobenzoic acid and $3, 4 -$dinitrobenzoic acid are stronger acids than benzoic acid.

Further, due to the presence of an additional ${NO}_{2}$​ at $m -$position with respect to $COOH$ group, $3, 4 -$dinitrobenzoic acid, the overall acid strength increase in the order:

$4 -$methoxy benzoic acid $<$ Benzoic acid $<$ $4 -$nitrobenzoic acid $<$ $3, 4 -$dinitrobenzoic acid

questions.q:
Which of the following statements is correct about \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\) ?
A. The hybridisation of central atom is \(s p^3\).
B. Its resonance structure has one \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{O}\) single bond and two \(\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}\) double bonds.
C. The average formal charge on each carbon atom is 0.67 units.
D. All \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{O}\) bond lengths are equal.
questions.solution:
The hybridisation of central atom is \(s p^2\). Since a net charge of -2 is shared over 3 oxygen atoms, hence formal charge \(=0.67\) units. In resonating structures bonds are not fixed and therefore, all bond lengths are equal.
Hence, options (c) and (d) are correct.

Hybridisation state of \($\mathrm{Be}$\) in \($\mathrm{BeF}}_{2}\) is \(s p\).
\(\begin{aligned}

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Observe the following statements
i. The dipole moment of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ is higher than the dipole moment of $\mathrm{NF}_3$.
ii. The dipole moment of chloroform is zero.
iii. Covalent bond character in $\mathrm{NaCl}$ is more compared to $\mathrm{CuCl}$.
questions.solution:
Only statement (i) is correct.
- i. The dipole moment of \($\mathrm{NH}}_{3}\) is higher than the dipole moment of \( \mathrm{NF}$}_{3}\). This is correct. In \($\mathrm{NH}}_{3}\), the bond dipoles of the three \( \mathrm{N}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds and the lone pair on nitrogen all point in the same general direction, adding up to a larger net dipole moment. In \(N F_3\), the bond dipoles of the three N-F bonds point towards the highly electronegative fluorine atoms, while the lone pair dipole points away. These dipoles oppose each other, resulting in a much smaller net dipole moment.
- if. The dipole moment of chloroform is zero. This is incorrect. Chloroform (\(\mathrm{CHCl}$}_{3}\)) is a tetrahedral molecule with three highly electronegative chlorine atoms and one less electronegative hydrogen atom. The bond dipoles do not cancel each other out, resulting in a significant net dipole moment.
- iii. Covalent bond character in NaCl is more compared to CuCl . This is incorrect. According to Fajan's rules, a smaller cation with a pseudo-noble gas configuration (like \(C u^{+}\)) has a greater polarizing power than a cation with a noble gas configuration (like \($\mathrm{Na}^{+}$\)). This increased polarizing power leads to a greater covalent character. Therefore, CuCl is more covalent than NaCl.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Assertion (A): Higher lattice enthalpy leads to greater stability of ionic compounds.
Reason (R) : Lattice enthalpy is a direct measure of the electrostatic forces of repulsion among the constituent ions in an ionic solid.
The correct answer is
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct, but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct, but (R) is correct
questions.solution: Assertion (A): Higher lattice enthalpy leads to greater stability of ionic compounds. This statement is correct. Lattice enthalpy is the energy released when gaseous ions combine to form one mole of a solid ionic compound. A more negative (higher in magnitude) lattice enthalpy signifies a stronger attraction between ions and thus a more stable ionic compound. Reason (R): Lattice enthalpy is a direct measure of the electrostatic forces of repulsion among the constituent ions in an ionic solid. This statement is incorrect. Lattice enthalpy is a measure of the strong electrostatic forces of attraction between the oppositely charged ions in the crystal lattice, not repulsion. Therefore, Assertion (A) is correct, but the Reason (R) is incorrect. The correct option is (3).

questions.q:
Identify the correct statements from the following :
a) Change in hybridisation affects the electronegativity of carbon
b) The p orbitals in ethene are mutually parallel
c) The number of $\sigma$ bonds in propyne is 6
d) Electromeric effect is a permanent effect
questions.solution:
Statements a, b, and c are correct.
- a) Change in hybridization affects electronegativity. Carbon's electronegativity increases with the percentage of s-character in its hybridization \($\left($s p \gt s p² \gt s p³\right)\).
- b) The p orbitals in ethene are parallel. The two unhybridized p-orbitals on the \(s p²\) hybridized carbon atoms are parallel to each other, allowing for side-by-side overlap to form the pi bond.
- c) Propyne has 6 sigma bonds. The structure (\(C H_3-C $\equiv$C H\)) contains three \($\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}$\) bonds, one \($\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}$\) single bond, and one \($\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}$\) bond within the triple bond, and one \($\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}$\) bond, for a total of 6 sigma bonds.
- d) The electromeric effect is a temporary effect. It only occurs in the presence of an attacking reagent.
Thus, the correct statements are a, b, and c.

questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{A}_2(\mathrm{ g})+\mathrm{B}_2(\mathrm{ g}) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{AB}(\mathrm{ g}) \\
& \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{[\mathrm{AB}]^2}{\left[\mathrm{ A}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{B}_2\right]} \\
& \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{1.4 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.4 \times 10^{-3}}{1.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 2.1 \times 10^{-3}} \\
& \mathrm{ K}_{\mathrm{c}}=0.622 \\
& \mathrm{ K}_{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{RT})^{\Delta \mathrm{n}} \\
& \Delta \mathrm{n}=0 \\
& \mathrm{ K}_{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}=0.622
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}

$\mathrm{A}_2 \mathrm{ B}_6(\mathrm{ g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{A}_2 \mathrm{ B}_4(\mathrm{ g})+\mathrm{B}_2(\mathrm{ g})\begin{aligned}
& \text{Initial } \begin{array}{l}
\mathrm{p}=4 \mathrm{ atm} \quad 0.0 \\
\begin{array}{l}
\text{Equilibrium } \\
=4 \alpha
\end{array} \quad \mathrm{p} \alpha=4 \alpha
\end{array}$ \quad $\mathrm{p} \alpha=4 \alpha \\
& \qquad \begin{array}{l}

=\frac{(4 \alpha)(4 \alpha)}{4(1-\alpha)}=\frac{4 \alpha^2}{1-\alpha} \approx 4 \alpha^2 \\
\Rightarrow \alpha=0.1
\end{array}$
\end{aligned}$
Therefore, \mathrm{P} \left(\mathrm{A}_2 \mathrm{ B}_6\right) at equilibrium =4(1-\alpha)\begin{aligned}& =4(1-0.1) \\
& =3.62
\end{aligned}$

yellow colourless deep red

$\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g})+\mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{ g})+\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{ g})$
Its $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}$ value is
questions.solution: \Rightarrow Number of moles of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ reacting $=40 \%$ of 1 mole $=0.4$ moles $($ degree of dissociation $=\alpha)\Rightarrow 0.4$ moles of $\mathrm{CO}$ and 0.4 moles of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ react. Let $\mathrm{C}=$ initial concentrations of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} and \mathrm{CO}$. \Rightarrow At equilibrium; $\begin{aligned} & {\left[\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right]=\frac{0.6 \mathrm{ mol}}{1 \mathrm{ L}}=0.6 \mathrm{M}} \\ & {[\mathrm{CO}]=\frac{0.6 \mathrm{ mol}}{1 \mathrm{ L}}=0.6 \mathrm{M}} \\ & {\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]=\left[\mathrm{CO}_2\right]=\mathrm{c} \alpha=1 \times 0.4=0.4 \mathrm{M}} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{CO}_2\right]}{\left[\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right]}=\frac{(0.4)(0.4)}{(0.6)(0.6)} \\ & =0.444 . \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
A $1.0 \mathrm{~L}$ of aqueous solution contains $1 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NaBr}, 1 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NaCl} and 1 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{M}$ NaI. To this solution, $1 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{M}$ aqueous $\mathrm{AgNO}_3$ solution is added drop wise. The order of precipitation of $\operatorname{Ag} X(X=\mathrm{Cl}, \mathrm{Br}, \mathrm{I})$ is
$\begin{aligned} & \left(K_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathrm{AgCl})=1.8=10^{-10} ; K_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathrm{AgBr})=5 \times 10^{-13} ;\right. \\ & \left.K_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathrm{AgI})=8.3 \times 10^{-17}\right)\end{aligned}$
questions.solution:
$K_{\mathrm{sp}}$ of any salt is equal to the multiplication of concentration of its ions.
For $\mathrm{AgCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-}K_{\mathrm{sp}}=\left[\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\right]1.8 \times 10^{-10}=10^{-10}\left[\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\right]\left[\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\right]=\frac{1.8 \times 10^{-10}}{10^{-10}}=1.8$
Similarly, for AgBr
$\left[\mathrm{Br}^{-}\right]=\frac{5 \times 10^{-13}}{10^{-10}}=5 \times 10^{-3}$
For AgI
$\mathrmI^{-}=\frac{8.3 \times 10^{-17}}{10^{-10}}=8.3 \times 10^{-7}$
Lesser is the concentration of ion, more easily they get precipitated.
So, order of precipitation is
$\mathrm{AgI} \gt \mathrm{AgBr} \gt \mathrm{AgCl}$

questions.q:
Assertion (A) : For an endothermic dissolution process, increase in temperature increases the solubility in a nearly saturated solution.
Reason (R) : In saturated solution dynamic equilibrium exists between dissolved solute and undissolved solute.
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and R is the correct explanation of $\mathrm{A}$
Both (A) and (R) are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of $\mathrm{A}$
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
questions.solution: Increase in temperature in an endothermic resolution process enhance the kinetic energy of the solvent molecules by allowing them to break apart more efficiently. This results into the more solubility of solute molecules.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The formation of ammonia from its constituent elements is an exothermic reaction. The effect of increase temperature on the reaction equilibrium is
options: The rate of the forward reaction becomes zero
questions.solution:
Consider the reaction of formation of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen by Haber's process:

${N}_{2}\left(g\right) + 3{H}_{2}\left(g\right)\overset{}{⇌}2{NH}_{3}\left(g\right); ∆ H = - 92. 4kJ$

The forward reaction is exothermic& while, the reverse reaction is endothermic. If the temperature of the system in equilibrium in increased, according to Le Chatelier's principle, the system tries to decrease the temperature by absorbing heat. So, an increase in temperature favours the endothermic reaction. Therefore, at higher temperature the yield of ammonia is low.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given $k_p$ for the reaction
$\frac{1}{2} C(g) \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2} A(g)+\frac{1}{2} B(g)$ at a fixed temperature is $0.25 \mathrm{ atm}^{-2}$. Find the $K_p$ for the reaction
$A(g)+B(g) \rightleftharpoons C(g)$ at the same temperature.
questions.solution:
For the reaction,
$\frac{1}{2} C(g) \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2} A(g)+\frac{1}{2} B(g)$
Given, $K_p=0.25 \mathrm{ atm}^{-2}$
We know that, $K_C=\frac{[\text{ Product }]^b}{[\text{ Reactant }]^a}$, where $a and b$ are stiochiometric coefficients.
Also, $K_p=K_C(R T)^{\Delta n_g}$
where, $\Delta n_g=b-a$
For above reaction, $K_{C_1}=\frac{[A]^{0.5}[B]^{0.5}}{[C]^{0.5}}\Delta n_g=1-0.5=0.5$
So, $K_{p_1}=K_{C_1}(R T)^{0.5}...(i)$
Similarly for reaction,
$A(g)+B(g) \rightleftharpoons C(g)$, at same temperature
$\begin{aligned}
K_{C_2} & =\frac{[C]}{[A][B]} \\
\Delta n_g & =1-2=-1 \\
K_{p_2} & =K_{C_2}(R T)^{-1}...(ii)
\end{aligned}$
Now, divide $K_{p_1} and K_{p_2}$, we get,

Using the data provided, find the value of equilibrium constant for the following reaction at $298K$ and $1$ atm pressure. ${NO}_{( g )} + \dfrac{1}{2}{O}_{2} ( g ) ⇌ {NO}_{2} ( g )$
${\Delta}_{f}{H}^{0}\left({NO}_{( g )}\right) = 90 .4 kJ . {mol}^{- 1}$

${\Delta}_{f}{H}^{0}\left({NO}_{2} ( g )\right) = 32 .48 kJ ⋅ {mol}^{- 1}$

${\Delta S}^{∘} @ 298K = - 70 .8 J ⋅ {K}^{- 1} ⋅ {mol}^{- 1}$

$antilog ⁡ ( 0 .50 ) = 3162$
questions.solution:
The given reaction is

${NO}_{( g )} + \dfrac{1}{2}{O}_{2} ( g ) ⇌ {NO}_{2} ( g )$

The enthalpy of the above reaction given by the difference of enthalpies of reactant side and product side.

Therefore,

${∆}_{c}H = {∆}_{f}H\left({NO}_{2}\right) - \left[{∆}_{f}H\left(NO\right) + \dfrac{1}{2}{∆}_{f}H\left({O}_{2}\right)\right]{∆}_{c}H = 32 . 8 - \left[90 . 4 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(0\right)\right]{∆}_{c}H = - 57 . 6{KJmol}^{- 1}$

Also, we know that Gibb's free energy can be determined by

$∆ G = ∆ H - T ∆ S ∆ G = 57600{Jmol}^{- 1} - 298 \times \left(- 70 . 8\right){JK}^{- 1}{mol}^{- 1} ∆ G = - 36501 . 5{Jmol}^{- 1}$

Again, Using relation of Gibb's free energy with equilibrium constant i.e.

$∆ G = - 2 . 303 \times 8 . 31 \times 298logk = - 36501 . 5{Jmol}^{- 1}K = 3 . 162 \times {10}^{6}$

questions.solution:
In this question, we have to assume that volume of the vessel is \(1 \mathrm{ L}\).
$\begin{array}{lcccc} \mathrm{NO}_{2}(g)+ \mathrm{CO}(g) & \rightleftharpoons&  \mathrm{NO}(g)+ \mathrm{CO}_{2}(g) \\ t=0 & 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ \text{mole } t=t_{\text{eq } } & 1-0.5 & 2-0.5 & 0.5 & 0.5 \\ & =0.5 & =1.5 & & \\ \text{Molar conc. } \left(\mathrm{mol} \mathrm{L}^{-1}\right) \frac{0.5}{1} \frac{0.5}{1} \frac{0.5}{1} \frac{0.5}{1}\\ & =0.5 & =1.5 & 0.5 & 0.5\end{array}$ \)
Given, \(\alpha=2 \times \frac{25}{100}=0.5\)
\(\Rightarrow K_C=\frac{[\mathrm{NO}]\left[\mathrm{CO}_2\right]}{\left[\mathrm{NO}_2\right][\mathrm{CO}]}=\frac{0.5 \times 0.35}{0.5 \times 1.5}=\frac{1}{3}=K_p\)
Because, \(\Deltan_g=( \mathrm{l}+\mathrm{l})-(\mathrm{l}+\mathrm{l})=0\) \begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow& K_p=K_C(R T)^{\Deltan_s}=K_C(R T)^0=K_C \\
\Rightarrow   K_p=$\frac{1}{3}$
\end{array}

\$(\begin{aligned}$p_T & =p-p_i+2 p_i \\ p_T & =p+p_i \Rightarrow p_i=p_T-p \\ p_i & =10.64-6.64 \\ & =4.00 $\mathrm{bar} \end{aligned}\) At equilibrium, \$(\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad$p_{\mathrm{N}_2$} $\mathrm{O}}_{4}} & =p-p_i=6.64-4 \\ & =2.64 \mathrm{bar}\\ p_{\mathrm{NO}_2} & =2 p_i=2 \times4 \\ & =8 \mathrm{bar}\\ \therefore \quad K_p $$=\frac{$\left[p_{\mathrm{NO}_2}\right]$^2}{$\left[p_{\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_4}\right]$}$\\ $$=\frac{[8]^2}{2.64}=$24.29 \end{aligned}\)

The equilibrium constant $\left(K_C\right)$ for the following equilibrium
$2 \mathrm{SO}_2(g)+\mathrm{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{SO}_3(g)$
at $563 \mathrm{~K}$ is 100 . At equilibrium, the number of moles of $\mathrm{SO}_3$ in the 10 litre flask is twice the number of moles of $\mathrm{SO}_2$, then the number of moles of oxygen is
questions.solution:
Let, number of moles of $\mathrm{SO}_2=x$ moles of $\mathrm{SO}_3=2 x2 \mathrm{SO}_2(g)+\mathrm{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{SO}_3(g)$
At equilibrium,
$\begin{aligned}
K_c & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{SO}_3\right]^2}{\left[\mathrm{SO}_2\right]^2\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]} \\
100 & =\frac{\left[\frac{2 x}{10}\right]^2}{\left[\frac{x}{10}\right]^2\left[\frac{n_{\mathrm{O}_2}}{10}\right]} \\
100 & =\frac{40}{n_{\mathrm{O}_2}} n_{\mathrm{O}_2}=\frac{40}{100}=0.4
\end{aligned}$
Hence, number of moles of oxygen $=0.4$

what is the equilibrium constant of
$\mathrm{HI}(g) \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{H}_2(g)+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I}_2(g) ?$
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{H}_2(g)+\mathrm{I}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{HI}(g) ; K\therefore \quad K=\frac{[\mathrm{HI}]^2}{\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{I}_2\right]}$ ...(i)
For the reaction,
$\mathrm{HI}(g) \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{H}_2(g)+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I}_2(g)$
Equilibrium constant,
$K^{\prime}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]^{1 / 2}\left[\mathrm{I}_2\right]^{1 / 2}}{[\mathrm{HI}]}$

$\left(K^{\prime}\right)^2=\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{I}_2\right]}{[\mathrm{HI}]^2}$  ...(ii)
On multiplying Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $K \cdot\left(K^{\prime}\right)^2=1K^{\prime}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}$

questions.solution:
$\begin{gathered}\mathrm{N}_2+2 \mathrm{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NO}_2 \\ K_1=\frac{\left[\mathrm{NO}_2\right]^2}{\left[\mathrm{ N}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]^2}\end{gathered}$ or $\quad 100=\frac{\left[\mathrm{NO}_2\right]^2}{\left[\mathrm{ N}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]^2} \quad \ldots$ (i)

$\begin{gathered}

\text{$ or $} \quad K_2^2=\frac{1}{100} \quad \text{ or } \quad K_2=\frac{1}{10}=0.1
\end{gathered}$

questions.q: In a $500 \mathrm{ mL}$ flask, the degree of dissociation of $\mathrm{PCl}_5$ at equilibrium is $40 \%$ and the initial amount is 5 moles. The value of equilibrium constant in $\mathrm{mol} \mathrmL^{-1}$ for the decomposition of $\mathrm{PCl}_5$ is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{PCl}_5 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl}_3+\mathrm{Cl}_2 \text{ initial moles } \\ & \left.5(1)^5 \alpha\right) \quad 5 \alpha \quad 5 \alpha \text{ moles at equilibrium } \\ & \frac{5(1-\alpha)}{0.5} \quad \frac{5 \alpha}{0.5} \quad \frac{5 \alpha}{0.5} \text{ conc at equilibrium } \\ & \alpha=40 \% \\ & =0.4 \\ & K_c=\frac{\left[\mathrm{PCl}_3\right]\left[\mathrm{Cl}_2\right]}{\left[\mathrm{PCl}_5\right]} \\ & =\frac{\left(\frac{5 \times 0.4}{0.5}\right)\left(\frac{5 \times 0.4}{0.5}\right)}{\left(\frac{5 \times 0.6}{0.5}\right)}=\frac{16}{6} \\ & =2.66 \mathrm{ mol} / \mathrm{L} \\ & \end{aligned}$

The equilibrium constant of the reaction
$2 \mathrm{SO}_3(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{SO}_2(g)+\mathrm{O}_2(g)$ would be

$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{SO}_2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2 & \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{SO}_3 \\ K_1 & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{SO}_3\right]}{\left[\mathrm{SO}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]^{1 / 2}} \\ 2 \mathrm{SO}_3 & \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{SO}_2+\mathrm{O}_2 \\ \mathrm{ K}_2 & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{SO}_2\right]^2\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]}{\left[\mathrm{SO}_3\right]^2}\end{aligned}$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii)
$\begin{aligned} K_2 & =\frac{1}{K_1^2} \\ K_2 & =\frac{1}{\left(5 \times 10^{-2}\right)^2}=\frac{1}{25 \times 10^{-4}} \\ & =\frac{100 \times 10^2}{25} \\ & =4 \times 10^2 \mathrm{ atm}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider the following reaction equilibrium:
$\mathrm{N}_2(g)+3 \mathrm{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_3(g)$
Initially, 1 mole of $\mathrm{N}_2$ and 3 moles of $\mathrm{H}_2$ are taken in a $2 \mathrm{~L}$ flask. At equilibrium state if, the number of moles of $\mathrm{N}_2$ is 0.6 , what is the total number of moles of all gases present in the flask?
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{N}_2(g)+3 \mathrm{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_3(g) \begin{array}{ll}1 \text{ mole } 3 \text{ mole } & 0 \text{ moles (2 L) (initially) } \\ 0.6 \text{ or } \quad(3-3 x) & 2 x \text{ moles } \\ (1-x) \text{ moles moles } & \text{ (at equilibrium) }\end{array}$
Number of moles of $\mathrm{N}_2=0.6=1-x$ \therefore x=1-0.6=0.4$
So, 3-3 x=3-3 \times 0.4=1.8$,
and $2 x=2 \times 0.4=0.8$
Therefore, the total number of moles at equilibrium.
$=(1+x)+(3-3 x)+2 x =0.6+1.8+0.8=3.2 $$\mathrm{ mol}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The rate constant of a first order reaction was doubled when the temperature was increased from 300 to 310 K . What is its approximate activation energy (in $\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ )? ( $\mathrm{R}=8.3 \mathrm{ J} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1} \mathrm{ K}^{-1} ; \log 2=0.3$ )
questions.solution:
According to Arrhenius theory. $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{K}=\mathrm{A} \times \mathrme^{-\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}} / \mathrm{RT}} \\ & \log \frac{\mathrm{ K}_2}{\mathrm{ K}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{2.303 \mathrm{R}}\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{ T}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{ T}_2}\right] \end{aligned}$
Given, $\begin{array}{ll} \mathrm{K}_1=\mathrm{x}, & \mathrm{ T}_1=300 \\ \mathrm{ K}_2=2 \mathrm{x} & \mathrm{ T}_2=310 \\ \log \frac{2 \mathrm{x}}{\mathrm{x}}=\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{2.303 \times 8.3}\left[\frac{1}{300}-\frac{1}{310}\right] \\ \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{\log 2 \times 2.303 \times 8.3 \times 300 \times 310}{10} \\ \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}=53.49 \mathrm{ kJ} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1} \end{array}$

The rate constant of a first order reaction is $3.46 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{ s}^{-1}$ at 298 K. What is the rate constant of the reaction at 350 K if its activation energy is $50.1 \mathrm{ kJ} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1} ?(\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{ J}\mathrmK^{-1} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1}$ )
$(\log 2=0.3010)$
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{K}_1=3.46 \times 10^{-2} \\ & \mathrm{ T}_1=298 \mathrm{ K} \\ & \mathrm{ K}_2=? \\ & \mathrm{ T}_2=350 \mathrm{ K} \\ & \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}=50.1 \mathrm{ kJ} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1} \\ & \mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1} \end{aligned}$
According to Arrhenius theory, $\begin{aligned} & \log \frac{\mathrm{K}_2}{\mathrm{ K}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{2.303 \mathrm{R}}\left[\frac{1}{\mathrm{ T}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{ T}_2}\right] \\ & \log \frac{\mathrm{K}_2}{3.46 \times 10^{-2}}=\frac{50.1 \times 10^3}{2.303 \times 8.314}\left[\frac{1}{298}-\frac{1}{350}\right] \\ & \log \frac{\mathrm{K}_2}{3.46 \times 10^{-2}}=1.30 \\ & \frac{\mathrm{ K}_2}{3.46 \times 10^{-2}}=10^{1.30}=20 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \mathrm{K}_2 & =3.46 \times 10^{-2} \times 20 \\ \mathrm{ K}_2 & =69.03 \times 10^{-2} \\\end{aligned}\therefore \quad \mathrm{K}_2=0.69 \mathrm{ s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Which of the following is correct with respect to the graph given?
$\begin{aligned} & {[R]=\text{ Concentration at time ' } t \text{ ' }} \\ & {[R]_0=\text{ Initial concentration }}\end{aligned}$
options: I, III represent first order and II represents zero order reaction
I, II represent zero order and III represents first order reaction
I, II, III all represent zero order reactions
I, II, III all represent first order reaction
questions.solution:
For a zero order reaction :-
Rate $=\mathrm{K}[\mathrm{A}]^0=\mathrm{K}$
Thus, the rate does not change with concentration. Therefore, I is of zero order reaction. For the integrated rate law of zero order :-
$\mathrm{C}=-\mathrm{kt}+\mathrm{C}_0$
Thus, the graph II is for a zero order reaction.
For a first order reaction:-
$\mathrm{t}=\frac{2.303}{\mathrm{ K}} \log \frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}$ or $\log \frac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}=\frac{\dot{\mathrm{K}}}{2.303} \mathrm{t}$
Thus, III is a graph for a first order reaction.

ment

questions.q: $P \rightarrow Q$ is a zero order reaction. If the concentration of $P$ decreases from $0.1 \mathrm{M}$ to 0.05 in 10 seconds, the concentration of $P$ after 15 seconds time is
questions.solution:
Given that, $P \rightarrow Q$ is a zero order reaction.
Initial concentration, $[A]_0=0.1 \mathrm{M}$
Final concentration, $[A]_t=0.05 \mathrm{M}$
Time taken, $t=10 \mathrm{ s}$
For, zero order reaction, $k=\frac{[A]_0-[A]_t}{t}=\frac{0.1-0.05}{10}=0.005 \mathrm{M} \mathrms^{-1}$
Now, for concentration of $P$ after 15 seconds,
$0.005=\frac{[0.05]-P}{15}$
On solving we will get, $P=0.025 \mathrm{M}$

$2 \mathrm{~N}_2 \mathrm{O}_5(g) \longrightarrow 4 \mathrm{NO}_2(g)+\mathrm{O}_2(g)$

Rate of disapperance of reactant $\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_5=$ Rate of apperance of products $\mathrm{NO}_2 and \mathrm{O}_2$.
For the reaction,
$\begin{aligned} & 2 \mathrm{~N}_2 \mathrm{O}_5(g) \longrightarrow 4 \mathrm{NO}_2(g)+\mathrm{O}_2(g) \\ & \quad-\frac{1}{2} \frac{d\left[\mathrm{~N}_2 \mathrm{O}_5\right]}{d t}=\frac{1}{4} \frac{d\left[\mathrm{NO}_2\right]}{d t}=\frac{d\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]}{d t}\end{aligned} \therefore \quad \frac{d\left[\mathrm{NO}_2\right]}{d t}=\frac{4}{2} \frac{d\left[\mathrm{~N}_2 O_5\right]}{d t} =2 \times 1.2 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-1} \left(\frac{d\left[\mathrm{~N}_2 \mathrm{O}_5\right]}{d t}\right)=2.4 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$

questions.solution:
Zero order reaction means that the rate of the reaction is proportional to zero power of the concentration of reactants.

Some enzyme catalysed reactions and reactions which occur on metal surfaces are a few examples of zero order reactions. The decomposition of gaseous ammonia on a hot platinum surface is a zero order reaction at high pressure.

Integrated rate equation for zero order reaction is given by the expression

$k = \dfrac{\left[R\right]0 -\left[R\right]t}{t}$

Where, k=rate constant

t=time in seconds

$\left[R\right]0$=Initial concentration of the reactants

$\left[R\right]t =$Concentration of the reactants after time, t.

$t = \dfrac{\left[R\right]0 -\left[R\right]t}{k} = \dfrac{0 . 10 - 0 . 075}{0 . 0030} = 8 . 33seconds$

factor.

questions.solution:
$2 A+B \longrightarrow 2 C+D$
Let order with respect to A and B$ are $x and y$ respectively.
$\therefore \quad$ Rate $=k[A]^x[B]^y7.2 \times 10^{-2}=k(0.3)^x(0.2)^y$ ...(i)

Dividing Eq. (i) by Eq. (ii), we get

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which statement among the following is incorrect?
options: Unit of rate of disappearance is $Ms^{- 1}$
Unit of rate of reaction is $Ms^{- 1}$
Unit of rate constant k depends upon order of reaction
Unit of rate constant k for a first order reaction is $Ms^{- 1}$
questions.solution:
Rate of disappearance of reaction of reactants is equal to the& $\dfrac{d\left[R\right]}{dt}$.

Concentration has the unit $M$. Time has the unit of second.

Hence, unit of rate of disappearance is $Ms^{- 1}$.

Rate of reaction is equal to the concentration per unit time. So, the unit of rate of reaction is $Ms^{- 1}$.

The unit of rate constant k depends upon order of reaction. Each order of reaction has the different unit of rate constant.

The unit of rate constant k for a first order reaction is $s^{- 1}$.

Hence, the incorrect statement is the unit of rate constant k for a first order reaction is $Ms^{- 1}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: In collision theory, \$e^{-E_{\mathrm{n}} / R T}$ corresponds to the fraction of molecules that have energy equal or greater than \(E_a\)$
The number of collisions of reacting molecules per second per unit volume of the reaction mixture is activated complex
Molecularity is the number of molecules involved in a complex reaction
A catalyst catalyses the non-spontaneous reaction
questions.solution:
(a) In collision theory, \(e^{-E_a / R T}\) corresponds to the fraction of molecules that have energy equal to or greater than \(E_a\) (activation - energy) is the correct statement because it is in accordance with Arrhenius theory.
(b) The number of collision of the reacting molecules per second per unit volume of the reaction mixture is activated complex is not a correct statement as activated complexes are formed during the reaction, which finally gives the product.
(c) Molecularity is the number of molecules involved in a complex reaction. This is also not correct as molecularity is defined as: The number of reacting species taking part in a reaction, which must collide simultancously in order to bring out the reaction.
(d) A catalyst, catalyses the non-spontaneous reaction. This is also not correct as a catalyst can catalyse the spontaneous as well as non-spontaneous reactions.
Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.

Given,

For first order reaction,
(i) half-life $\left(t_{1 / 2}\right)$ at temperature $300 \mathrm{ K}=50 \mathrm{ s}$
(ii) half-life $\left(t_{1 / 2}\right)$ at temperature $400 \mathrm{ K}=10 \mathrm{ s} \begin{aligned}$& \therefore \quad K_1($\text{ at }300 \mathrm{ K})=\frac{0.693}{50}=0.014 \mathrm{ s}^{-1}$\\
& $\text{$ and } K_2($\text{ at }400 \mathrm{ K})=\frac{0.693}{10}=0.07 \mathrm{ s}^{-1}$\\
& $\left.\qquad \because$ K=0.693 / t_{(1 / 2)} $\text{$ for $lst order reaction }\right]
\end{aligned}$ where, $K_1 and K_2$ are rate constant at $300 \mathrm{ K}$ and $400 \mathrm{ K}$ respectively.
Also, according to Arrhenius theory

$\log\frac{K_2}{K_1}=\frac{E_a}{2.303 R} \left[\frac{T_2-T_1}{T_1 \cdot T_2}\right]where, $ E_a=$ activation energy

\begin{aligned}

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The reaction $X \rightarrow$ products is a first order reaction. In 40 minutes, the concentration of $X$ changes from $1.0 \mathrm{M}$ to $0.25 \mathrm{M}$. What is the initial rate of reaction when $[X]=0.1 \mathrm{M}$ ? $(\log 4=0.60)$

Given, (concentration) $a=1.0 \mathrm{M}, a-x=0.25 \mathrm{M}, t=40$ minutes For a first order reaction, $\begin{aligned} k & =\frac{2.303}{t} \log \frac{a}{a-x}\\
& =\frac{2.303}{40} \log \frac{1}{0.25}=\frac{2.303}{40} \log4 \\
& =\frac{2.303 \times 2 \times 0.3010}{40}\\
& =0.03466 \mathrm{ min}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$ Now, Initial rate $\begin{aligned}& =k[A] \\
& =0.03466(0.1) \\
& =0.003466 \mathrm{ mol}/ \mathrm{L}/ \mathrm\min\\
& =3.466 \times10^{-3} \mathrm{ mol}/ \mathrm{L}/ \mathrm\min\\
& =3.47 \times10^{-3} \mathrm{ mol}/ \mathrm{L}/ \mathrm\min
\end{aligned}$ According to options given, any option cannot match with answer. But (d) can be the correct answer.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The rate equation for a first-order reaction is given by $\left[R\right] = \left[R\right]0e^{- kt}$. A straight line with positive slope is obtained by plotting ($\left[R\right]0 =$~Initial concentration of the reactant, $\left[R\right] =$ concentration of the reactant at time~$t$)
questions.solution:
First-order reaction is the rate of reaction is proportional to the first power of the concentration of the reactant $R$.

$R \to P$

Rate $= - \dfrac{d\left[R\right]}{dt} = kR$

Rate equation, $\left[R\right] =\left[R\right]0e^{- kt}$

Comparing with $y = mx + c$, if we plot $lnR$ against $t$, we get a straight line with a slope $= - k$ and intercept $= \ln \left[{R}_{0}\right]$.

Also,

$k = \dfrac{2. 303}{t}\log \left[{R}_{0}\right]\left[R\right] ⇒ \log \left[{R}_{0}\right] \left[R\right] = \dfrac{kt}{2. 303}$

If we plot a graph between $\log\left[{R}_{0}\right]\left[R\right]$ Vs $t$, slope $= \dfrac{k}{2. 303}.

$

questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: The first ionization enthalpies of $\mathrm{Na}, \mathrm{Mg}$ and $\mathrm{Si}$ are respectively 496,737 and $786 \mathrm{KJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$. What would be the first ionization enthalpy of $\mathrm{Al}$ in $\mathrm{KJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ ?
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{Na}, \mathrm{Mg}, \mathrm{Al}$ and $\mathrm{Si}$ lie in the same period $\left(3^{\text{rd }}\right.$ period) and therefore the effective nuclear charge increases as $\mathrm{Na} \lt  \mathrm{Mg} \lt  \mathrm{Al} \lt  \mathrm{Si}$ because of which their ionization enthalpy (first) is also supposed to increase in this manner.
However, the configuration of $\mathrm{Al}$ is $1 s^2 2 s^2 \cdot 2 p^6 3 s^2 3 p^1$ in which the loss of one $3 \mathrm{p}$ - electron results in a stable, fully-filled configuration.
This stable configuration is not as stable as that of $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ which is $1 s^2 2 s^2 2 p^6$ and therefore the first ionization energy of $\mathrm{Al}$ will be higher than that of $\mathrm{Na}$ but lower than that of $\mathrm{Mg}$.
\Rightarrow  First ionization energy$ of \mathrm{Al}=575 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$.

questions.q:

The correct answer is
options: Both statements I and II are correct
Both statements I and II are not correct
Statement I is correct but statement II not correct
Statement I is not correct but statement II is correct
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{Al}$ atom is smaller than $\mathrm{Mg}$ atom as $\mathrm{Al}$ lies to the right of $\mathrm{Mg}$ and it has greater effective nuclear charge. A cation is smaller than its parent atom so $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ is smaller than $\mathrm{Al}$ and therefore $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ is smallest in size.
Thus, statement I is correct.
Among lanthanides there is a gradual decrease in the atomic and ionic radii as we move from left to right due to lanthanoid contraction.
As per the latest data from rsc.org; the atomic radii of Sm, Eu and Gd are:- $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Sm}=236 \mathrm{pm},185 \mathrm{pm} \text{ (covalent) }\\ \mathrm{Eu}=235 \mathrm{pm},183 \mathrm{pm} \text{ (covalent) }\\ \mathrm{Gd}=234 \mathrm{pm},182 \mathrm{pm} \text{ (covalent) }
\end{aligned}$ Thus, the radii of lanthanides decreases gradually with europium following the same trend.
Thus, statement II is false.

questions.q:
Observe the following statements.
Statement (A) In general, the ionisation potential value decreases on moving down in the group.
Statement (B) The lst ionisation potential of sodium is greater from that of potassium. Correct answer is
questions.solution:
Ionisation energy is the energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom. Ionisation potential decreases as we move down in the group. The atomic number increases in a group and hence the number of shells also increases. Thus, outermost electrons are far away from nucleus and can be removed easily.
Hence, statement A is correct
The outer electron in potassium is in $4 s$-orbital, which is further away from the nucleus than the $3 s$-orbital of sodium. This means that less energy is needed to remove the outermost electron. Therefore, first ionisation potential of sodium is greater than potassium.
Hence, statement (b) is also correct.

Therefore, Ge forms stable compound in $(+4)$ O.S. and $\mathrm{Pb}$ in $(+2)$ O.S. $\therefore$ (II) $\ $ (III) are correct.

$\therefore \quad$ (IV) is incorrect.

We know that the electron gain enthalpy increases from left to right and decreases from top to bottom. So here, Fluorine& has maximum electron gain enthalpy. Now in ${2}^{nd}$ period size of elements are too small so inter-electronic repulsion is& maximum and due to this reason it is slightly difficult to add the electron in elements of ${2}^{nd}$ group therefore after fluorine sulphur have higher electron gain enthalpy. Hence, the final order will be:

$F > S > O > N$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: In second period of the long form of the periodic table, an element $X$ has second lowest first ionization enthalpy and element $Y$ has second highest first ionization enthalpy values. What are $X$ and $Y$ ?
questions.solution:
The order of ionization enthalpy of elements of 2nd period in long form of periodic table is $Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne$.

Generally, on going left to right in a period, ionization energy increases, but there are some exceptions to this. For example, Be has more ionization energy than B, due to fulfilled s-orbital. And N has more ionization energy than O due to half filled p-subshell.

So,In second period of the long form of the periodic table, the element $B$ has second lowest first ionization enthalpy and element $F$& has second highest first ionization enthalpy values.&

questions.q: Which of the following tetrahalides does not exist?
questions.solution: Group-14 elements can form halides of formula ${MX}_{2}$ and ${MX}_{4}$ (where $X = F, Cl, Br, I$). Except carbon, all other members react directly with halogen under suitable condition to make halides. Most of the ${MX}_{4}$ are covalent in nature. The central metal atom in these halides undergoes ${sp}^{3}$ hybridisation and the molecule is tetrahedral in shape. ${PbI}_{4}$ does not exist because $Pb — I$ bond initially formed during the reaction does not release enough energy to unpair $6s^{2}$ electrons and excite one of them to higher orbital to have four unpaired electrons around lead atom.

questions.q:
The formation of oxide ion $\mathrm{O}^{2-}$ from oxygen atom requires an exothermic reaction, followed by an endothermic step as shown below. The process of formation of $\mathrm{O}^{2-}$ in gas phase is unfavorable $\left(\Delta H^{\ominus}=+\right.$ ve )$, even though it has stable configuration of the nearest noble gas neon. This is because
$\begin{aligned} & $\mathrm{O}$(g)+e^{-} \longrightarrow $\mathrm{O}^{-}$(g) ; \Delta H^{\ominus}=-141 $\mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ \\ & $\mathrm{O}^{-}$(g)+e^{-} \longrightarrow $\mathrm{O}^{2-}$(g) ; \Delta H^{\ominus}=+760 $\mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$\end{aligned}

oxygen is more electronegative than neon

electron repulsion in oxide ion is more which over comes the stability achieved by noble gas configuration.
questions.solution:
The process of formation of $\mathrmO^{2-}$ in the gas phase is unfavorable even through $\mathrmO^{2-}$ is isoelectronic with neon. It is due to that electronic repulsion outweighs the stability gained by achieving noble gas configuration. The formation of oxide ion, $\mathrmO^{2-}(g)$ from oxygen atom require first an exothermic and then endothermic step.

$\begin{aligned}$& $\mathrm{O}($g)+e^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrmO^{-}(g) ; $\Delta H^{\ominus}=-141 \mathrm{~kJ}\mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\\
& \mathrmO^{-}(g)+e^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrmO^{2-}(g) ; $\Delta H^{\ominus}=+760 $\mathrm{~kJ}\mathrm{~mol}^{-1}

Zn.

Greater the oxidation state, lesser will be the ionic radii. $\mathrmS^{2-}$ acquire very high charge in it. It increases our ionic radii than $\mathrmK^{+}$. Therefore, $\mathrmS^{2-}$ is very big in size.

questions.q: In the modern periodic table, the acidic nature of oxides
options: increases from left to right and decreases from top to bottom
decreases from right to left and increases from top to bottom
remains same across a period and increases from top to bottom
decreases from left to right and remains the same down the group
questions.solution:
More the electropositivity of central atom, the more basic is the oxide and more electronegative central atom, more acidic is the oxide.
As we know, the electronegativity is the property of the element to attract electrons pairs. Hence, acidic character of the oxides "decreases down the group" because the electronegativity decreases down the group. Electronegativity decreases down the group because the "distance between the nucleus and valences shell electron increases. Hence, acidic nature of oxides increases left to right and decreases from top to bottom.

questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Assertion (A)
The first ionisation energy of Be is greater than that of $\mathrm{B}$.
Reason (R) $2 p$ orbital has lower energy than $2 s$ orbital.
options: Both $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{R}$ are true and $\mathrm{R}$ is a correct explanation for $\mathrm{A}$.
Both $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{R}$ are true but $\mathrm{R}$ is not a correct explanation for $\mathrm{A}$.
questions.solution:
The first IE of Be is greater than that of B because Be has stable complete electronic configuration $\left(1 s^2 2 s^2\right)$, which require more energy to remove the first electron from its valence shell, whereas, B has electronic configuration $1 s^2 2 s^2 3 s^1$ which require lesser energy than that of Be. So, $\mathrm{A}$ is true, but $\mathrm{R}$ is false.

questions.solution: Magnesium has the atomic number of $12$. It has the electronic configuration of~$\left[Ne\right]3s^{2}$. It has the fully filled orbitals. So, it has the high ionisation energy. The atomic number of the aluminium is $13$. It has the electronic configuration of~$\left[Ne\right]3s^{2}3p^{1}$. It has the low value of the first ionisation energy. So, the first ionisation energy of magnesium is higher than the aluminium because magnesium has the fully filled orbital. Hence,~The first ionization enthalpies of $Mg and Al$ can be expected to be~${IE}_{1} ( Mg ) = 737 . 7kJ . {mol}^{- 1}, {IE}_{1} ( Al ) = 577 . 5kJ . {mol}^{- 1}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: The order of screening effect among $s, p, d$ and $f$-orbitals of a given shell of an atom in its outer shell electrons is
questions.solution:
$s$ has the greatest effect to reduce the force of attraction between the outermost electron and nucleus due to its effective charge density followed by $p > d > f$.
So, according to the screening effect, $s$ orbital being close to the nucleus lacks screening from any other orbital as it is the first and the closest orbital. $p$ orbital electrons are loosely bound with greater size than $s$ block elements as they undergo screening from $s$ orbital electrons.
Similarly, $d$-orbital electrons undergo screening from $s$ and $p$-block orbitals and finally $f$ orbital also undergoes screening from all the other orbitals. Hence, the $f$-block elements are generally big in size with less nuclear charge acting on their outermost electrons.
Thus, the order of screening effect of electrons of $s, p, d$ and $f$ orbitals of a given shell of an atom on its outer shell electrons is $s > p > d > f$.
Hence, the correct option is (1).

However, the electron gain enthalpy of $\mathrm{F}$ is less negative than $\mathrm{CI}$ due to electron-electron repulsion in small-sized $\mathrm{F}$ atom. Thus, the correct order is $\mathrm{F} < \mathrm{CI} > \mathrm{Br} > \mathrm{l}$.
$\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{CI}, \mathrm{Br}$ and $\mathrm{I}$ have $\Delta e_g H$ values (in $\mathrm{kJ}^{\mathrm{Jmol}} \mathrmI^{-1}$ )
$-328,-349,-325$ and -295 respectively. That order of arrangement does not agree with the variation of property.
Hence, the correct option is (3).

questions.q: Calculate the energy required to convert all atoms in \(4.8 $\mathrm{~g}$\) of \($\mathrm{Mg}$\) to \($\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$\) in the vapour state. \($\mathrm{IE}}_{1}\) and \( \mathrm{IE}$}_{2}\) of \($\mathrm{Mg}$\) are \(740 $\mathrm{~kJ}$/ $\mathrm{mol}$\) and \(1450 $\mathrm{~kJ}$/ $\mathrm{mol}$\) respectively.
questions.solution:
For 1 mole of \($\left(\mathrm{Mg} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\right)$ \(\mathrm{IE}=\mathbb{E E}_$1+\mathrm{IE}_{2}=(740+1450)=2190  \mathrm{ kJ}/ \mathrm{mol}\).
Number$ of $mole in \(4.8 \mathrm{ g}\) of \( \mathrm{Mg}=4.8 / 24=0.2  \mathrm{ mol}\)
For 1 mole energy required \(=2190 \mathrm{ kJ}/ \mathrm{mol}$
For 0.2 mole energy required \(=2190 \times0.2=438  \mathrm{ kJ}\)
Thus, for \(4.8 \mathrm{ g}\) of \($\mathrm{Mg}$ to $\(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ conversion, energy required is \(438  $\mathrm{ kJ}$.
Hence, the correct option is (d).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: The second ionisation energies of \($\mathrm{Li}, \mathrm{Be}, \mathrm{B}$\) and \($\mathrm{C}$\) are in the order
questions.solution:
The second ionisation energy is the energy required to remove an electron from a \($\mathrm{I}+$\) cation in the gaseous state.
\(X^{+}(g)  → X^{2+}(g)+e^{-}\)
Just like the first ionisation energy, the second ionisation energy is affected by size, effective nuclear charge, and electron configuration. Li has highest \($\mathrm{IE}}_{2}\) than because the second electron remove from stable noble gas configuration and \(B\) has higer \( \mathrm{IE}$}_{2}\) than \($\mathrm{C}$\) due to the extra stability of the \(2 s²\) subshell in the \(\mathrmB^{+}\)ion. Therefore, the order is \($\mathrm{Li}  \gt  \mathrm{B}  \gt  \mathrm{C}  \gt  \mathrm{Be}$\)
Hence, the correct option is (b).

3. Shielding effect as well as ionisation energy decrease down the group. So, statement 3 is incorrect.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Assertion (A) Boron has a smaller first ionisation enthalpy than beryllium.
Reason (R) The penetration of a \(2 s\)-electron to the nucleus is more than the \(2 p\)-electron hence, \(2 p\)-electron is more shielded by the inner core of electrons than \(2 $\mathrm{ s}$\)-electrons.
options: Assertion and Reason both are correct statements but Reason is not correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is correct statement but Reason is wrong statement.
Assertion and Reason both are correct statements and Reason is correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion and Reason both are wrong statements.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) Electronic configuration of boron \((Z=5)\) is [He] \(2 s² 2 p¹\). So, in first ionisation ( \(1 \mathrm{IE}_{1}\) or \(\Delta_i H_1\) ) removal will take place from unpaired \(p^1\)-electron. Whereas that of Be will be from paired \(2 s^2\)-electrons which requires more energy.
Electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{Be}(Z=4):[ \mathrm{He}]2 s^2\) So, the Assertion is a correct statement.
Reason (R) \(s\)-orbital is being symmetrical in shape (spherical), it shields nuclear force (nuclear charge) strongly. So, \(2 p^1\)-electron of \(B\) is experiences lesser nuclear attractive force for ionisation. As a result,
\(\mathrm{IE}}_{1} \text{ or } \Delta_i H_1: \mathrm{B}  <  \mathrm{Be}\)
So, the Reason is correct explanation for Assertion.

Which of the following statements are correct for classification of elements?
I. The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
II. Non-metallic elements are less in number than the metallic elements.
III. The first ionisation energies of elements along a period do not vary in a regular manner.
IV. The ground state electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Pd}(Z=46)$ is $[\mathrm{Kr}] 4 d^8 5 s^2$.
questions.solution:
(I, II) Properties of elements are periodic function of their atomic number. Number of non-metals are less as compared to number of metallic elements.
(III) In periodic table, first ionisation energy of elements along a period do not vary in regular manner due to effective nuclear charge.
(IV) Ground state electronic configuration of $\operatorname{Pd}[Z=46]$ is $[\mathrm{Kr}] 4 d^{10} 5 s^0$.

Thus, option (b) is correct.

questions.solution:
On moving down the group electron gain enthalpy decreases. Oxygen due to its small size causes electron-electron repulsions in relatively small \(2 p\)-subshell. Hence, incoming electrons cannot allow to enter easily, as in case of other elements of this group that's why oxygen has the lowest electron gain enthalpy.
Therefore, correct order of electron gain enthalpy,
\($\mathrm{S}  \gt  \mathrm{Se}  \gt  \mathrm{Te}  \gt  \mathrm{O} .$\)

II. Tendency to form stable super oxides increases from \($\mathrm{Li}$\) to \($\mathrm{Cs}$\) down the group.
III. Low solubility of \($\mathrm{LiF}$\) is due to its high lattice energy.
IV. Solubility of carbonates of group-2 elements increases down the group.
questions.solution:
(II) On moving down in the group the size of the atom increases. The positive charge around the ion gets weaken. The bigger atom can stabilise the bigger superoxide ion with less negative field.
(III) Due to smaller size of \(\mathrmF^{-}\)ion, the lattice energy increases. While, hydration enthalpy is less than that of lattice energy. Hence, LiF has very low solubility.
Statements (II, III) are correct.
Thus, correct option is (c).

questions.q: In photoelectric effect, if the energy required to overcome the attractive forces on the electron, (work functions) of $\mathrm{Li}, \mathrm{Na}$ and $\mathrm{Rb}$ are $2.41 \mathrm{eV}$, $2.30 \mathrm{eV}$ and $2.09 \mathrm{eV}$ respectively, the work function of ' $\mathrm{K}$ ' could approximately be in $\mathrm{eV}$
questions.solution:
As the size of atom (element) increases, energy required to overcome the attractive force on outermost electron decreases.
$\mathrm{Li}, \mathrm{Na}, \mathrm{K}$ and $\mathrm{Rb}$ are the members of same group and have the following order of size
$\mathrm{Li} < \mathrm{Na} < \mathrm{K} < \mathrm{Rb}$
Thus, the energy in case of $\mathrm{K}$ is intermediate of $\mathrm{Rb}$ and $\mathrm{Na}$, i.e.,

questions.solution:
The electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Na}, \mathrm{Ne}, \mathrm{Mg}$ and $\mathrm{Al}$ after the removal of an electron is as
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Na}^{+}: 1 s^2, 2 s^2, 2 p^6 \\
& \mathrm{Ne}^{+}: 1 s^2, 2 s^2, 2 p^5 \\
& \mathrm{Mg}^{+}: 1 s^2, 2 s^2, 2 p^6, 3 s^1 \\
& \mathrm{Al}^{+}: 1 s^2, 2 s^2, 2 p^6, 3 s^2
\end{aligned}$
The ionisation energy decreases as the size of the atom/ion increases. Further ionisation energy increases with increase in nuclear charge. Since, $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ gives a stable electronic configuration hence its $\mathrm{IE}_2$ is highest among the given species and therefore the correct order of their $\mathrm{IE}_2$ is
$\mathrm{Mg} < \mathrm{Al} < \mathrm{Ne} < \mathrm{Na}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Which one of the following order is correct for the first ionisation energies of the elements?
questions.solution:
First ionisation energy increases in a period. Thus, the first IE of the elements of the second period should be as follows
$\mathrm{Be} < \mathrm{B} < \mathrm{N} < \mathrm{O}$
But in practice, the elements do not follow the above order. The first IE of these elements is
$\mathrm{B} < \mathrm{Be} < \mathrm{O} < \mathrm{N}$
The lower IE of $\mathrm{B}$ than that of $\mathrm{Be}$ is because in $\mathrm{B}  \left(1 s², 2 s² 2 p¹\right)$, electron is to be removed from $2 p$ which is easy while in $\operatorname{Be}  \left(1 s², 2 s²\right)$, electron is to be removed from $2 s$ which is difficult. The low IE of $\mathrm{O}$ than that of $\mathrm{N}$ is because of the half-filled $2 p$ orbitals in $\mathrm{N}  \left(1 s², 2 s² 2 p³\right).$

Given,
Atomic number of element $B=Z$
(\because$ noble gas \quad \therefore$ belong to zero group)
Atomic number of element $A=Z-1$
(ie, halogens)
Atomic number of element $C=Z+1$
(ie, group IA)
Atomic number of element $D=Z+2$
(ie, group IIA)
$\because$ Element $B$ is a noble gas
$\therefore$ Element $A$ must be a halogen ie, have highest electron affinity.
and element $C$ must be an alkali metal and exist in +1 oxidation state.
and element $D$ must be an alkaline earth metal with +2 oxidation state.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The hybridisation of metals involved in the following complexes, respectively are $\left[\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{CN})_6\right]^{3-},\left[\mathrm{CoF}_6\right]^{3-}$
questions.solution:
In $\left[\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{CN})_6\right]^{3-}, \mathrm{Mn}$ is in +3 oxidation state.
As $\mathrm{CN}^{-}$is a strong field ligand, it causes pairing of two $3 d$ electrons, thereby making two $d$-orbitals vacant, namely $d_{x^2-y^2} and d_{z^2}$. These two $d$-orbitals and one $4 s$ and three $4 p$-orbitals hybridise and give $d^2 s p^3$-hybridisation. In $\left[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{F})_6\right]^{3-}, \mathrm{Co}$ is in +3 oxidation state.
As $\mathrmF^{-}$is a weak field ligand, so it cannot cause the pairing of unpaired $3 d$-electrons. Thus, one $4 s$, three $4 p$-orbitals and two $4 d$-orbitals hybridise and give $s p^3 d^2$-hybridisation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The crystal filed theory is successful in explaining which of the following?

I. Ligands as point charges;

II. Formation and structures of complexes.

III. colour;

IV. Magnetic properties:

V. covalent character of metal-ligand bonding.
questions.solution: The crystal field theory (CFT) is an electrostatic model which considers the metal-ligand bond to be ionic arising purely from electrostatic interactions between the metal ion and the ligand. Ligands are treated as point charges in case of anions or point dipoles in case of neutral molecules.& The colour in the coordination compounds can be readily explained in terms of the crystal field theory. However, the crystal field model is successful in explaining the formation, structures, colour and magnetic properties of coordination compounds to a large extent. However, from the assumptions that the ligands are point charges, it follows that anionic ligands should exert the greatest splitting effect.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following is correct related to the colours of ${TiCl}_{3}  \left(X\right) \left[Ti   \left({H}_{2}$ O\right)^{6}\right]{Cl}_{3}$\left(Y\right)$
questions.solution:
Atomic number of Titanium is 22.

Electronic configuration of Ti is& $\left[Ar\right]3d^{2}4s^{2}$

The colour of transition metal compounds is due to the presence of unpaired electrons in their metal ions which are responsible for d-d transitions.

The colour in the coordination compounds can be readily explained in terms of the crystal field theory. Consider, for example, the complex [Ti(H2O)6 ]3+, which is violet in colour. This is an octahedral complex where the single electron (Ti3+ is a 3d1 system) in the metal d orbital is in the t2g level in the ground state of the complex. The next higher state available for the electron is the empty eg level. If light corresponding to the energy of blue-green region is absorbed by the complex, it would excite the electron from t2g level to the eg level (t2g1 eg0 → t2g 0 eg1 ). Consequently, the complex appears violet in colour. The crystal field theory attributes the colour of the coordination compounds to d-d transition of the electron.

It is important to note that in the absence of ligand, crystal field splitting does not occur and hence the substance is colourless. For example, removal of water from [Ti(H2O)6 ]Cl3 on heating renders it colourless.Hence TiCl3& is colourless.

On other hand, $\mathrm{CoCl}_3 \cdot 5 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ dissociates into $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$, $3 \mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ ions and $5 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ molecules.
Hence, only $\mathrm{PtCl}_4 \cdot 6 \mathrm{NH}_3$ gives maximum number of ions in aqueous solution.

The nickles with strong field ligands formed the square planar complex and tetrahedral with the weak field ligand.& $\left[Ni ( Cl{)}_{4}\right]2 -$~is a tetrahedral complex. 1.

questions.solution:
The crystal field splitting in the tetrahedral field is smaller than in the octahedral field.
For most purposes the relationship between tetrahedral and octahedral crystral field splitting may be represented as :
\(\Delta_t=$\frac{4}{9} \Delta_$o ; \Delta_o=$\frac{9}{4}\left(\Delta_$t\right)\)
If$ the CFSE of tetrahedral complex \(\left(\Delta_$t\right)\)$ of \(\left[$M L_4\right]^{n+}\) is \(x $\mathrm{eV}$, the CFSE of octahedral complex \($\left[$M L_6\right]^{n+}\) will be \(\Delta_o=$\frac{9 x}{4}$.

questions.q: Identify the pair of elements in which number of electrons in $(n-1)$ shell is same
questions.solution:
1. Fe electronic configuration $=\left[\mathrm{Fe} \Rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{p}^6 3 \mathrm{~s}^2\right.$ $\left.3 \mathrm{p}^6 4 \mathrm{~s}^2 3 \mathrm{~d}^6\right]$ Here $(n-1)$ shell is $3 d$ which have 6 electron. 2. mn electronic configuration $\left[\mathrm{Mn} \Rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{p}^6 3 \mathrm{~s}^2\right.$ $\left.3 \mathrm{p}^6 4 \mathrm{~s}^2 3 \mathrm{~d}^5\right]$ ( $\mathrm{n}-1$ ) shell have 5 electrons 3. Zn electronic configuration $\left[\mathrm{Zn} \Rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{p}^6 3 \mathrm{~s}^2\right.$ $3 \mathrm{p}^6 4 \mathrm{~s}^2 3 \mathrm{~d}^{10}$ ] [ $\mathrm{n}-1$ ) shell have 10 electron] 4. Sc electronic configuration $\left[\mathrm{Sc} \Rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{p}^6 3 \mathrm{~s}^2 3 \mathrm{p}^6\right.$ $4 \mathrm{~s}^2 3 \mathrm{~d}^1$ ] $(n-1)$ shell have 1 electron. Kelectronic configuration is $\left[\mathrm{K} \Rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{p}^6 3 \mathrm{~s}^2 3 \mathrm{p}^6 4 \mathrm{~s}^1\right]$ $(n-1)$ shell have 6 electron. Cr electronic configuration is $\left[\mathrm{Cr} \Rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{p}^6 3 \mathrm{~s}^2\right.$ $\left.3 p^6 4 s^1 3 d^5\right]$ Here $(n-1)$ shell have 5 electron.
So $\mathrm{Mn}, \mathrm{Cr}$ have same number of electron in $(\mathrm{n}-1)$ shell.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The formula of nickel oxide is $\mathrm{Ni}_{0.98} \mathrm{O}_{1.00^{{}^{\circ}}}$. What is the approximate percentage of $\mathrm{Ni}^{+2}$ in it?
questions.solution:
Let there be 100 formula units of $\mathrm{Ni}_{0.98} \mathrm{O}_{100}$. Thus, for $100 \mathrmO^{2-}$ ions, there are 98 nickel ions $\left(\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\right.$ or $\left.\mathrm{Ni}^{3+}\right)$.
Let $\mathrm{x}=$ number of $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$ ions.
\Rightarrow  Number of $\mathrm{Ni}^{3+}$ ions $=98-\mathrm{x}$.
For an electrically neutral compound:-
$\begin{aligned} & 2 x+3(98-x)+100(-2)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow x=94\end{aligned}$
So, $\%$ of $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}=\frac{94}{98} \times 100=96 \%$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Which of the following statements are correct?
I. $\quad \mathrm{P}$ is having least negative electron gain enthalpy among $\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{S}, \mathrm{Cl}$, and $\mathrm{F}$
II. In $\mathrm{Eu}, \mathrm{Yb}$ Lanthanoid contraction is not observed
III. $\mathrm{Ce}(\mathrm{OH})_3$ is most basic among lanthanoid hydroxides
IV. The radii of $\mathrm{Na}$ and $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ are $95 \mathrm{pm}, 186 \mathrm{pm}$ respectively
questions.solution:
Europium $(\mathrm{Eu})=[\mathrm{Xe}] 4 \mathrm{f}^7 5 \mathrm{ d}^0 6 \mathrm{ s}^2, 185 \mathrm{pm}$ Ytterbium $(\mathrm{Yb})=[\mathrm{Xe}] 4 \mathrmf^{14} 5 \mathrm{ d}^0 6 \mathrm{ s}^2, 170 \mathrm{pm}$ In these two elements, the atomic radii do not show expected decrease due to lanthanoid contraction but instead show an increased value.
This is due to an electron entering into the $4 \mathrm{f}$-orbital(inner shell) and giving rise to very stable half-filled and fullyfilled configurations that results in greater screening of the valence electrons (higher screening constant $\sigma$ ) Thus, Statement II is correct.
The value of electron gain enthalpy is more negative for more electronegative elements.
The electronegativity follows the order :$\mathrm{P} < \mathrm{S} < \mathrm{Cl} < \mathrm{F}$.
Thus, $\mathrm{P}$ has the least negative electron gain enthalpy and therefore Statement I is correct.
$\mathrm{Ce}(\mathrm{OH})_3$ is most basic hydroxide due to largest cation size which results in $\mathrm{Ce}(\mathrm{OH})_3$ being most ionic.
Thus, III is also correct.
The cation formed is always smaller than the parent atom or ion and thus $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ will be smaller than $\mathrm{Na}$.
Thus, IV is incorrect.

questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} / \mathrm{Cu}^{{}^{\circ}}=+0.34 \mathrm{ V}, \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{I}_2 / \mathrmI^{-}}^{{}^{\circ}}=0.54 \\ & 2 \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}+4 \mathrmI^{-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{CuI}+\mathrm{I}_2\end{aligned}$
Despite the above values of the standard reduction potentials, $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ is able to oxidize iodide to $\mathrm{I}_2$ due to all the species like $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}, \mathrm{Cu}^{+}$, and $\mathrm{CuI}$ being present together in the solution.

questions.q: Which of the following elements are not regarded as transition elements?
questions.solution:
Transition elements are characterised by partially filled $(n-1) d$ subshells. $\mathrm{Zn}, \mathrm{Cd}, \mathrm{Hg}, \mathrm{Cu}$ and $\mathrm{Ag}$ all have completely filled $(n-1) d$ subshell. But $\mathrm{Zn}, \mathrm{Cd}$, and $\mathrm{Hg}$ are not considered as transition metals as in their most common oxidation state, i.e. +2 , they have $d^{10}$ configuration. Whereas $\mathrm{Cu}$ and $\mathrm{Ag}$ when exists in +2 oxidation state have $d^9$ configuration.
Electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Zn}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 d^{10} 4 s^2$
Electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Cd}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 d^{10} 4 s^2$
Electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Hg}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 d^{10} 4 s^2$
Electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Cu}$ is $[\mathrm{A} r] 3 d^{10} 4 s^1$
Electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Ag}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 d^{10} 4 s^1$

questions.solution: The transition metals and their compounds are known for their catalytic activity. This activity is ascribed to their ability to adopt multiple oxidation states and to form complexes. Catalysts at a solid surface involve the formation of bonds between reactant molecules and atoms of the surface of the catalyst (first row transition metals utilise 3d and 4s electrons for bonding). This has the effect of increasing the concentration of the reactants at the catalyst surface and also weakening of the bonds in the reacting molecules (the activation energy is lowering).

Identify the correct statements from the following :
I. The ionic radius of \($\mathrm{Pr}^{3+}, \mathrm{Dy}^{3+}$\) and \($\mathrm{Sm}^{3+}$\) follow the order, \($\mathrm{Sm}^{3+}  \gt  \mathrm{Pr}^{3+}  \gt  \mathrm{Dy}^{3+}$\).
II. \($\mathrm{Eu}^{2+}$\) acts as strong reducing reagent.
III. Pu exhibits +7 oxidation state.
questions.solution:
(i) The ionic radius of lanthanoids follow the following relation:
Ionic radius \(\propto \frac{1}{\text{ atomic number }}Atomic number \((Z)\) for $\(\mathrm{Pr}=59\)
Atomic number \((Z)\) for $\(\mathrm{Sm}=$62\)
Atomic number \((Z)\) for \(D y=66\)
and has ionic radii for positive ions as given below:
$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Pr}^{3+}& =1.013 Å \\
\mathrm{Sm}^{3+}& =0.964 Å \\
\mathrm{Dy}^{3+}& =0.908 Å
\end{aligned}\)
Thus, statement (i) is not correct.
(ii) Element Eu \((Z=63)\) can exist in \((+) 2\) and \((+) 3\) oxidation state.
\(\therefore(+)\) 3oxidation state is the most common oxidation state for lanthanoids.
Thus, (+) 2oxidation state oxides oxidises to (+) 3 easily and \(\mathrm{Eu}^{2+} can act as strong reducing agent.
Hence, the statement (II) is correct.
(iii) The electronic configuation for
\(\text{(Pu), }(Z=94)=5 f⁶ 6 d⁰ 7 s²\)
Therefore, it can use maximum of \(6+2=8\) electrons.
Thus, can show +7 oxidation state.
Thus, statement (III) is also correct.
Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

& \Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{ S}^{{}^{\circ}}=100 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1} \\
& \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{cell}^{{}^{\circ}}=1.0 \mathrm{ V} \\
& \mathrm{n}=2 \\
& \Delta \mathrmG^{{}^{\circ}}=-\mathrm{nFE}^{{}^{\circ}} \\
&=-2 \times 96500 \times 1 \mathrm{ J} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1} \\
&=-193 \mathrm{ kJ} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1} \\
& \therefore \quad \Delta \mathrmG^{{}^{\circ}}=\Delta \mathrmH^{{}^{\circ}}-\mathrm{T} \Delta \mathrm{ S}^{{}^{\circ}} \\
& \Delta \mathrmH^{{}^{\circ}}=\Delta \mathrm{G}+\mathrm{T} \Delta \mathrm{ S} \\
&=-193+\frac{300 \times 100}{1000} \\
&=-193+30 \\
& \Delta \mathrmH^{{}^{\circ}}=-163 \mathrm{ kJ} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider the cell reaction, at 300 K
$\mathrm{A}(s)+\mathrmB^{2+}(a q) \rightleftharpoons \mathrmA^{2+}(a q)+\mathrm{B}(s)$
Its $\mathrmE^{{}^{\circ}}$ is 1.0 V . The $\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrmH^{{}^{\circ}}$ of the reaction is $-163 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. What is $\Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrmS^{{}^{\circ}}$ (in J K${ }^{-1}$ ) of the reaction?
$\left(\mathrm{F}=96500 \mathrm{C} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$
questions.solution:
Given,
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{E}^{{}^{\circ}}=1.0 \mathrm{ V} \\
& \Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^{{}^{\circ}}=-163 \mathrm{ kJ} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1} \\
& \mathrm{n}=2 \\
& \mathrm{ T}=300 \mathrm{k} \\
& \therefore \quad \Delta \mathrm{G}^{{}^{\circ}}=-\mathrm{nFE}{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \\
& =-2 \times 96500 \times 1.0 \\
& =193000 \mathrm{CV} \quad[1 \mathrm{ J}=1 \mathrm{CV}] \\
& =\frac{193000}{1000} \mathrm{ kJ} \quad\left[1 \mathrm{ kJ}=10^3 \mathrm{ J}\right] \\
& \Delta \mathrm{G}^{{}^{\circ}}=193 \mathrm{ kJ} \\
& \therefore \quad \Delta \mathrm{G}=\Delta \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{T} \Delta \mathrm{ S} \\
& \text{ or, } \Delta \mathrm{S}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{H}-\Delta \mathrm{G}}{\mathrm{ T}} \\
& \Rightarrow \Delta S=\frac{-163+193}{300}=\frac{30}{300}=0.1 \mathrm{ kJ} \mathrm{ K}^{-1} \\
& \therefore \quad \Delta \mathrm{ S}=0.1 \times 10^3 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \\
& \Delta \mathrm{ S}=100 \mathrm{JK}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
What is the molar conductivity of $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{CO}_2 \mathrm{H}$ at infinite dilution?
Given that,
$\wedge_{\mathrmm^{\mathrm{o}}\left(\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{CO}_2\right)_2 \mathrm{Ba}=\mathrm{x}_1 \mathrm{ S} \mathrm{ cm}^2 \mathrm{ mol}^{-1}\begin{aligned} & \wedge_{\mathrmm^{\mathrm{o}}\left(\mathrm{BaCl}_2\right)=\mathrm{x}_2 \mathrm{ S} \mathrm{ cm}^2 \mathrm{ mol}^{-1} \\ & \wedge_{\mathrmm^{\mathrm{o}}(\mathrm{HCl})=\mathrm{x}_3 \mathrm{ S} \mathrm{ cm}^2 \mathrm{ mol}^{-1}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which condition among the following holds true at the state of half-completion for the reaction $A \rightleftharpoons B$ ?
questions.solution:
Equilibrium condition in the course of a reversible chemical reaction is in which no net change in the amounts of reactants and products occurs.
At equilibrium, the reaction is half completed, $[A]=[B]$
Thus, $\frac{[B]}{[A]}=1$
According to standard free Gibbs energy,

$\begin{aligned}\Delta G^{{}^{\circ}} & =-R T \ln K \\
$\Delta G^{{}^{\circ}} & =-R T \ln (1) \\
{$\left[\Delta$G^{{}^{\circ}}\right.} & =0]
\end{aligned}

Hence, at equilibrium condition,$ the reaction is half-completed i.e.,A \rightleftharpoons B$.

questions.q: In the electrolysis of a ${CuSO}_{4}$ solution, how many grams of $Cu$ are plated out on the cathode, in the time that is required to liberate $5. 6L$ of ${O}_{2} ( g )$, measured at $1atm$ and $273K$, at the anode?

The mole of oxygen =& $\dfrac{Givenvolume}{Molarvolume} = \dfrac{5 . 6}{22 . 4} = 0 . 25mol$

Equivalent of oxygen = $n - factor \times mole$

$n - factor = 4$

Equivalent of oxygen=$4 \times 0 . 25 = 1$

So, Equivalent of oxygen =& Equivalent of copper

Equivalent mass of copper=& $\dfrac{Molarmass}{n - factor} = \dfrac{63 . 5}{2}$
