questions.q: If $u + iv = \dfrac{3i}{x + iy + 2},$ then $y =$
questions.solution:
Given,

$u + iv = \dfrac{3i}{x + iy + 2}$

$⇒ u - iv = \dfrac{- 3i}{x + 2 - iy}$

$⇒ \left(u + iv\right) \times \left(u - iv\right) = \left\{\dfrac{3i}{\left(x + 2\right) + iy}\right\}\left\{\dfrac{- 3i}{\left(x + 2\right) - iy}\right\}$

$⇒ {u}^{2} + {v}^{2} = \dfrac{9}{{\left(x + 2\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}}$

$⇒ {\left(x + 2\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2} = \dfrac{9}{{u}^{2} + {v}^{2}} . . . \left(i\right)$

Now, 

$u + iv = \dfrac{3i}{x + iy + 2}$

            $= \left\{\left(\dfrac{3i}{x + iy + 2}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{x + 2 - iy}{x + 2 - iy}\right)\right\}$

             $= \left(\dfrac{3y + i\left(x + 2\right)}{{\left(x + 2\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}}\right)$

              $= \left\{\dfrac{3y}{{\left(x + 2\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}}\right\} + i\left\{\dfrac{\left(x + 2\right)}{{\left(x + 2\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}}\right\}$

Comparing real and imaginary part, we get

$u = \dfrac{3y}{{\left(x + 2\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}} . . . \left(ii\right)$

By $\left(i\right) \text{ and } \left(ii\right)$, we get

$y = \dfrac{3u}{{u}^{2} + {v}^{2}}$.

questions.q: Let A  $\left(3 - i\right)$, B   $\left(2 + i\right)$ be two points in the Argand plane. If the point $P$ represents the complex number $z = x + iy,$ which satisfies $\left| z - 3 + i\right| = \left| z - 2 - i\right|,$ then the locus of the point $P$ is
options: the ellipse with $AB$ as major axis
questions.solution:
Given,

$A\left(3 - i\right) ⇒ A ≡ \left(3, - 1\right)$

$B\left(2 + i\right) ⇒ B ≡ \left(2, 1\right)$

Now,

$\left|z - 3 + i\right| = \left|z - 2 - i\right|$

$⇒ \left|z - \left(3 - i\right)\right| = \left|z - \left(2 + i\right)\right| ≡ \left\{\left|z - A\right| = \left|z - B\right|\right\}$

$⇒ \left|z - \left(3 - i\right)\right| = \left|z - \left(2 + i\right)\right| ≡ \left\{\left|P - A\right| = \left|P - B\right|\right\}$

Therefore, we get $AP = BP$.

Point $P$ is moving along the line $CM$ such that $AP = BP$.

Hence, locus of the point $P$ is the perpendicular bisector of line $AB$.

questions.q: If $a = cos\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right) + isin\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right),$ then $Re \left(a + a^{2} + a^{3} + a^{4} + a^{5}\right) =$
questions.solution:
We have,

$a = cos\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right) + isin\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right)$

Then,

${a}^{2} = {\left\{cos\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right) + isin\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right)\right\}}^{2}$

      $= cos\left(\dfrac{16\pi}{11}\right) + isin\left(\dfrac{16\pi}{11}\right)$

${a}^{3} = cos\left(\dfrac{24\pi}{11}\right) + isin\left(\dfrac{24\pi}{11}\right)$

${a}^{4} = cos\left(\dfrac{32\pi}{11}\right) + isin\left(\dfrac{32\pi}{11}\right)$

${a}^{5} = cos\left(\dfrac{40\pi}{11}\right) + isin\left(\dfrac{40\pi}{11}\right)$

Now, 

$= a + {a}^{2} + {a}^{3} + {a}^{4} + {a}^{5}$

$= cos\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right) + isin\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right) + cos\left(\dfrac{16\pi}{11}\right) + isin\left(\dfrac{16\pi}{11}\right) + cos\left(\dfrac{24\pi}{11}\right) + isin\left(\dfrac{24\pi}{11}\right) + cos\left(\dfrac{32\pi}{11}\right) + isin\left(\dfrac{32\pi}{11}\right) + cos\left(\dfrac{40\pi}{11}\right) + isin\left(\dfrac{40\pi}{11}\right)$

$= \left\{cos\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right) + cos\left(\dfrac{16\pi}{11}\right) + cos\left(\dfrac{24\pi}{11}\right) + cos\left(\dfrac{32\pi}{11}\right)\right\} + cos\left(\dfrac{40\pi}{11}\right) + i\left\{sin\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right) + sin\left(\dfrac{16\pi}{11}\right) + sin\left(\dfrac{24\pi}{11}\right) + sin\left(\dfrac{32\pi}{11}\right) + sin\left(\dfrac{40\pi}{11}\right)\right\}$

  $= \left\{\dfrac{cos\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11} + 4 \cdot \dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right)}{sin\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right)} \times sin\left(\dfrac{5 \times 8\pi}{11}\right)\right\} + \text{Imaginary part}$

$= \dfrac{cos\left(\dfrac{40\pi}{11}\right)sin\left(\dfrac{40\pi}{11}\right)}{sin\left(\dfrac{8\pi}{11}\right)} + \text{Imaginary part}$        $= \left(- \dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \text{Imaginary part}$   

Therefore, $\text{Re}\left(a + {a}^{2} + {a}^{3} + {a}^{4} + {a}^{5}\right) = \dfrac{- 1}{2}$

$\begin{aligned} &\text{ Let }z=x+i y \text{, so } \\ & \qquad|z|^2+1=\left|z^2-1\right|\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}& \Rightarrow x²+y²+1=\sqrt{\left(x^2-y^2-1\right)^2+4 x^2 y^2}\\

questions.q: If $a=\cos \left(\frac{8 \pi}{11}\right)+i \sin \left(\frac{8 \pi}{11}\right)$, then $\operatorname{Re}\left(a+a^2+a^3+a^4+a^5\right)=$
questions.solution:
$a=\cos \left(\frac{8 \pi}{11}\right)+i \sin \left(\frac{8 \pi}{11}\right) \Rightarrow a=e^{\frac{i 8 \pi}{11}}$
$\Rightarrow a$ is 11 th root of unity and all roots are $1, a, a^2, \ldots, a^{10}$
Now, $\quad a^{10}=\frac{a^{10} \cdot a}{a}=\frac{a^{11}}{a}=\frac{1}{a}=\bar{a}$
Similarly, $a^9=\overline{a^2}, a^8=\overline{a^3}, a^7=\overline{a^4}, a^6=\overline{a^5}$,
We know that,
Sum of $n$ roots of unity $=0$
$$
\begin{gathered}
1+a^1+a^2+a^3+\ldots+a^{10}=0 \\
\Rightarrow a+a^2+a^3+a^4+a^5+a^6+a^7+a^8 \\
a^9+a^{10}=-1 \\
\Rightarrow(a+\bar{a})+\left(a^2+\overline{a^2}\right)+\left(a^3+\overline{a^3}\right) \\
+\left(a^4+\overline{a^4}\right)+\left(a^5+\overline{a^5}\right)=-1 \\
\Rightarrow 2 \operatorname{Re}(a)+2 \operatorname{Re}\left(a^2\right)+2 \operatorname{Re}\left(a^3\right)+2 \operatorname{Re}\left(a^4\right)+2 \operatorname{Re}\left(a^5\right) \\
=-1[z+\bar{z}=2 \operatorname{Re}(z)] \\
\Rightarrow 2 \operatorname{Re}\left(a+a^2+a^3+a^4+a^5\right)=-1 \\
\Rightarrow \operatorname{Re}\left(a+a^2+a^3+a^4+a^5\right)=-\frac{1}{2}
\end{gathered}
$$

& \left(z^{n-1}+z^{n-2}+\ldots . .+z^2+z+1\right)=\left(z-z_1\right) \\
& \left(z-z_1\right)=\left(z-z_{n-1}\right)
\end{aligned}$
Put $z=1$, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& (1+1+\ldots .+n \text{ times }) \\
& =\left(1-z_1\right)\left(1-z_2\right)+\ldots .\left(1-z_{n-1}\right) \\
& n=\left(1-z_1\right)\left(1-z_2\right) \ldots\left(1-z_{n-1}\right)
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The common roots of the equations $z^3+2 z^2+2 z+1=0, z^{2014}+z^{2015}+1=0$ are
questions.solution:
Given equation,
$\begin{aligned}
& z^3+2 z^2+2 z+1=0 \\
& (z+1)\left(z^2+z+1\right)=0
\end{aligned}$
Its roots are $-1, \omega$ and $\omega^2$.
Let $f(z)=z^{2014}+z^{2015}+1=0$
Put $z=-1, \omega$ and $\omega^2$ respectively, we get
$f(-1)=(-1)^{2014}+(-1)^{2015}+1=0=1 \neq 0$
Therefore, -1 is not a root of the equation $f(z)=0\begin{aligned}
& \text{ Again, } f(\omega)=(\omega)^{2014}+(\omega)^{2015}+1 \\
& =\left(\omega^3\right)^{671} \cdot \omega+\left(\omega^3\right)^{671} \cdot \omega^2+1 \\
& =\omega+\omega^2+1 \\
& =\omega^2+\omega+1 \\
& =0
\end{aligned}$
Therefore, $\omega$ is a root of the equation $f(z)=0$
Similarly,
$\begin{aligned}
& f\left(\omega^3\right)=\left(\omega^2\right)^{2014}+\left(\omega^3\right)^{2015}+1 \\
& =\left(\omega^3\right)^{1342} \cdot \omega^2+\left(\omega^3\right)^{1343} \cdot \omega+1 \\
& =\omega^2+\omega+1 \\
& =0
\end{aligned}$
Hence $\omega$ and $\omega^2$ are the common roots of $z^{2014}+z^{2015}+1=0$

questions.q: The least positive integer $n$ for which $(1+i)^n=(1-i)^n$, is

Given, $(1+i)^n=(1-i)^n \begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow \quad $\frac{(1+i)^n}{(1-i)^n}=1 \\ \text{$ and $} \Rightarrow \quad\left[\frac{(1+i) \times(1+i)}{(1-i) \times(1+i)}\right]^ n=1 \\

questions.solution:

& \Rightarrow \quad-2 x²=2 x² \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 4 x²=0 \Rightarrow x=0 \\
& \therefore \quad z=x+i y=0+i y \\
& \Rightarrow \quad z=i y \quad \Rightarrow \quad(x, y)=(0, y) \\
&

questions.q: If $z=1+i \sqrt{3}$ then $|\operatorname{Arg} z|+|\operatorname{Arg} \bar{z}|$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$z=1+i \sqrt{3}$
Let $1+i \sqrt{3}=r(\cos \theta+i \sin \theta)$
Then, $\quad r \cos \theta=1\ldots$ (i)
$r \sin \theta=\sqrt{3}\ldots$ (ii)
Eq. (i) + Eq. (ii), we get $r^2\left(\sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^2 \theta\right)=3+1\left(\because \sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^2 \theta=1\right)r^2=4r=2$
Eq. (ii) \div Eq. (i), we get
$\tan \theta=\sqrt{3}\Rightarrow \quad \tan \theta=\tan \frac{\pi}{3}\Rightarrow \quad \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$
So, $z=(1+i \sqrt{3})=2\left\{\cos \frac{\pi}{3}+i \sin \frac{\pi}{3}\right\}$
Then $\bar{z}=(1-i \sqrt{3})=2\left\{\cos \frac{\pi}{3}-i \sin \frac{\pi}{3}\right\}=2\left\{\cos \left(\frac{-\pi}{3}\right)+i \sin \left(\frac{-\pi}{3}\right)\right\}$
So, $\quad \operatorname{Arg} z=\frac{\pi}{3}\operatorname{Arg} \bar{z}=-\frac{\pi}{3}|\operatorname{Arg} z|+|\operatorname{Arg} \bar{z}|=\left|\frac{\pi}{3}\right|+\left|\frac{-\pi}{3}\right|=\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{2 \pi}{3}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text{ Given that, }=\frac{9+6 i}{13} \\ & \qquad \begin{aligned} X_n & =\cos \frac{\pi}{2^n}+i \sin \frac{\pi}{2^n}=\operatorname{cis} \frac{\pi}{2^n} \\ \therefore \quad \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} X_n & =\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \operatorname{cis} \frac{\pi}{2^n} \\ & =\operatorname{cis} \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot \operatorname{cis} \frac{\pi}{2^2} \cdot \operatorname{cis} \frac{\pi}{2^3} \ldots. \\ & =\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{2^2}+\frac{\pi}{2^3}+\ldots..\right) \\ & =\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{\frac{\pi}{2}}{1-\frac{1}{2}}\right)=\operatorname{cis} \pi \\ & =-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Given that period of $\frac{\cos n x}{\sin \left(\frac{x}{n}\right)}$ is $4 \pi$.
We know
Period of $\quad \cos n x=\frac{2 \pi}{n}$
and period of $\sin \left(\frac{x}{n}\right)=2 n \pi\begin{array}{ll}\therefore \text{ Period of } & \frac{\cos n x}{\sin\left(\frac{x}{n}\right)} \text{ is } 2 n \pi . \\ \Rightarrow & 2 n \pi=4 \pi \Rightarrow n=2\end{array}$

questions.solution:
We have,
Let $\begin{gathered}x⁴-x²+x-1=0 \\
\alpha=\frac{1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}, \beta=\frac{1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}\\
\alpha+\beta=\frac{1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}+\frac{1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}=1 \\
\alpha \beta=\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)=\frac{1+3}{4}=1
\end{gathered} Then equation is $ x^2-(\alpha+\beta) x+\alpha \beta=0
\Rightarrow \quad x²-x+1=0 Now, divide $ x^4-x^2+x-1$ by $x^2-x+1$,
We get, $x^2-1\therefore$ The real roots are $x^2-1=0$
x= \pm$1$

$f(x)$ is differentiable $\forall x \in \mathbb{R} \Rightarrow f(x)$ is continuous $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{+}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} f(x) \Rightarrow \lim _{x \rightarrow 2}\left(6 x^3+1\right)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 2}(3 x-3) \\

& \Rightarrow a+b-\frac{13}{8}=0 \Rightarrow a+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{13}{8}=0 \Rightarrow a=\frac{11}{8} \\
& \therefore a-b=\frac{11}{8}-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{9}{8}
\end{aligned}$

If a real valued function
$f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}\frac{2 x^2+(k+2) x+9}{3 x^2-7 x-6} & , \text{ for } x \neq 3 \\ l & , \text{ for } x=3\end{array}\right.x=3$ and $l$ is a finite value, then $l-k=$
questions.solution:
Since, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=3 \Rightarrow \lim _{x \rightarrow 3} f(x)=f(3)$ Now, $\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{2 x^2+(k+2) x+9}{3 x^2-7 x-6}$ For this limit to exist, we must have $\begin{aligned} & \lim _{x \rightarrow 3} 2 x^2+(k+2) x+9=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 18+3 k+6+9=0 \Rightarrow k=-11 \end{aligned}$
So, $\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{2 x^2-9 x+9}{3 x^2-7 x-6}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 3} \frac{4 x-9}{6 x-7}=\frac{3}{11}=l$ Thus, $l-k=\frac{3}{11}+11=\frac{124}{11}$

questions.q: The function $f(x)=|x-24|$ is
options: continuous on $[0,25]$, but not differentiable on $[0,25]$.
questions.solution:
$\begin{gathered}f(x)=|x-24|=\left\{ \begin{array}{cc}-x+24, & x < 24 \\ x-24, & x \geq 24\end{array} \right. \\ \lim _{x \rightarrow 24^{-}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 24}(-x+24)=0\end{gathered} \lim _{x \rightarrow 24^{+}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 24}(x-24)=0 \text{ and } f(24)=0\therefore f$ is continuous on [ 0,25$]$.
Also, $\lim _{x \rightarrow 24^{-}} \frac{f(x)-f(24)}{x-24}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 24} \frac{-x+24+0}{x-24}=-1\lim _{x \rightarrow 24^{+}} \frac{f(x)-f(24)}{x-24}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 24} \frac{x-24}{x-24}=1\therefore f$ is not differentiable on $[0,25]$.

b, & x=0 \\

questions.solution:
$f(x)\left\{$\begin{array}{cc}(1+|$\sin x$|)^{$\frac{a}{|$\sin x$|}$} & , $\frac{-\pi}{6}$ < x < 0 \\ b & x=0 \\ e^{$\frac{$\tan 2$ x}{$\tan 3$ x}$} & , \quad 0 < x < $\frac{\pi}{6}$\end{array}$\right.$
For $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=0\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} f(x)=f(0)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}} f(x) \qquad...\mathrm{(i)} \\
& \lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{-}}(1+|\sin x|)^{\frac{a}{|\sin x|}} \\
& =e^{\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(|\sin x| \frac{a}{|\sin x|}\right)}=e^a \qquad \mathrm{(1^{\infty} form)}
\end{aligned}$
Now, $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} e^{\frac{\tan 2 x}{\tan 3 x}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} e^\frac{\left(\frac{\tan 2 x}{2 x} \cdot 2 x\right)}{\left(\frac{\tan 3 x}{3 x} \cdot 3 x\right)}=e^{\frac{2}{3}}\therefore$ From (i)
$e^a=b=e^{\frac{2}{3}} \Rightarrow a=\frac{2}{3}, b=e^{\frac{2}{3}}$

questions.solution:
Given the function
$f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}\frac{2 x e^{\frac{1}{2 x}}-3 x e^{\frac{-1}{2 x}}}{e^{\frac{1}{2 x}}+4 e^{-\frac{1}{2 x}}} & \text{ if } x \neq 0 \\ 0 & \text{ if } x=0\end{array}\right.\begin{aligned} & \text{ L.H.D. }=f^{\prime}(0)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(0-h)-f(0)}{-h} \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(-h)-f(0)}{-h}\end{aligned}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{-2 h e^{\frac{-1}{2 h}}+3 h e^{\frac{1}{2 h}}-0}{-h\left(e^{\frac{-1}{2 h}}+4 e^{\frac{1}{2 h}}\right)}\left.=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{2 e^{\frac{-1}{2 h}}-3 e^{\frac{1}{2 h}}}{\left(e^{\frac{-1}{2 h}}+4 e^{\frac{1}{2 h}}\right.}\right)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{2 e^{\frac{-2}{2 h}}-3}{e^{\frac{-2}{2 h}}+4}\right)\begin{aligned} & =\frac{0-3}{0+4}=\frac{-3}{4} \text{ and, R.H.D. }=\mathrm{f}^{\prime}\left(0^{+}\right) \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(0+h)-f(0)}{h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(h)-0}{h}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{0-3}{0+4}=\frac{-3}{4} \text{ and, R.H.D. }=\mathrm{f}^{\prime}\left(0^{+}\right) \\ & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(0+h)-f(0)}{h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(h)-0}{h}\end{aligned}\left.=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{2 h e^{\frac{1}{2 h}}-3 h e^{\frac{-1}{2 h}}}{h\left(e^{\frac{1}{2 h}}+4 e^{\frac{-1}{2 h}}\right.}\right)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{2-3 e^{-\frac{1}{h}}}{1+4 e^{\frac{-1}{h}}}\right)=\frac{2-0}{1+0}=2$
Since $\left(f^{\prime}\left(0^{-}\right) \neq f^{\prime}\left(0^{+}\right)\right.$
So, $f(x)$ is not differentiable at $x=0$

\(\begin{aligned}

& =\lim _{x \rightarrow 1}\left(x^2+x+1\right)=3
\end{aligned}\)
\(\therefore\) LHD \( ≠ \) RHD
So, \(f(x)\) is not differentiable at \(x=1\)

Given function \(f: R \rightarrow R\), such that

30, & \text{ if } x \geq 5

\(a+b=5\) ...(i)
If \(f\) is continuous at \(x=3\), then
\(\Rightarrow \quad \begin{gathered}

a+2 b=15 \quad \ldots (ii)
\end{gathered}\)
and if \(f\) is continuous at \(x=5\), then
\(b+25=30 \Rightarrow b=5\) ...(iii)
From Eqs. (ii) and (iii), we get
\(a=5\) ...(iv)
but \(a=5\) and \(b=5\) doesn't satisfy the Eq. (i). so, \(f: R \rightarrow R\) is not continuous for any values of \(a\) and \(b\).
Hence, option (4) is correct.

questions.q: If the function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}\dfrac{sin ( a + 1 ) x + sinx}{x} & , x 0\end{cases}\right$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$, then $a + b =$
questions.solution:
Given:

$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}\dfrac{sin ( a + 1 ) x + sinx}{x} & , x 0\end{cases}\right$

Since, $f\left(x\right)$ is continuous on $R$

Therefore, $f\left(x\right) is continuous at $x = 0$.

Thus, $\lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}f $\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}f\left(x\right) = f\left(x\right)

Now,

$\lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}f $\left(x\right)$ = f $\left(x\right)$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}\left\{\dfrac{sin ( a + 1 ) x + sinx}{x}\right\} = b$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}\left[\left(\left(a + 1\right)\dfrac{sin ( a + 1 ) x}{\left(a + 1\right)x}\right) + \dfrac{sinx}{x}\right] = b$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}\left(\left(a + 1\right)\dfrac{sin ( a + 1 ) x}{\left(a + 1\right)x}\right) + \lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}\left(\dfrac{sinx}{x}\right) = b$

$⇒ a + 1 + 1 = b$

$⇒ b = a + 2 . . . \left(i\right)$

And,

$\lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}f\left(x\right) = f\left(x\right)

$⇒ \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}$\left\{\dfrac{\sqrt{x + {x}^{2}} - \sqrt{x}}{{x}^{\dfrac{3}{2}}}\right\}$ = b$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}$\left\{\dfrac{\sqrt{1 + x} - 1}{x}\right\}$ = b$

Using L'Hospital rule, we have

$\lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}$\left\{\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{1 + x}} - 0}{1}\right\}$ = b$

$⇒ b = $\dfrac{1}{2}$ . . . $\left(ii\right)$

Putting in $\left(i\right)$, we get $a = \dfrac{- 3}{2}$.

Therefore, $a + b = - 1$.

options: $f$ is continuous but not differentiable on $D$
$f$ is differentiable but not continuous on $D$
questions.solution:
Given:

$f ( x ) = \dfrac{| x |}{1 - | x |}$

Now,

$\text{LHL} = \lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}f\left(x\right)$

        $= \lim_{h \to 0}f\left(0 - h\right)$

        $= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\left|0 - h\right|}{1 - \left|0 - h\right|} = 0$

$\text{RHL} = \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}f\left(x\right)$

          $= \lim_{h \to 0}f\left(0 + h\right)$

           $= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\left|0 + h\right|}{1 - \left|0 + h\right|} = 0$

$\lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}f\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}f\left(x\right) = f\left(0\right)$

Hence, $f\left(x\right)$ is continuous at $x = 0$.

Using differentiation:

$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}\dfrac{- x}{1 + x}, x 0\end{array}\right$

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}\dfrac{- 1}{1 + x} + \dfrac{x}{{\left(1 + x\right)}^{2}}; x 0\end{array}\right$

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}\dfrac{- 1}{{\left(1 + x\right)}^{2}}; x 0\end{array}\right$

$\text{LHD} \ne \text{RHD}$ at $x = 0$.

Hence, $f\left(x\right)$ is differentiable in $D$ except at $x = 0$.

$\begin{aligned}& \text{We have, } f(x)=\frac{|x|}{1-|x|}=\left\{$\begin{array}{l}
$\frac{-x}{1+x}$, x < 0 \\
$\frac{x}{1-x}$, x \geq 0
\end{array}$\right. \\
& \text{ LHD }(\text{ at } x=0)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(0-h)-f(0)}{-h} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(-h)-0}{-h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{h}{\frac{1-h}{-h}} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{-1}{1-h}=-1 \\
& \text{ RHD }(\text{ at } x=0)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(0+h)-f(0)}{h} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(h)-0}{h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{h}{1-h}
\end{aligned} So, $ f(x)$ is not differentiable at $x=0$.
Hence, $f(x)$ is differentiable on $D$ except at $x=0$.$

fails to be continuous is(are)
questions.solution:
Given function,
$f(x)=\left\{ \begin{array}{cc}
1-x, & x < 1 \\
(1-x)(2-x), & 1 \leq x \leq 2 \\
3-x & x > 2
\end{array} \right.$
For $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=1$.
$\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{x \rightarrow 1^{+}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 1^{+}} f(x)=f(1) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 1^{+}}(1-x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 1^{+}}(1-x)(2-x) \\
& (1-1)=(1-1)(2-1)=0
\end{aligned}$ and $f(1)=(1-1)(2-1)=0\therefore f(x)$ is continuous at $x=1$.
Now, at $x=2, \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} f(x)=f(2)\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}}(1-x)(2-x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{+}}(3-x) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad(1-2)(2-2)=(3-2) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 0 \neq 1 \\
& \therefore \quad f(x) \text{ is discontinuous at } x=2
\end{aligned}\therefore f(x)$ is discontinuous at $x=2$.

L.H.S. $=\int_0^{2 \pi}\left(\sin ^4 x+\cos ^4 x\right) d x\begin{aligned}
& =\int_0^{2 \pi} \sin ^4 x d x+\int_0^{2 \pi} \cos ^4 x d x=2 \int_0^\pi \sin ^4 x d x+2 \int_0^\pi \cos ^4 x d x \\
& =2 \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sin ^4 x d x+4 \int_0^{\pi / 2} \cos ^4 x d x \\
& =4\left(\frac{3 \times 1}{4 \times 2}\right) \frac{\pi}{2}+4\left(\frac{3 \times 1}{4 \times 2}\right) \frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{3 \pi}{2} \\
& \text{ R.H.S. }=K \int_0^\pi \sin ^2 x d x+L \int_0^{\pi / 2} \cos ^2 x d x \\
& =2 K \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sin ^2 x d x+L \int_0^{\pi / 2} \cos ^2 x d x \\
& =2 K\left(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{\pi}{2}\right)+L\left(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{\pi}{2}\right)=(K) \frac{\pi}{2}+\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) \frac{\pi}{2} \\
& \therefore \text{$ For $R.H.S. }=\text{ L.H.S. } \\
& \frac{3 \pi}{2}=(K) \frac{\pi}{2}+\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) \frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow 3=K+\frac{L}{2}
\end{aligned}$Since, $K, L \in \mathbb{N}  possible values are
$\therefore(K, L)=(2,2),(1,4)So, two ordered pairs$ of (K, L)$ are possible.

questions.solution:
$\mathrm{I}=729 \int_1^3 \frac{1}{x^3\left(x^2+9\right)^2} d x$
Let $\frac{1}{x^3\left(x^2+9\right)^2}=\frac{\mathrm{A}}{x}+\frac{\mathrm{B}}{x^2}+\frac{C}{x^3}+\frac{\mathrm{D} x+\mathrm{E}}{x^2+9}+\frac{\mathrm{F} x+\mathrm{G}}{\left(x^2+9\right)^2}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 1=x^3\left(x^2+9\right)(\mathrm{D} x+\mathrm{E})+x^3(\mathrm{ F} x+\mathrm{G}) \\ & \qquad+x^2\left(x^2+9\right)^2 \mathrm{ A}+x\left(x^2+9\right)^2 \mathrm{ B}+\left(x^2+9\right)^2 \mathrm{C} \\ & \Rightarrow 1=x^6(\mathrm{ A}+\mathrm{D})+x^5(\mathrm{ B}+\mathrm{E})+x^4(18 \mathrm{ A}+\mathrm{C}+9 \mathrm{D}+\mathrm{F}) \\ & +x^3(18 \mathrm{ B}+9 \mathrm{E}+\mathrm{G})+x^2(81 \mathrm{ A}+18 \mathrm{C})+81 x \mathrm{ B}+81 \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}$
On comparing, $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{A}+\mathrm{D}=0, \mathrm{ B}+\mathrm{E}=0 ; 18 \mathrm{ A}+\mathrm{C}+9 \mathrm{D}+\mathrm{F}=0 \\ & 18 \mathrm{ B}+9 \mathrm{E}+\mathrm{G}=0,81 \mathrm{ A}+18 \mathrm{C}=0 \\ & 81 \mathrm{ B}=0,81 \mathrm{C}=1 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{ A}=\frac{-2}{729}, B=0, C=\frac{1}{81}, D=\frac{2}{729}, E=0, F=\frac{1}{81} \\ & \mathrm{G}=0 \\ & \therefore \mathrm{I}=\int_1^3 \frac{-2}{x} d x+9 \int_1^3 \frac{1}{x^3} d x+2 \int_1^3 \frac{x}{x^2+9} d x+9 \int_1^3 \frac{x}{\left(x^2+9\right)^2} d x \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \mathrm{I} & =\left[\log \frac{1}{x^2} \frac{-9}{2} \frac{1}{x^2}+\log \left(x^2+9\right) \frac{-9}{2\left(x^2+9\right)}\right]_1^3 \\ \mathrm{I} & =\left[\log \left(\frac{x^2+9}{x^2}\right)-\frac{9}{2} \frac{1}{x^2}-\frac{9}{2} \frac{1}{x^2+9}\right]_1^3 \\ \mathrm{I} & =\left[\log 2-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4}-\log 10+\frac{9}{2}+\frac{9}{20}\right]=\left[\log \frac{1}{5}+\frac{21}{5}\right] \\ & \Rightarrow a=\frac{21}{5}, b=\frac{1}{5} \Rightarrow a-b=\frac{20}{5}=4\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & f(x)=\left\{$\begin{array}{cc}$\frac{6 x^2+1}{4 x^3+2 x+3}$, & 0 < x < 1 \\ x^2+1, & 1 \leq x \leq 2 \\ \int_0^2 f(x) d x=\int_0^1 f(x) d x+\int_1^2 f(x) d x\end{array}$\right. \\ & =\int_0^1 \frac{6 x^2+1}{4 x^3+2 x+3} d x+\int_1^2\left(x^2+1\right) d x\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2} \int_0^1 \frac{12 x^2+2}{4 x^3+2 x+3} d x+\int_1^2\left(x^2+1\right) d x \\ & =\left[\frac{1}{2} \log \left(4 x^3+2 x+3\right)\right]_0^1+\left[\frac{x^3}{3}+x\right]_1^2 \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \log 9-\frac{1}{2} \log 3+\frac{8}{3}+2-\frac{1}{3}-1=\frac{1}{2} \log 3+\frac{10}{3}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: $\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} n^4\left[\frac{1}{n^5}+\frac{1}{\left(n^2+1\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}+\frac{1}{\left(n^2+4\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}+\frac{1}{\left(n^2+9\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}+\ldots+\right]=$
questions.solution:
Since,
$\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} n^4\left[\frac{1}{n^5}+\frac{1}{\left(n^2+1\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}+\frac{1}{\left(n^2+4\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}+\ldots.+\frac{1}{\left(n^2+n^2\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}\right]=\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} n^4 \sum_{r=0}^n \frac{1}{\left(n^2+r^2\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}=\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{r=0}^n \frac{n^5}{\left(n^2+r^2\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}=\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{r=0}^n \frac{1}{\left(1+\frac{r^2}{n^2}\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}=\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\left(1+x^2\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}} d x$
Let $I=\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\left(1+x^2\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}} d x$
Let $\tan \theta=x \Rightarrow \sec ^2 \theta d \theta=d x\Rightarrow I=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\sec ^2 \theta d \theta}{\left(1+\tan ^2 \theta\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{1}{\sec ^3 \theta} d \theta=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \cos ^3 \theta d \theta=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \cos \theta\left(1-\sin ^2 \theta\right) d \theta$
Let $\sin \theta=t \Rightarrow \cos \theta d \theta=d t\Rightarrow \mathrm{I}=\int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}\left(1-t^2\right) d t=\left(t-\frac{t^3}{3}\right)_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{2} \cdot 3}\right)-0 \Rightarrow I=\frac{6-1}{6 \sqrt{2}}=\frac{5}{6 \sqrt{2}}$

questions.q:
Consider the following statements (A) and (B)
(A) $\int_a^b \frac{d}{d x}(f(x)) d x=\frac{d}{d x} \int_a^b(f(x)) d x$
(B) $\frac{d}{d x}\left(\int f(x) d x\right)=f(x)+C$ Which one of the following is true?
questions.solution:
$\int_a^b \frac{d}{d x}(f(x)) d x=\int_a^b d(f(x))=f(b)-f(a)$ ...(i)
and $\frac{d}{d x} \int_a^b f(x) d x=\frac{d}{d x}[\mathrm{~A}$ constant $]=0$ ...(ii)
$\left\{\because \int_a^b f(x) d x\right.$ will necessarily give a constant value
Hence $\int_a^b \frac{d}{d x}(f(x)) d x \neq \frac{d}{d x} \int_a^b f(x) d x$
Therefore statement ' $\mathrm{A}$ ' is false.
Now consider

$\frac{d}{d x}\left(\int$f(x) d x\right)=$\frac{d}{d x}\left(g(x)+C_1\right)

where \int f(x) d x=g(x)+C_1 \begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow $\frac{d}{d x} \intf(x) d x=g^{\prime}(\mathrm{x})+0\left\{\because \frac{d}{d x}(\text{ constant })=$0\right. \\
& =g^{\prime}(x)
\end{aligned}

Clearly statement ' $\mathrm{B}$ ' is also false.

questions.q: $\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\sum_{n=0}^4\left(\frac{n \pi}{4}+x\right)}{\cos x+\sin x} d x=$
questions.solution:
Let $f=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\sum_{n=0}^4 \frac{\pi \pi}{4}+x}{\cos x+\sin x} d r$
$\operatorname{since} \sum_{x=1}^4\left(\frac{\operatorname{ex}}{4}+x\right)=(0+1+2+3+4) \frac{\pi}{4}+(1+1+1+1+1) x$ $=\frac{5 \pi}{2}+5 x=5\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+x\right)$
Hence, $f=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{5\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+x\right) d x}{\sqrt{2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cos x+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sin x\right)}$
$\Rightarrow I=\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+x\right) \sec \left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) d x$ ...(i)
Replacing $(x)$ by $\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)$ we get
$$
I=\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left[\frac{\pi}{2}+\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)\right] \sec \left[\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)-\frac{\pi}{4}\right] d x
$$
$I=\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}[\pi-x] \sec \left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) d x$ ...(ii)
$\{\because \sec (-\alpha)=\sec \alpha\}$
Adding equations (i) \& (ii), we get
$$
2 I=\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(\frac{3 \pi}{2}\right) \sec \left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) d x
$$
$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow I=\frac{15 \pi}{4 \sqrt{2}}\left[\log \left|\sec \left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)+\tan \left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right|\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ & \Rightarrow I=\frac{15 \pi}{4 \sqrt{2}} \log \left|\frac{\sqrt{2}+1}{\sqrt{2}-1}\right|=\frac{15 \pi}{4 \sqrt{2}} \log \left|(\sqrt{2}+1)^2\right| \\ & \Rightarrow I=\frac{15 \pi}{2 \sqrt{2}} \log |\sqrt{2}+1|\end{aligned}$

& \Rightarrow \int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{2}}[2 \sin x] \mathrm{dx}=\pi \neq0
\end{aligned}

$\thereforeA is false
(R) From $the graph of 2 \sin x$, it is clear that $2 \sin x$ is decreasing function in the interval $\left[\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3 \pi}{2}\right]$

From $\mathrm{eq}^{\mathrm{n}}$ (i) \& (ii), we get
$\begin{aligned} & A=\frac{1}{3}, B=-1 \\ & A+B=\frac{1}{3}-1=-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Assertion (A): $\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \left(\sin ^$6 x+\cos ^6 x\right) d x$ lies in the interval \left(\frac{\pi}{8}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)
Reason (R): \sin ^6 x+\cos ^6 x$ is a periodic function with period $\frac{\pi}{2}$
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of $A$
Both $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{R}$ are true but $\mathrm{R}$ is not the correct explanation of $\mathrm{A}$
A is false, R is true
questions.solution:
Let $I=\int_0^{\pi / 2}\left(\sin ^6 x+\cos ^6 x\right) d x\begin{aligned}
& I=\int_0^{\pi / 2}\left(\left(\sin ^2 x\right)^3+\left(\cos ^2 x\right)^3\right) d x \\
& =\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(1-\frac{3}{4}(\sin 2 x)^2\right) d x
\end{aligned}$
Since $\frac{1}{4} \leq 1-\frac{3}{4}(\sin 2 x)^2 \leq 1$ for $x \in\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\Rightarrow \int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{1}{4} d x \leq \int_0^{\pi / 2}\left(1-\frac{3}{4}(\sin 2 x)^2\right) d x \leq \int_0^{\pi / 2} 1 d x\Rightarrow \frac{\pi}{8} < \mathrm{I} < \frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow$ Assertion is correct
and $f\left(x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\sin ^6\left(x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)+\cos ^6\left(x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\sin ^6 x+\cos ^6 x\Rightarrow$ Period of $\sin ^6 x+\cos ^6 x$ is $\frac{\pi}{2}$ since reason $R$ is correct.

questions.q: If $u(n)=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(1+\sin t)^n \sin 2 t d t, n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $u(4)=$

Given $u(n)=\int_0^{\pi / 2}(1+\sin t)^n \sin 2 t d t\Rightarrow \mathrm{u}(\mathrm{n})=2 \int_0^{\pi / 2}(1+\sin \mathrm{t})^{\mathrm{n}} \sin \mathrm{t} \cos \mathrm{t} d \mathrm{t}$
Let $1+\sin \mathrm{t}=\mathrm{u} \Rightarrow \cos \mathrm{tdt}=\mathrm{du}\begin{aligned}

& =2\left(\frac{2^6}{6}-\frac{2^5}{5}\right)-2\left(\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{5}\right) \\
& =\frac{128}{15}+\frac{1}{15}=\frac{129}{15}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Given that $\frac{d}{d x}\left[\int_0^{\phi(x)} f(t) d t\right]=\phi^{\prime}(f(x)) f^{\prime}(x)$. If $\int_0^{3^3} f(t) d t=x^2 \sin 2 \pi x$, then the value of $f(8)$ is
questions.solution:
$\int_0^{x^3} f(t) d t=x^2 \sin 2 \pi x$
Differentiating both sides, we get
$\frac{d}{d x}\left[\int_0^{x^3} f(t) d t\right]=\frac{d}{d x}\left[x^2 \sin 2 \pi x\right]\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow f\left(x^3\right) \cdot 3 x^2=2 x \cdot \sin (2 \pi x)+2 \pi x^2 \cos (2 \pi x) \\ & \Rightarrow f\left(x^3\right)=\frac{2 x}{3 x^2}[\sin (2 \pi x)+x \pi \cos (2 \pi x)] \\ & \Rightarrow f\left(x^3\right)=\frac{2}{3 x}[\sin (2 \pi x)+x \pi \cos (2 \pi x)]\end{aligned}$
Put $x=2$ :
$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow f(8)=\frac{2}{3 \times 2}[\sin (4 \pi)+2 \pi \cos (4 \pi)] \\ & =\frac{1}{3}[0+2 \pi \cdot 1] \Rightarrow f(8)=\frac{2 \pi}{3} .\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $\int_0^{2024 \pi} \frac{2023^{\sin ^2 x}}{2023^{\sin ^2 x}+2023^{\cos ^2 x}} d x=k$, then $\left(\frac{2 k}{\pi}+1\right)=$
questions.solution:
Given : $\int_0^{2024 \pi} \frac{2023^{\sin ^2 x}}{2023^{\sin ^2 x}+2023^{\cos ^2 x}} d x=k$ ....(i)
Let $I=\int_0^{2024 \pi} \frac{2023^{\sin ^2 x}}{2023^{\sin ^2 x}+2023^{\cos ^2 x}} d x$ ...(ii)
$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow I=2024 \int_0^\pi \frac{2023^{\sin ^2 x}}{2023^{\sin ^2 x}+2023^{\cos ^2 x}} d x \\ & \Rightarrow I=2024 \times 2 \int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{2023^{\sin ^2 x}}{2023^{\sin ^2 x}+2023^{\cos ^2 x}} d x \\ & \Rightarrow I=2024 \times 2 \int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{2023^{\sin ^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}}{2023^{\sin ^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}+2023^{\cos ^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}} d x\end{aligned}\Rightarrow \quad I=2024 \times 2 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{2023^{\cos ^2 x}}{2023^{\sin ^2 x}+2023^{\cos ^2 x}} d x$ ...(iii)
Adding (ii) and (iii) :
$2 I=2024 \times 2 \int_0^{\pi / 2} 1 d x\Rightarrow \quad 2 I=2024 \times 2 \times \frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow I=1012 \pi$
From eqns. (i) and (ii) :
$k=\mathrm{I} \Rightarrow k=1012 \pi$
Now, $\frac{2 k}{\pi}+1=\frac{2 \times 1012 \pi}{\pi}+1=2024+1=2025$.

questions.solution: $\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\left[1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}}+\ldots \ldots \ldots \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right]\begin{aligned} & =\lim _{\mathrm{n} \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{n}}} \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{\mathrm{n}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{r}}}=\lim _{\mathrm{n} \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{n}}} \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{\mathrm{n}} \frac{1}{\left(\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{r}}{\mathrm{n}}}\right) \times \sqrt{\mathrm{n}}} \\ & =\lim _{\mathrm{n} \rightarrow \infty}\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}}\right) \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{\mathrm{n}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{r}}{\mathrm{n}}}} \\ & =\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{x}}} \mathrm{dx} ; \frac{\mathrm{r}}{\mathrm{n}}=\mathrm{x} \\ & =\left[\frac{\mathrmx^{-\frac{1}{2}+1}}{-\frac{1}{2}+1}\right]_0^1=\left[2(\mathrm{x})^{\frac{1}{2}}\right]_0^1=2\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Assertion (A)

\int_2^e$\left(\frac{1}{\log _e x}-\frac{1}{   \left(\log _$ ex\right)^2}\right)$ d x=e-2 \log _2 e

Reason (R)

\int_a^b e^x\left(f(x)+f^{\prime}(x)\right) d x=e^b f(b)-e^a f(a)
$
options: A and $R$ are true, $R$ is the correct explanation to $A$.
$A$ and $R$ are false, $R$ is not the correct explanation to $\mathrm{A}$.
$A$ is true and $R$ is false, $R$ is not the correct explanation to $\mathrm{A}$.
$\mathrm{A}$ is false and $\mathrm{R}$ is true, $\mathrm{R}$ is not the correct explanation to $\mathrm{A}$.
questions.solution:
Assertion
Let $I=\int_2^e\left(\frac{1}{\log _e x}-\frac{1}{\left(\log _e x\right)^2}\right) d x$
Let $\log _e x=y$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \quad x & =e^y \\
\Rightarrow \quad d x & =e^y d y \\
I & =\int_{\log _e 2}^1 e^y\left[\frac{1}{y}+\left(\frac{-1}{y^2}\right)\right] d y
\end{aligned}
$$
[Using the formula $\int_a^b e^x\left[f(x)+f^{\prime}(x)\right] d x=\left[e^x f(x)\right]_a^b$ ]
$$
\begin{aligned}
I & =\left[e^y \frac{1}{y}\right]_{-\log e^2}^1 \\
& =e-\frac{2}{\log _e 2}=e-2 \log _2 e
\end{aligned}
$$
Hence, Assertion and Reason both are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & I=\int_0^\pi\left(\cos ^2\left(\frac{3 \pi}{8}-\frac{x}{4}\right)-\cos ^2\left(\frac{11 \pi}{8}+\frac{x}{4}\right)\right) \cdot d x \\ & I=\int_0^\pi\left(\cos \left(\frac{3 \pi}{8}-\frac{x}{4}\right)-\cos \left(\frac{11 \pi}{8}+\frac{x}{4}\right)\right) \\ & \left(\cos \left(\frac{3 \pi}{8}-\frac{x}{4}\right)+\cos \left(\frac{11 \pi}{8}+\frac{x}{4}\right)\right) \cdot d x \\ & I=\int_0^\pi\left(2 \cos \left(\frac{14 \pi}{8 \times 2}\right) \cos \left(-\pi-\frac{x}{2}\right)\right)\end{aligned}\begin{gathered}\left(-2 \sin \left(\frac{14 \pi}{8 \times 2}\right) \sin \left(-\pi-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) d x \\ I=\int_0^\pi 2 \cos \left(\frac{7 \pi}{8}\right)\left(-\cos \frac{x}{2}\right)\left(=2 \sin \left(\frac{14 \pi}{8}\right)\left(\sin \frac{x}{2}\right)\right) d x \\ I=\int_0^\pi\left(2 \cos \frac{7 \pi}{8} \sin \frac{7 \pi}{8}\right)\left(-2 \sin \frac{x}{2} \cos \frac{x}{2}\right) d x \\ I=-\int_0^\pi \sin \frac{7 x}{4} \sin x d x \\ I=-\sin \left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \int_0^\pi \sin x d x \\ I=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-\cos x) \int_0^\pi=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\cos \pi-\cos 0) \\ I=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-1-1)=\frac{-2}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}\end{gathered}$

questions.solution:
Let $\quad I=\int_{-\pi}^\pi\left[\frac{2 x(1+\sin x)}{\left(1+\cos ^2 x\right)}\right] d x=\int_{-\pi}^\pi\left[\frac{2 x}{\left(1+\cos ^2 x\right)}\right] d x+\int_{-\pi}^\pi\left[\frac{2 x(\sin x)}{\left(1+\cos ^2 x\right)}\right] d xI=I_1+I_2$
Take $I_1=\int_{-\pi}^\pi\left[\frac{2 x}{\left(1+\cos ^2 x\right)}\right] d x\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad f(x)=\left[\frac{2 x}{1+\cos ^2 x}\right] \\ & \Rightarrow f(-x)=\left[\frac{2(-x)}{1+\cos ^2(\pi-\mathrm{x})}\right]\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & =-\left[\frac{2\left({ }^x\right)}{1+(-\cos x)^2}\right] \\ & =-\left[\frac{2\left({ }^x\right)}{1+\cos ^2 x}\right]\end{aligned}=-f\left({ }^x\right)\Rightarrow \quad I_1=\int_{-\pi}^\pi \frac{2 x}{1+\cos ^2 x} d x=0 \quad($ since $f(x)$ is an odd function)
Again consider
$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \mathrm{g}(\mathrm{X})=\frac{2 \mathrm{x} \sin \mathrm{x}}{1+\cos ^2 \mathrm{x}} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{g}(-\mathrm{x})=\frac{2(-\mathrm{x}) \sin (-\mathrm{x})}{1+\cos ^2(-\mathrm{x})}\end{aligned}=\frac{2(\mathrm{x}) \sin (\mathrm{x})}{1+\cos ^2(\mathrm{x})}[$ since $\sin (-x)=-\sin x, \cos (-x)=\cos x]=\mathrm{g}\left({ }^{\mathrm{X}}\right)\Rightarrow \quad I_2=\int_{-\pi}^\pi \frac{2 x \sin x}{1+\cos ^2 x} d x=2 \times 2 \int_0^\pi \frac{x \sin x}{1+\cos ^2 x} d x=4 \int_0^\pi \frac{x \sin x}{1+\cos ^2 x} d x$...(i)
[since $\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x})$ is an even function]
Then,
$\Rightarrow \quad I_2=4 \int_0^\pi \frac{(\pi-\mathrm{x}) \sin (\pi-\mathrm{x})}{1+\cos ^2(\pi-\mathrm{x})} d x=4 \int_0^\pi \frac{(\pi-\mathrm{x}) \sin (\mathrm{x})}{1+\cos ^2(\mathrm{x})} d x$  ...(ii)
$\left[\int_0^a f(x) d x=\int_0^a f(a-x) d x\right]$
Adding (i)and (ii), we get
$\Rightarrow \quad 2 I_2=4 \pi \int_0^\pi \frac{\sin \mathrm{x}}{1+\cos ^2 \mathrm{x}} \mathrm{dx}$
Substitute $\cos x=z-\sin x d x=d z$
when $x \rightarrow 0, z \rightarrow 1$ and
when $x \rightarrow \pi, \mathrm{z} \rightarrow-1\Rightarrow \quad 2 I_2=-4 \pi \int_1^{-1} \frac{d z}{1+z^2}$\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & 2 $\mathrm{I}_2=-4$ \pi $\left[\tan ^{-1} \mathrm{z}\right]_1^{-1}$ \\ \Rightarrow & 2 $\mathrm{I}_2=-4$ \pi $\left[-\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{4}$\right]$ \\ \Rightarrow & 2 \mathrm{I}_2=$2$ \pi^2 \\ \Rightarrow & \mathrm{I}_2=\pi^2\end{array} \Rightarrow \quad $I=I_1+I_2\begin{aligned}$& =0+$\pi^$2 \\ & =$\pi^$2\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
$\int_0^\pi \frac{x \tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} d x$
Let $I=\int_0^\pi \frac{x \tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} d x...(i)\begin{aligned} \because \quad \int_a^b f(x) d x & =\int_a^b f(a+b-x) d x \\ \Rightarrow \quad I & =\int_0^\pi \frac{(\pi-x) \tan (\pi-x)}{\sec (\pi-x)+\tan (\pi-x)} d x \\ I & =\int_0^\pi \frac{(\pi-x)(-\tan x)}{-\sec x-\tan x} d x \\ I & =\int_0^\pi \frac{(\pi-x) \tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} d x...(ii)\end{aligned}$
Adding Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\begin{aligned}2 I & =\int_0^\pi \frac{x \tan x+(\pi-x) \tan x}{\sec x+\tan x}d x \\
2 I & =\int_0^\pi \frac{\pi \tan x}{\sec x+\tan x}d x \\
I & =\frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^\pi \frac{\tan x}{\sec x+\tan x}d x=\frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^\pi \frac{\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}}{\frac{1}{\cos x}+\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}}\\
& =\frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^\pi \left(\frac{\sin x}{1+\sin x} \times \frac{1-\sin x}{1-\sin x}\right)d x \\
& =\frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^\pi \frac{\sin x(1-\sin x)}{1-\sin ^2 x}d x \\
& =\frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^\pi \frac{\sin x-\sin ^2 x}{\cos ^2 x}d x
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}
I= & \frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^\pi \left(\frac{\sin x}{\cos ^2 x}-\frac{\sin ^2 x}{\cos ^2 x}\right)d x \\
& \frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^\pi\left(\secx \tan x-\tan ^2 x\right) d x \\
& \frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^\pi\left\{\sec x \tan x-\left(\sec ^2 x-1\right)\right\} d x
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}I & =\frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^\pi\left(\secx \tan x-\sec ^2 x+1\right) d x \\ & =\frac{\pi}{2}[\secx-\tan x+x]_0^\pi\\ & =\frac{\pi}{2}\left\{(\sec \pi-\tan \pi+\pi)-\frac{\pi}{2}\right.\\ & =\frac{\pi}{2}\{(-1-0+\pi)-(1-0+0)\} \\ & =\frac{\pi}{2}(\ppi-1-1)=\frac{\pi}{2}(\pi-2) \\ I & =\frac{\pi(\pi-2)}{2}\end{aligned}$

Let \(I=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\sin ^2 x}{\sin x+\cos x} d x\) ...(i)

\(\begin{aligned}

\Rightarrow I & =\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{2}}[\log (\sqrt{2}+1)-\log (\sqrt{2}-1)] \\
& =\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{2}}[2 \log (\sqrt{2}+1)]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \log (\sqrt{2}+1)
\end{aligned}\)

questions.q: If \(A_n=\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}} e^{-x} \cdot \cos ^n x d x\), then \(\frac{A_4-A_6}{A_4}=\)
questions.solution:
We have,
\(\begin{aligned}
& A_6=\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\infty} e^{-x} \cos ^6 x d x \\
& =\left[-e^{-x} \cos ^6 x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\infty}-\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\infty}\left(-e^{-x}\right) 6 \cos ^5 x(-\sin x) d x \\
& =0-6 \int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\infty} e^{-x} \cos ^5 x \sin x d x \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{A_6}{-6}=\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\infty} e^{-x} \cos ^5 x \sin x d x \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{-1}{6} A_6=\left[-e^{-x} \cos ^5 x \sin x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\infty} \\
& -\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\infty}\left(-e^{-x}\right)\left[5 \cos ^4 x(-\sin x) \sin x+\cos ^5 x \cdot \cos x\right] d x \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{-1}{6} A_6=0+\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\infty} e^{-x}\left[-5 \cos ^4 x\left(1-\cos ^2 x\right)+\cos ^6 x\right] d x \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{-1}{6} A_6=-5 \int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\infty} e^{-x} \cos ^4 x d x+6 \int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\infty} e^{-x} \cos ^6 x d x \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{-1}{6} A_6=-5 A_4+6 A_6 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 5 A_4=\frac{37}{6} A_6 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad A_6=\frac{30}{37} A_4 \\
& \therefore \quad \frac{A_4-A_6}{A_4}=\frac{A_4-\frac{30}{37} A_4}{A_4}=\frac{7}{37}
\end{aligned}\)

(i) and (ii), we get $\begin{aligned}$2 I & =\int_0^{$\pi$/ 2} $\frac{\left(\sin ^3 x \cos x+\cos ^3 x \sin x\right)}{\cos ^4 x+\sin ^4 x}$d x \\ & =\int_0^{$\pi$/ 2} $\frac{\sin x \cos x\left(\sin ^2 x+\cos ^2 x\right)}{\cos ^4 x+\sin ^4 x}$d x \\ & =\int_0^{$\pi$/ 2} $\frac{\sin x \cos x}{\sin ^4 x+\cos ^4 x}$d x \\ & =\int_0^{$\pi$/ 2} $\frac{\sin x \cos x}{\cos ^4 x\left(\tan ^4 x+1\right)}$d x \\ & =\int_0^{$\pi$/ 2} $\frac{\tan ^4 \sec ^2 x}{\left(\tan ^4 x+1\right)}$d x \end{aligned} Let $\tan ^2 x=t$ Differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get $\begin{array}{ll}$& 2 \tan x \sec ^2 x d x=d t \\ \therefore & \tan x \sec ^2 x d x=$\frac{d t}{2}$\\ \Rightarrow & 2 I=$\frac{1}{2} \int_$0^{$\infty$} $\frac{d t}{t^2+1}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\tan ^{-1}$t\right]_0^{$\infty$} \\ \Rightarrow & 2 I=$\frac{1}{2}\left[\tan ^{-1}(\infty)-\tan ^{-1}($0)\right]=$\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{\pi}{2}$\\ & 2 I=$\frac{\pi}{4} \Rightarrow$I=$\frac{\pi}{8} \end{array}$

questions.q: \(\int_{\log _c 2}^x $\frac{d t}{\sqrt{e^t-1}}=\frac{\pi}{6} \Rightarrowx=$\)
questions.solution:
Given integral
$$\begin{aligned}& I=\int_{\log _e 2}^x \frac{d t}{2 \sqrt{e^t-1}}=\frac{\pi}{6} \quad \text{(given)}\\
& \Rightarrow \quad \int_{\log _e 2}^x \frac{e^{-\frac{t}{2}}}{\sqrt{1-\left(e^{-t / 2}\right)^2}} d t=\frac{\pi}{6}\\
& \text{put } e^{-t / 2}=u \text{, at } t=\log _e 2 u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ and at } t=x \text{, }\\
& u=e^{-x / 2} \text{ and } e^{-t / 2} d t=-2 d u \\
& \text{so, } I=\int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}^{e^{-x / 2}} \frac{-2 d u}{\sqrt{1-u²}}=\frac{\pi}{6}\\
& \Rightarrow\left[-2 \sin ^{-1} u\right] \int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}^{e^{-\frac{x}{2}}}=\frac{\pi}{6} \Rightarrow \sin ^{-1}\left( e^{-x / 2}\right)-\frac{\pi}{4}=-\frac{\pi}{12}\\
& \Rightarrow \sin ^{-1}\left( e^{-x / 2}\right)=\frac{\pi}{6} \Rightarrow e^{-x / 2}=\sin \frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{1}{2}\\
& \Rightarrow-\frac{x}{2}=\log _ e\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\log _ e(2) \Rightarrow x=2 \cdot \log _ e(2) \text{. }\\
\end{aligned}$$\)
Hence, option (1) is correct.

questions.q: If $a$ and $b$ are positive integers such that $b > a,$ then $\lim_{n \to \infty}\left[\dfrac{1}{na} + \dfrac{1}{na + 1} + \dfrac{1}{na + 2} + \ldots + \dfrac{1}{nb}\right] =$

We have,

$\lim_{n \to \infty} \left[\dfrac{1}{na} + \dfrac{1}{na + 1} + \dfrac{1}{na + 2} + \ldots + \dfrac{1}{nb}\right]

$= \lim_{n \to $\infty}\left[\dfrac{1}{na} + \dfrac{1}{na + 1} + \dfrac{1}{na + 2} + \ldots + \dfrac{1}{na + n \left($ b - a\right)}\right]

$= \lim_{n \to \infty}\left[\dfrac{1}{na} + \dfrac{1}{na + 1} + \dfrac{1}{na + 2} + \ldots + \dfrac{1}{na + n \left(b - a\right)}\right]$

$= \lim_{n \to \i infty}\dfrac{1}{n}\$ left[$\dfrac{1}{a} +$+$1\left(a + \dfrac{1}{n}\right) +1 \left($ a + $\dfrac{2}{n}\right) + \ldots + \dfrac{1}{a + \dfrac{n\left(b - a\right)}{n}}\right]$

$= \lim_{n \to $\infty}\mathop{∑}_{r = 0}^{n $\left( b - a\right)}\d$ dfrac{1}{n}\$left(\dfrac{1}{a + \dfrac{r}{n}}\right)$

Now, replacing $\dfrac{1}{n}$ \todx, $\dfrac{r}{n}$ \tox$$ and converting limits, we get

$= {∫}_{0}^{b - a} \$ left($\dfrac{dx}{a + x}\right)$

$= {log $\left(a + x\right)$}_{0}^{b - a}$

$= log\$left($\dfrac{b}{a}$\right).$$

questions.q: ${∫}_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{xtanx}{secx + tanx}dx =$
questions.solution:
Let

$I = {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{xtanx}{secx + tanx}dx$

$= {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{\left(\pi - x\right)tan\left(\pi - x\right)}{sec\left(\pi - x\right) + tan\left(\pi - x\right)}\right\}dx$

$= {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{\left(\pi - x\right)\left(- tanx\right)}{- secx - tanx}\right\}dx$

$= {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{\left(\pi - x\right)\left(\tan x\right)}{secx + tanx}\right\}dx$

$= {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{\pi\left(\tan x\right)}{secx + tanx}\right\}dx - {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{x\left(\tan x\right)}{secx + tanx}\right\}dx$

$= {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{\pi\left(\tan x\right)}{secx + tanx}\right\}dx - I$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{tanx}{secx + tanx}\right\}dx$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\left(\dfrac{sinx}{cosx}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{cosx}\right) + \left(\dfrac{sinx}{cosx}\right)\right\}dx$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{sinx}{1 + sinx}\right\}dx$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{sinx\left(1 - sinx\right)\left(1 - \sin^{2}x\right)\right\}dx$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left\{\dfrac{sinx}{\cos^{2}x} - \dfrac{\sin^{2}x}{\cos^{2}x}\right\}dx$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left(tanxsecx - \tan^{2}x\right)dx$

$⇒ 2I = \pi{secx - tanx + x}_{0}^{\pi}$

$⇒ 2I = \pi \left[ \left(sec \pi -$ tan $\pi + \pi\right) - \left(sec0 - tan0 + 0\right)\right]$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{\pi\left(\pi - 2\right)}{2}.$

 $=$\lim _{x \rightarrow$ \infty}  $\$left[$\frac{1}{n a}+\frac{1}{n a+1}+\frac{1}{n a+2}+$\ldots+$\frac{1}{n a+n(b-a)}\right]$\\
 $$=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{r=0}^{(b-a) n} \frac{1}{n a+r}=\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{r=0}^{(b-a) n} \frac{1}{a+\frac{r}{n}}$\\

questions.q: For $n \geq 2$, let $I_n=\int_0^{\pi / 4} \tan ^n x d x$ and $F_n=I_n+I_{n-2}$. Then, $F_n-F_{n+1}=$

F_{n+1} & =\frac{1}{n}

questions.solution:
$Given that,
\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty}\left\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2-1^2}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2-2^2}}+\ldots+\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2-(n-1)^2}}\right\} \\
& \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty}\left\{\frac{1}{n \sqrt{1-\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^2}}+\frac{1}{n \sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2}{n}\right)^2}}+\ldots+\frac{1}{n \sqrt{1-\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)^2}}\right\} \\
& \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty}\left\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^2}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2}{n}\right)^2}}+\ldots+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)^2}}\right\} \\
& \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{r=1}^{n-1} \frac{1}{n \sqrt{1-\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^2}=\int_0^1 \frac{d x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}}=\left[\sin ^{-1} x\right]_0^1 \\
& =\sin ^{-1} 1-\sin ^{-1} 0=\frac{\pi}{2}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: $\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\left(\frac{x+\frac{\pi}{4}}{2-\cos 2 x}\right) d x$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given, $\mathrm{I}=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{x+\frac{\pi}{4}}{2-\cos ^2 x} d x\mathrm{I}=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{x+\frac{\pi}{4}}{2-\cos ^2 x} d x+\frac{\pi}{4} \int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{1}{2-\cos ^2 x} d x$
Let, $I_1=\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{x}{2-\cos ^2 x} d xf(x)=\frac{x}{2-\cos ^2 x}f(-x)=\frac{-x}{2-\cos 2(-x)}=\frac{-x}{2-\cos 2 x}=-f(x)f(x)$ is an odd function.
Thus, $I_1=0$
Let $I_1=\frac{\pi}{4} \int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{1}{2-\cos 2 x} d xg(x)=\frac{\pi}{4(2-\cos 2 x)}g(-x)=\frac{\pi}{4(2-\cos 2(-x))}=\frac{\pi}{4(2-\cos 2 x)}=g(x)\therefore \quad g(x)$ is an even function
Thus, $\mathrm{I}_2=2 \times \frac{\pi}{4} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{d x}{2-\cos 2 x}$
Now, $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_2=\frac{\pi}{4} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{d x}{2-\frac{1-\tan ^2 x}{1+\tan ^2 x}}\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{I}=\frac{\pi}{4} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{1+\tan ^2 x}{2+\tan ^2 x-1+\tan ^2 x} d x \\
& \mathrm{I}=\frac{\pi}{4} \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \frac{\sec ^2 x}{1+3 \tan ^2 x} d x
\end{aligned}$
Put $\tan x=t \Rightarrow \sec ^2 x d x=d t$
Limits : $x=0 \quad \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}=0\begin{aligned}
& x=\frac{\pi}{4} \quad \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}=1 \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{I}=\frac{\pi}{4} \int_0^1 \frac{d t}{1+3 t^2} \\
& \mathrm{I}=\frac{\pi}{2} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\left[\tan ^{-1} \sqrt{3} t\right]_0^1 \\
& \mathrm{I}=\frac{\pi}{2 \sqrt{3}}\left[\tan ^{-1}(\sqrt{3})-\tan ^{-1}(0)\right] \\
& \mathrm{I}=\frac{\pi}{2 \sqrt{3}}\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=\frac{\pi^2}{6 \sqrt{3}}
\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Let $I=\int_0^{\pi / 4} \frac{\sin x+\cos x}{3+\sin 2 x} d x$
Put $\sin x-\cos x=t(\sin x+\cos x) d x=d t$
Limits:
$\begin{aligned}
& x=0 \\
& \Rightarrow t=\sin \theta-\cos \theta=-1 \\
& x=\frac{\pi}{4} \Rightarrow t=\sin \frac{\pi}{4}-\cos \frac{\pi}{4}=0 \\
& \sin 2 x=1-1+\sin 2 x \\
& =1-(1-\sin 2 x) \\
& =1-\left(\sin ^2 x+\cos ^2 x-2 \sin x \cos x\right) \\
& =1-(\sin x-\cos x)^2 \\
& =1-t^2
\end{aligned}$
Now, $I=\int_{-1}^0 \frac{d t}{3+1-t^2}=\int_{-1}^0 \frac{d t}{(2)^2-(t)^2}\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{1}{4}\left[\log \left(\frac{2+t}{2-t}\right)\right]_{-1}^0 \\
& =-\frac{1}{4} \log \frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{4} \log 3
\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
$I=\int_{-1}^1 \frac{\sqrt{1+x+x^2}-\sqrt{1-x+x^2}}{\sqrt{1+x+x^2}+\sqrt{1-x+x^2}} d x$
Let $f(x)=\frac{\sqrt{1+x+x^2}-\sqrt{1-x+x^2}}{\sqrt{1+x+x^2}+\sqrt{1-x+x^2}}$
Replacing $x$ by $-x$, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& f(-x)=\frac{\sqrt{1-x+x^2}-\sqrt{1+x+x^2}}{\sqrt{1-x+x^2}+\sqrt{1+x+x^2}} \\
& =\frac{\sqrt{1+x+x^2}-\sqrt{1-x+x^2}}{\sqrt{1+x+x^2}+\sqrt{1-x+x^2}}=-f(x)
\end{aligned}$
So, $f(x)$ is an odd function.
$\therefore \quad \int_{-1}^1 f(x) d x=0$

questions.solution:
Given:

$A = \left[\begin{cases}- 2 & x & 1 \\ x & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & - 1\end{cases}\right]$

Also,

$det\left(A\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left|\begin{cases}- 2 & x & 1 \\ x & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & - 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ - 2\left(- 1 - 3\right) - x\left(- x - 2\right) + \left(3x - 2\right) = 0$

$⇒ x^{2} + 5x + 6 = 0$

$⇒ \left(x + 2\right)\left(x + 3\right) = 0$

$⇒ x = - 2, - 3$

So, $l^{3} - m^{3} = \left(- 2\right)^{3} - \left(- 3\right)^{3} = - 8 + 27 = 19$

questions.q: If $\left|\begin{cases}x & x^{2} & 1 + x^{3} \\ y & y^{2} & 1 + y^{3} \\ z & z^{2} & 1 + z^{3}\end{cases}\right| = 0$ and x, y, z are all distinct, then $xyz =$
questions.solution:
Given,

If $\left|\begin{cases}x & x^{2} & 1 + x^{3} \\ y & y^{2} & 1 + y^{3} \\ z & z^{2} & 1 + z^{3}\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$\left|\begin{cases}x & x^{2} & 1 \\ y & y^{2} & 1 \\ z & z^{2} & 1\end{cases}\right| + \left|\begin{cases}x & x^{2} & x^{3} \\ y & y^{2} & y^{3} \\ z & z^{2} & z^{3}\end{cases}\right| = 0$

Taking~$x, y, z$~from& ${C}_{1}, {C}_{2}, {C}_{3}$~respectively&

$\left|\begin{cases}x & x^{2} & 1 \\ y & y^{2} & 1 \\ z & z^{2} & 1\end{cases}\right| + xyz\left|\begin{cases}1 & x & x^{2} \\ 1 & y & y^{2} \\ 1 & z & z^{2}\end{cases}\right| = 0$

By interchanging the columns twice

$\left|\begin{cases}x & x^{2} & 1 \\ y & y^{2} & 1 \\ z & z^{2} & 1\end{cases}\right| + xyz\left|\begin{cases}x & x^{2} & 1 \\ y & y^{2} & 1 \\ z & z^{2} & 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$\left|\begin{cases}x & x^{2} & 1 \\ y & y^{2} & 1 \\ z & z^{2} & 1\end{cases}\right|\left(1 + xyz\right) = 0$

${R}_{1} \to {R}_{1} - {R}_{2} & {R}_{2} \to {R}_{2} - {R}_{3}$

$\left|\begin{cases}x - y & x^{2} - y^{2} & 1 - 1 \\ y - z & y^{2} - z^{2} & 1 - 1 \\ z & z^{2} & 1\end{cases}\right|\left(1 + xyz\right) = 0$

$\left|\begin{cases}x - y & \left(x - y\right)\left(x + y\right) & 0 \\ y - z & \left(y - z\right)\left(y + z\right) & 0 \\ z & z^{2} & 1\end{cases}\right|\left(1 + xyz\right) = 0$

$\left(x - y\right)\left(y - z\right)\left|\begin{cases}1 & \left(x + y\right) & 0 \\ 1 & \left(y + z\right) & 0 \\ z & z^{2} & 1\end{cases}\right|\left(1 + xyz\right) = 0$

${R}_{1} \to {R}_{1} - {R}_{2}$

$\left(x - y\right)\left(y - z\right)\left|\begin{cases}1 - 1 & \left(x + y - y - z\right) & 0 \\ 1 & \left(y + z\right) & 0 \\ z & z^{2} & 1\end{cases}\right|\left(1 + xyz\right) = 0$

$\left(x - y\right)\left(y - z\right)\left|\begin{cases}0 & \left(x - z\right) & 0 \\ 1 & \left(y + z\right) & 0 \\ z & z^{2} & 1\end{cases}\right|\left(1 + xyz\right) = 0$

$\left(x - y\right)\left(y - z\right)\left[\left(- x + z\right) \times 1\right]\left(1 + xyz\right) = 0$

$\left(x - y\right)\left(y - z\right)\left(z - x\right)\left(1 + xyz\right) = 0$

$⇒ 1 + xyz = 0\left\{∵ x \ne y \ne z\right\}$

Hence,~$xyz = - 1$

Applying ${R}_{1} \to {R}_{1} + {R}_{2} + {R}_{3}$

$△ = \left|\begin{cases}b + c + b + c & a + c + a + c & a + b + a + b \\ b & c + a & b \\ c & c & a + b\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ △ = 2\left|\begin{cases}b + c & a + c & a + b \\ b & c + a & b \\ c & c & a + b\end{cases}\right|$

Applying ${R}_{1} \to {R}_{1} - {R}_{2}$

$⇒ △ = 2\left|\begin{cases}b + c - b & a + c - ( c + a ) & a + b - b \\ b & c + a & b \\ c & c & a + b\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ △ = 2\left|\begin{cases}c & 0 & a \\ b & c + a & b \\ c & c & a + b\end{cases}\right|$

Applying ${R}_{3} \to {R}_{3} - {R}_{1}$

$⇒ △ = 2\left|\begin{cases}c & 0 & a \\ b & c + a & b \\ 0 & c & b\end{cases}\right|$

Applying ${R}_{2} \to {R}_{2} - {R}_{3}$

$⇒ △ = 2\left|\begin{cases}c & 0 & a \\ b & a & 0 \\ 0 & c & b\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ △ = 2 \left[c \left(ab - 0\right) - 0 + $a$\left(bc - 0\right)\right]$

$⇒ △ = 2 \left[abc + abc\right]$

$⇒ △ = 4abc.$

Then the value of $n$ is
questions.solution:
$\left|\begin{cases}a & a + 1 & a - 1 \\ - b & b + 1 & b - 1 \\ c & c - 1 & c + 1\end{cases}\right| + \left|\begin{cases}a + 1 & b + 1 & c - 1 \\ a - 1 & b - 1 & c + 1 \\ \left(- 1\right)n + 2a & \left(- 1\right)n - 1b & \left(- 1\right)nc\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left|\begin{cases}a & a + 1 & a - 1 \\ - b & b + 1 & b - 1 \\ c & c - 1 & c + 1\end{cases}\right| + \left(- 1\right)n\left|\begin{cases}a + 1 & b + 1 & c - 1 \\ a - 1 & b - 1 & c + 1 \\ a & - b & c\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left|\begin{cases}a & a + 1 & a - 1 \\ - b & b + 1 & b - 1 \\ c & c - 1 & c + 1\end{cases}\right| + \left(- 1\right)n\left|\begin{cases}a + 1 & a - 1 & a \\ b + 1 & b - 1 & - b \\ c - 1 & c + 1 & c\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left|\begin{cases}a & a + 1 & a - 1 \\ - b & b + 1 & b - 1 \\ c & c - 1 & c + 1\end{cases}\right| + \left(- 1\right)n\left|\begin{cases}a & a + 1 & a - 1 \\ - b & b + 1 & b - 1 \\ c & c - 1 & c + 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ ( 1 + \left(- 1\right)n ) \left|\begin{cases}a & a + 1 & a - 1 \\ - b & b + 1 & b - 1 \\ c & c - 1 & c + 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

Hence,~$n$ is an odd integer.

questions.solution:
Given equation is& $\left|\begin{cases}1 & - 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 6 & 4 \\ 1 & 3x & x^{2}\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ 6x^{2} - 12x + 3\left(x^{2} - 4\right) + \left(3x - 6\right) = 0$

$⇒ 6x^{2} - 12x + 3x^{2} - 12 + 3x - 6 = 0$

$⇒ 9x^{2} - 9x - 18 = 0$

$⇒ 9\left(x^{2} - x - 2\right) = 0$

questions.q: If ${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, . . . , {a}_{9}$ are in $G . P . ,$ then $\left|\begin{cases}log{a}_{1} & log{a}_{2} & log{a}_{3} \\ log{a}_{4} & log{a}_{5} & log{a}_{6} \\ log{a}_{7} & log{a}_{8} & log{a}_{9}\end{cases}\right|$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given& ${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3}, . . . , {a}_{9}$ are in& $G . P . ,$ hence, by the definition of $G . P . ,$ we have& $\dfrac{a2}{a1} = \dfrac{a3}{a2} = \dfrac{a4}{a3} = . . . \dfrac{a9}{a8} = r,$ where& $r$ is the common ratio of the& $G . P .$

Now, let $△ = \left|\begin{cases}log{a}_{1} & log{a}_{2} & log{a}_{3} \\ log{a}_{4} & log{a}_{5} & log{a}_{6} \\ log{a}_{7} & log{a}_{8} & log{a}_{9}\end{cases}\right|$

Applying ${C}_{2} \to {C}_{2} - {C}_{1}, {C}_{3} \to {C}_{3} - {C}_{2},$ we get

$△ = \left|\begin{cases}log{a}_{1} & log{a}_{2} - log{a}_{1} & log{a}_{3} - log{a}_{2} \\ log{a}_{4} & log{a}_{5} - log{a}_{4} & log{a}_{6} - log{a}_{5} \\ log{a}_{7} & log{a}_{8} - log{a}_{7} & log{a}_{9} - log{a}_{8}\end{cases}\right|$

Using $logm - logn = log\left(\dfrac{m}{n}\right),$ we get

$⇒ △ = \left|\begin{cases}log{a}_{1} & log\left(\dfrac{a2}{a1}\right) & log\left(\dfrac{a3}{a2}\right) \\ log{a}_{4} & log\left(\dfrac{a5}{a4}\right) & log\left(\dfrac{a6}{a5}\right) \\ log{a}_{7} & log\left(\dfrac{a8}{a7}\right) & log\left(\dfrac{a9}{a8}\right)\end{cases}\right|$

Using the relation defined above, we get

$⇒ △ = \left|\begin{cases}log{a}_{1} & log\left(r\right) & log\left(r\right) \\ log{a}_{4} & log\left(r\right) & log\left(r\right) \\ log{a}_{7} & log\left(r\right) & log\left(r\right)\end{cases}\right|$

Thus, the determinant has& ${C}_{2} = {C}_{3},$ and we know that if two rows/columns of a determinant are same then its value is zero.

So,& $△ = \left|\begin{cases}log{a}_{1} & log{a}_{2} & log{a}_{3} \\ log{a}_{4} & log{a}_{5} & log{a}_{6} \\ log{a}_{7} & log{a}_{8} & log{a}_{9}\end{cases}\right| = 0 .$

=(a-b)(a-c)$\left| \begin{array}{ccc}b c & b+c & 1 \\

 \begin{aligned}\Delta& =(a-b)(a-c)$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}b c & b+c & 1 \\

questions.q: Let \(M=$\left[\begin{array}{ll}$1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]\) and \(N=$\left[\begin{array}{ll}$1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{array}\right]\). Then \(N M^{10} N^{-1}=\)
questions.solution:
\begin{aligned}M & =$\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 1 \\
0 & 1
\end{array}\right] \\
M² & =\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 1 \\
0 & 1
\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 1 \\
0 & 1
\end{array}\right] \\
M² & =\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 2 \\
0 & 1
\end{array}\right] \\
M³ & =\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 3 \\
0 & 1
\end{array}\right] \\
& \vdots \\
M^{10} & =\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 10 \\
0 & 1
\end{array}\right] \\
N & =\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\
0 & 2
\end{array}\right] \\
|N| & =2-0=2 \\
\operatorname{Adj}^N & =\left[\begin{array}{ll}2 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{array}\right] \\
N^{-1} & =\frac{1}{|N|} \text{ Adj A } \\
N^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2}\left[\begin{array}{ll}2 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{array}\right] \\
N^{-1} & =\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\
0 & \frac{1}{2}
\end{array}\right]
\end{aligned}$
Consider,
\begin{aligned}
$\mathbf{N}$\cdot $\mathbf{M}^{10}$ \cdot $\mathbf{N}^{-1}$& =$\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\
0 & 2
\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & 10 \\
0 & 1
\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\
0 & \frac{1}{2}

& =$\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & 10 \\
0 & 2
\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\
0 & \frac{1}{2}
\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 5 \\
0 & 1

\end{aligned}\)
Hence, option (a) is correct.$

k-4 & 2 k-9 & 3 k-16 \\
k-8 & 2 k-27 & 3 k-64
\end{array}$\right|=0\)$
questions.solution:
It is given that,
\$(\left|\begin{array}{ccc}k-2 & 2 k-3 & 3 k-4 \\
k-4 & 2 k-9 & 3 k-16 \\
k-8 & 2 k-27 & 3 k-64
\end{array}\right|=0\)
On applying, \(R_2 \longrightarrow R_2-R_1\) and \(R_3 \longrightarrow R_3-R_1\), we get
\begin{aligned}& \Rightarrow \quad\left|\begin{array}{ccc}k-2 & 2 k-3 & 3 k-4 \\
-2 & -6 & -12 \\
-6 & -24 & -60
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \$ quad$\left| $\begin{array}{ccc}k-2 & 2 k-3 & 3 k-4 \\
1 & 3 & 6 \\
1 & 4 & 10
\end{array}$ \right|$=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad(k-2)[30-24]-(2 k-3)[10-6]+(3 k-4)[4-3]=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 6 k-12-8 k+12+3 k-4=0 \Rightarrow k=4
\end{aligned}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
If \(x=\alpha, y=\beta, z=\gamma\) is the solution, for the system of equations
$\begin{aligned}
2 x-y+8 z & =13 \\
3 x+4 y+5 z & =18 \\
5 x-2 y+7 z & =20
\end{aligned}\)
then \(\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha=\)$
questions.solution:
According to Cramer's rule,
\(\begin{aligned}
& x=\alpha=\frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta},y=\beta=\frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} \text{ and }z=\gamma=\frac{\Delta_3}{\Delta}\\
& \text{where } \begin{aligned}
\Delta& =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}2 & -1 & 8 \\
3 & 4 & 5 \\
5 & -2 & 7
\end{array}\right| \\
& =2(28+10)+1(21-25)+8(-6-20) \\
& =76-4-208=76-212=-136
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}
\Delta_1 & =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}13 & -1 & 8 \\
18 & 4 & 5 \\
20 & -2 & 7
\end{array}\right| \\
& =13(28+10)+1(126-100)+8(-36-80) \\
& =(13 \times 38)+26-(8 \times 116) \\
& =494+26-928=-408 \\
\Delta_2 & =\left|\begin{array}{lll}2 & 13 & 8 \\
3 & 18 & 5 \\
5 & 20 & 7
\end{array}\right| \\
& =2(126-100)-13(21-25)+8(60-90) \\
& =(2 \times 26)+(13 \times 4)-(8 \times 30) \\
& =52+52-240=-136 \\
\Delta_3 & =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}2 & -1 & 13 \\
3 & 4 & 18 \\
5 & -2 & 20
\end{array}\right| \\
& =2(80+36)+1(60-90)+13(-6-20) \\
& =(2 \times 116)-30-(13 \times 26) \\
& =232-30-338=-136
\end{aligned}\)
So, \(\alpha=3, \beta=1, \gamma=1\)
\(\therefore \quad \alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha=3+1+3=7\)
Hence, option (c) is correct.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the system of simultaneous linear equations \(x+y+z=a, x-y+b z=2\), \(2 x+3 y-z=1\) has infinitely many solutions, then \(b-5 a=\)
questions.solution:
Given that system of linear equations
\(\begin{aligned}
x+y+z & =a \quad \ldots (i)\\
x-y+b z & =2 \quad \ldots (ii) \\
2 x+3 y-z & =1 \quad \ldots (iii)
\end{aligned}\)
has infinitely many solutions,
\(\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 1 & 1 \\
1 & -1 & b \\
2 & 3 & -1
\end{array}\right]=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 1(1-3 b)-1(-1-2 b)+1(3+2=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 1-3 b+1+2 b+5=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \\
& -b=-7 \\
& \Rightarrow \\
& b=7
\end{aligned}\)
Adding Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
\(\quad \begin{aligned}
2 x+8 z & =a+2 \\
\Rightarrow x+4 z & =\frac{a+2}{2}  \quad \ldots (iv)
\end{aligned}\)
Multiply Eq. (i) by 3 then subtract Eq. (iii) from it,
\(\begin{aligned}
3 x+3 y+3 z & =3 a \\
-2 x \pm 3 y \mp z & =-1 \\
\hline x+4 z & =3 a-1 \quad \ldots (v)
\end{aligned}\)
By Eqs. (iv) and (v), we get
\($\begin{array}{rlrl} 
& & \frac{a+2}{2} & =3 a-1 \\
\Rightarrow & & a+2 & =6 a-2 \\
\Rightarrow & 6 a-a & =4 \\
\Rightarrow & & 5 a & =4 \\
\therefore & b-5 a & =7-4=3
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a+b+2 c & a & b \\ c & 2 a+b+c & b \\ c & a & a+2 b+c\end{array}$\right|=2$, then $a^3+b^3+c^3-3 a b c=
options: $1-3 a b-3 b c-3 c a$
$1-2 a b-2 b c-2 c a$
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}$& $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}$a+b+2 c & a & b \\
c & 2 a+b+c & b \\
c & a & a+2 b+c
\end{array}\right|=2 \\
& \Rightarrow 2(a+b+c)$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}$1 & a & b \\
1 & b+c+2 a & b \\
1 & a & c+a+2 b
\end{array}\right|=2
\end{aligned}

[Applying $C_1 \rightarrow C_1+C_2+C_3$ and taking $2(a+b+c)$ common from $\left.C_1\right]$
\Rightarrow 2(a+b+c)$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}$1 & a & b \\
0 & b+c+a & 0 \\
0 & 0 & c+a+b
\end{array}\right|=2

[Applying $R_2 \rightarrow R_2-R_1$ and $R_3 \rightarrow R_3-R_1$ ]

$\begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow \quad 2(a+b+c)^3=2 \quad $\text{ [expanding along }$C_1 $\text{ ] }$\\
& \Rightarrow \quad(a+b+c)^3=1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad a+b+c=1 \\
&
\end{aligned}

Now, $a^3+b^3+c^3-3 a b c$
$\begin{aligned}$& =(a+b+c)$\left($a^2+b²+c²-a b-b c-c a\right) \\

 $\begin{aligned}2 x+3|y|+5[z] & =0 \\

and
According to Cramer's rule,
\(x=\frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta},|y|=\frac{\Delta_2}{\Delta} \text{ and }[z]=\frac{\Delta_3}{\Delta}\)
where,
 \begin{aligned}\Delta& =$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}2 & 3 & 5 \\

questions.solution:
Given system of linear equations is
 \begin{aligned}x+2 y+3 z & =6 \\
x+3 y+5 z & =9 \\
$\text{$ and } \quad2 x+5 y+\lambda z & =\mu
\end{aligned} \)
Now, according to Cramer's rule,
 \begin{aligned}& \Delta=$\left|\begin{array}{lll}1 & 2 & 3 \\
1 & 3 & 5 \\
2 & 5 & \lambda
\end{array} \right|=1$(3 \lambda-25)-2(\lambda-10)+3(5-6) \\
& =\lambda-8 \\
& \Delta_1=$\left|\begin{array}{lll}6 & 2 & 3 \\
9 & 3 & 5 \\
\mu & 5 & \lambda
\end{array}\right|=6(3 \lambda-25)-2(9 \lambda-5 \mu) \\
& +3(45-3 \mu)=\mu-15 \\
& \Delta_2=\left|\begin{array}{lll}1 & 6 & 3 \\
1 & 9 & 5 \\
2 & \mu & \lambda
\end{array}\right|=1(9 \lambda-5 \mu)-6(\lambda-10)+3(\mu-18) \\
& =3 \lambda-4 \mu+6
\end{aligned}\)
and
\(\Delta_3=\left|\begin{array}{lll}1 & 2 & 6 \\
1 & 3 & 9 \\
2 & 5 & \mu
\end{array}\right|=1(3 \mu-45)-2(\mu-18)+6(5-6) = \mu - 15\)
Now, if \(\lambda=8\) and \(\mu  ≠ 15\), then system of linear equations has no solution.
If \(\lambda  ≠ 8\) and \(\mu \in R\), then system of linear equations has unique solution.
And, if \(\lambda=8\) and \(\mu=15\), then system of linear equations has infinite number of solutions, because \(\Delta_2=3 \lambda-2 \mu+6\) is also be zero. Hence, option (2) is correct.$

questions.q: If \(f(x), f^{\prime}(x) f^{\prime \prime}(x)\), are positive functions and \(f(0)=1, f^{\prime}(0)=2\), then the solution of the differential equation \($\left|$\begin{array}{ll}f(x) & f^{\prime}(x) \\ f^{\prime}(x) & f^{\prime \prime}(x)\end{array}$\right|=0\) is$
questions.solution:
\(\begin{aligned}
& \text{Since, }\left|\begin{array}{ll}f(x) & f^{\prime}(x) \\
f^{\prime}(x) & f^{\prime \prime}(x)
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad f(x) f^{\prime \prime}(x)-\left(f^{\prime}(x)\right)^2=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad f(x) f^{\prime \prime}(x)=\left(f^{\prime}(x)\right)^2 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{f^{\prime \prime}(x)}{f^{\prime}(x)}=\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}\\
\end{aligned}\)
On, integrating both sides, we get
\(\begin{aligned}
& \int \frac{f^{\prime \prime}(x)}{f^{\prime}(x)}d x=\int \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}d x \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \log _e\left(f^{\prime}(x)\right)=\log _e(f(x))+c \\
 \text{ and }  \because \quad f(0)=1 \text{ and }f^{\prime}(0)=2 \\
 \text{ and }  \therefore \quad c=\log _e 2 \\
 \text{ and }  \log _e\left(f^{\prime}(x)\right)=\log _e(f(x))+\log _e 2 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad f^{\prime}(x)=2 f(x) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}=2 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \int \frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}d x=\int2 d x \Rightarrow \log _e f(x)=2 x+c \\
& \because \quad f(0)=1 \text{, so }c=0 \\
& \because \quad \log _e f(x)=2 x \Rightarrow f(x)=e^{2 x} \\
\end{aligned}\)
Hence, option (1) is correct.

questions.q: The system of equations $3 x+2 y+z=6$, $3 x+4 y+3 z=14$ and $6 x+10 y+8 z=a$, has infinite number of solutions, if $a$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given system of equation is

$\begin{gathered}$3 x+2 y+z=6 \\
3 x+4 y+3 z=14 \\
6 x+10 y+8 z=a \\
A=$\left[\begin{array}{rrr}$3 & 2 & 1 \\
3 & 4 & 3 \\
6 & 10 & 8
\end{array}\right], B=$\left[\begin{array}{r}$6 \\
14 \\
a

\end{gathered}

Here, $\quad A=\left[\begin{array}{rrr}3 & 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & 3 \\ 6 & 10 & 8\end{array}\right], B=\left[\begin{array}{r}6 \\ 14 \\ a\end{array}\right]$
$\begin{aligned}$& C_{11}=(32-30)=2, C_{12}=-(24-18)=-6, \\
& C_{13}=(30-24)=6 \\
& C_{21}=-(16-10)=-6, C_{22}=(24-6)=18, \\
& C_{23}=-(30-12)=-18 \\
& C_{31}=(6-4)=2, C_{32}=-(9-3)=-6, \\
& C_{33}=(12-6)=6
\end{aligned}

$\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{adj}$A & =$\left[\begin{array}{lll}$C_{11} & C_{12} & C_{13} \\
C_{21} & C_{22} & C_{23} \\
C_{31} & C_{32} & C_{33}
\end{array}\right]^{\prime}=$\left[\begin{array}{rrr}$2 & -6 & 6 \\
-6 & 18 & -18 \\
2 & -6 & 6
\end{array}\right]^{\prime} \\
& =$\left[\begin{array}{rrr}$2 & -6 & 2 \\
-6 & 18 & -6 \\
6 & -18 & 6
\end{array}\right]
\end{aligned}

So,

$\begin{aligned}$& $\text{ A) }$B=$\left[\begin{array}{rrr}$2 & -6 & 2 \\
-6 & 18 & -6 \\
6 & -18 & 6
\end{array}\right]$\left[\begin{array}{r}$6 \\
14 \\
a
\end{array}\right] \\
& =$\left[\begin{array}{c}$12-84+2 a \\
-36+252-6 a \\
36-252+6 a
\end{array}\right]=$\left[\begin{array}{c}
-$72+2 a \\
216-6 a \\
-216+6 a
\end{array}\right] \\
& |A|=$\left|\begin{array}{rrr}$3 & 2 & 1 \\
3 & 4 & 3 \\
6 & 10 & 8
\end{array}\right| \\
& =3(32-30)-2(24-18)+1(30-24) \\
& =3(2)-2(6)+6=6-12+6=0 \\
&
\end{aligned}

and
We know that, if $|A|=0$ and $(\operatorname{adj} A) \cdot B=0$, then the system of equations is consistent and has an infinite number of solutions.

$\begin{gathered}
(\operatorname{adj}$A) $\cdot$B=0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad$\left[\begin{array}{c}
-$72+2 a \\
216+6 a \\
-216+6 a
\end{array}\right]=$\left[\begin{array}{l}$0 \\
0 \\
0
\end{array}\right]
\end{gathered}

On comparing, we get

$\begin{aligned}$2 a-72 & =0 \\
a & =36
\end{aligned}

\therefore \quad a=36

then $f(2012)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given, $f(x)=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & x & x+1 \\ 2 x & x(x-1) & x(x+1) \\ 3 x(x-1) & x(x-1)(x-2) & (x-1)(x)(x+1)\end{array}\right|$
Taking $x$ and $x(x-1)$ common from $R_2$ and $R_3$ and $(x+1)$ common from $C_3=x \times x(x-1) \times(x+1)\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & x & 1 \\ 2 & (x-1) & 1 \\ 3 & (x-2) & 1\end{array}\right|$
(applying $C_2 \rightarrow C_1+C_2$ )
$\begin{aligned} & =x^2\left(x^2-1\right)\left|\begin{array}{lll}1 & x+1 & 1 \\ 2 & x+1 & 1 \\ 3 & x+1 & 1\end{array}\right| \\ & =x^2\left(x^2-1\right)(x+1)\left|\begin{array}{lll}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right|=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad f(x)=0 \\ & \therefore \quad f(2012)=0\end{aligned}$

Given that, $a \alpha^2+2 b \alpha+c \neq 0$ and that the system of equations
$\begin{aligned} & (a \alpha+b) x+a y+b z=0 \\ & (b \alpha+c) x+b y+c z=0 \\ & (a \alpha+b) y+(b \alpha+c) z=0\end{aligned}$
has a non-trivial solution, then $a, b and c$ lie in
questions.solution:
Given system of equations is
$\begin{aligned}(a \alpha+b) x+a y+b z & =0 \\ (b \alpha+c) x+b y+c z & =0\end{aligned}$
and $(a \alpha+b) y+(b \alpha+c) z=0$
For non-trivial solution,
$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a \alpha+b & a & b \\ b \alpha+c & b & c \\ 0 & a \alpha+b & b \alpha+c\end{array}\right|=0$
Applying $R_3 \rightarrow R_3-\alpha R_1-R_2\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a \alpha+b & a & b \\ b \alpha+c & b & c \\ -\left(a \alpha^2+2 b \alpha+c\right) & 0 & 0\end{array}\right|=0 \\ & \Rightarrow-\left(a \alpha^2+2 b \alpha+c\right)\left(a c-b^2\right)=0\end{aligned}\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow a c-b^2=0 & \left(\because a \alpha^2+2 b \alpha+c \neq 0\right) \\ \Rightarrow a c=b^2\end{array}$
Hence, $a, b$ and $c$ are in GP.

If the system of equations
$(k+1)^3 x+(k+2)^3 y =(k+3)^3(k+1) x+(k+2) y =k+3x+y =1$
is consistent, then the value of $k$ is
questions.solution:
System of equations
$(k+1)^3 x+(k+2)^3 y=(k+3)^3(k+1) x+(k+2) y=(k+3)x+y=1$ is consistent.
Since, the given system of equations are consistent. Then $D=0$ and Also, $\left(D_1=D_2=D_3=0\right)$ have infinitely many solutions. By Crammer Rule
$D=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}(k+1)^3 & (k+2)^3 & (k+3)^3 \\(k+1) & (k+2) & (k+3) \\1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right|=0\because \quad C_2 \rightarrow C_2-C_1C_3 \rightarrow C_3-C_1D=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}(k+1)^3 & (k+2)^3-(k+1)^3 & (k+3)^3-(k+1)^3 \\ (k+1) & (k+2)-(k+1) & (k+3)-(k+1) \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right|=0D=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}(k+1)^3 & \left(3 k^2+9 k+7\right) & \left(6 k^2+24 k+26\right) \\ (k+1) & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right|=0$
Expand with $r$ to $R_32\left(3 k^2+9 k+7\right)-2\left(3 k^2+12 k+13\right)=0\Rightarrow 3 k^2+9 k+7-3 k^2-12 k-13=0\Rightarrow \quad-3 k-6=0 \Rightarrow 3 k=-6\Rightarrow \quad k=-2$

is

Write given system of equations in matrix form $A X=B$.
$\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$
Now,
$\begin{aligned} & |A|=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{array}\right| \\ & =1(6+1)+1(3+2)+1(1-4) \\ & =7+5-3 \\ & =9 \neq 0\end{aligned}$
Since, $|A| \neq 0$. So, the given system of equations has only trivial solution. So, there is no non-trivial solution.

Match the following elements of $\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 \\ 3 & -4 & 6\end{array}$\right]$ with their co-factors and choose the correct answer.
$\begin{array}{lcll} & $\text{ Element }$ & & $\text{ Co-factor }$ \\ $\text{ A. }$ & -1 & $\text{ (1) }$ & -2 \\ $\text{ B. }$ & 1 & (2) & 32 \\ $\text{ C. }$ & 3 & (3) & 4 \\ $\text{ D. }$ & 6 & $\text{ (4) }$ & 6 \\ & & $\text{ (5) }$ & -6\end{array}
questions.solution:
Let $A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 \\ 3 & -4 & 6\end{array}\right]$
Cofactor of $(-1)=-\left|\begin{array}{ll}0 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{array}\right|=6$
Cofactor of $(1)=\left|\begin{array}{cc}4 & 2 \\ -4 & 6\end{array}\right|=24+8=32$
Cofactor of $(3)=\left|\begin{array}{cc}-1 & 0 \\ 4 & 2\end{array}\right|=-2-0=-2$
Cofactor of $(6)=\left|\begin{array}{cc}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 4\end{array}\right|=4-0=4\therefore$ Option (3) is correct.

If $\left|$\begin{array}{ccc}$\cos$(A+B) & -$\sin$(A+B) & $\cos 2$ B \\ $\sin A$ & $\cos A$ & $\sin B$ \\ -$\cos A$ & $\sin A$ & $\cos B\end{array}$\right|=0$
then $B$ is equal to$
questions.solution:
$We have,
\left|\begin{array}{ccc}\cos (A+B) & -\sin (A+B) & \cos 2 B \\\sin A & \cos A & \sin B \\-\cos A & \sin A & \cos B\end{array}\right|=0\Rightarrow \quad \cos (A+B)[\cos A \cos B-\sin A \sin B]+\sin (A+B)[\sin A \cos B+\cos A \sin B]+\cos 2 B\left[\sin ^2 A+\cos ^2 A\right]=0\Rightarrow \quad \cos (A+B) \cos (A+B)+\sin (A+B) \sin (A+B)+\cos 2 B=0\Rightarrow \cos ^2(A+B)+\sin ^2(A+B)+\cos 2 B=0\Rightarrow \quad 1+\cos 2 B=0\Rightarrow \quad 1+2 \cos ^2 B-1=0\Rightarrow \quad \cos ^2 B=0 \Rightarrow \cos ^2 B=\cos ^2 \frac{\pi}{2}\Rightarrow \quad B=n \pi \pm \frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}(2 n \pm 1)\therefore \quad B=\frac{\pi}{2}(2 n+1)$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The general solution of the differential equation $x d y-y d x=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} d x$ is
questions.solution:
$x d y-y d x=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} d x$
Dividing by $x d x$ both sides $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{y}{x}+\sqrt{1+\frac{y^2}{x^2}}$
Let $y=v x \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=v+x \frac{d v}{d x}$ Hence, $v+x \frac{d v}{d x}=v+\sqrt{1+v^2}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow x \frac{d v}{d x}=\sqrt{1+v^2} \Rightarrow \frac{d v}{\sqrt{1+v^2}}=\frac{d x}{x} \\ & \Rightarrow \log \left(v+\sqrt{1+v^2}\right)=\log x+\log c \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{y}{x}+\sqrt{1+\frac{y^2}{x^2}}=c x \Rightarrow y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=c x^2 . \end{aligned}$

questions.q: The sum of the order and degree of the differential equation $x\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}=\left(1+\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^{\frac{4}{3}}$ is
questions.solution:
$x\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^{1 / 2}=\left(1+\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^{4 / 3}$
Squaring both sides $x^2\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)=\left(1+\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^{8 / 3}$
Cubing both sides $x^6\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^3=\left(1+\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^8$
So, degree $=3$, order $=2 \Rightarrow$ Sum $=3+2=5$.

Multiplying (i) by 2 and Subtracting from (ii) $\begin{aligned} & \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}-\frac{2 d y}{d x}=\frac{2 d y}{d x}-4 y \Rightarrow \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}-\frac{4 d y}{d x}+4 y=0 \\ & \Rightarrow y^{\prime \prime}-4 y^{\prime}+4 y=0 \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The difference of the order and degree of the differential equation $\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^{-\frac{7}{2}}\left(\frac{d^3 y}{d x^3}\right)^2-\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^{-\frac{5}{2}}\left(\frac{d^4 y}{d x^4}\right)=0$ is
questions.solution:
Given differential equation
$\begin{aligned}
& \left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^{-\frac{7}{2}} \cdot\left(\frac{d^3 y}{d x^3}\right)^2-\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^{-\frac{5}{2}} \cdot\left(\frac{d^4 y}{d x^4}\right)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^{-7} \cdot\left(\frac{d^3 y}{d x^3}\right)^4-\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^{-5} \cdot\left(\frac{d^4 y}{d x^4}\right)^2=0 \\
& \Rightarrow\left(\frac{d^3 y}{d x^3}\right)^4 \cdot\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^5-\left(\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}\right)^7 \cdot\left(\frac{d^4 y}{d x^4}\right)^2=0
\end{aligned}$
So, order $=4$, degree $=2$
Now, order - degree $=4-2=2$.

Let $y=\frac{1}{t} \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=-\frac{1}{t^2} \frac{d t}{d x}\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow-\frac{1}{t^2} \frac{d t}{d x}+\frac{1}{t x}+\frac{1}{t^2}=0 \Rightarrow \frac{d t}{d x}-\frac{t}{x}=1 \\

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The solution of $x d y-y d x=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} d x$ when $y(\sqrt{3})=1$ is
questions.solution:
Since, $x d y-y d x=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} d x\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow x d y=\left(y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\right) d x \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}{x}
\end{aligned}$
Let $y=v x \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=v+x \frac{d v}{d x}$
So, $v+x \frac{d v}{d x}=\frac{v x+\sqrt{x^2+v^2 x^2}}{x}\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow x \frac{d v}{d x}=\sqrt{1+v^2} \Rightarrow \int \frac{d v}{\sqrt{1+v^2}}=\int \frac{1}{x} d x \\
& \Rightarrow \log \left(v+\sqrt{v^2+1}\right)=\log x c \\
& \Rightarrow y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=xc
\end{aligned}$
Since, $y(\sqrt{3})=1 \Rightarrow 1+\sqrt{4}=3 c \Rightarrow c=1$
So, $y+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=x$

So, I.F. $=e^{\int \frac{\sec ^2 y}{\tan y} d y}=e^{\ln (\tan y)}=\tan y$

questions.q: The general solution of the differential equation $(x-y-1) d y=(x+y+1) d x$ is
questions.solution:
Given differential equation
$\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{x+y+1}{x-y-1}\begin{aligned} & \text{ Let } \mathrm{x}=X+h, y=Y+k \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d Y}{d X} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{d Y}{d X}=\frac{X+Y+h+k+1}{X-Y+h-k-1}\end{aligned}$
Since, $h+k+1=0h-k-1=0$
After solving this we get
$h=0, k=-1$
So, $\frac{d Y}{d X}=\frac{X+Y}{X-Y} \Rightarrow(X-Y) d Y=(X+Y) d X\Rightarrow X d Y-Y d X=X d X+Y d Y\Rightarrow \int \frac{X d Y-Y d X}{X^2\left(1+\frac{Y^2}{X^2}\right)}=\int \frac{X d X+Y d Y}{X^2+Y^2}\begin{aligned} & \int d \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{Y}{X}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \int d\left(\log \left(X^2+Y^2\right)\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{Y}{X}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \log \left(X^2+Y^2\right)+C\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{y+1}{x}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \log \left(x^2+(y+1)^2\right)+\mathrm{C} \\ & \Rightarrow \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{y+1}{x}\right)-\frac{1}{2} \log \left(x^2+y^2+2 y+1\right)=\mathrm{C}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let $\mathrm{a}$ and $\mathrm{b}$ be arbitrary constants and $\mathrm{C}$ be a fixed constant. If $y=a e^{2 x}+b x e^{2 x}+C$ is the general solution of a differential equation, then the order of that differential equation is
questions.solution:
Given $y=a e^{2 x}+b x e^{2 x}+c$  ...(i)
$\Rightarrow \quad y_1=2 a e^{2 x}+b   \left[2 x e^{2 x}+e^{2 x}\right] ...(ii)
$\Rightarrow \quad y_2=4 a e^{2 x}+b   $\left[4 x e^{2 x}+4 e^{2 x}\right]$ ...(iii)
Now eliminating arbitrary constant $a, b$ from eqs (i), (ii) \& (iii), we get the require differential equations.
$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}y-c & -e^{2 x} & -x e^{2 x} \\ y_1 & -2 e^{2 x} & -(2 x+1) e^{2 x} \\ y_2 & -4 e^{2 x} & -(4 x+4) e^{2 x}\end{array}\right|=0$ ...(iv)
Since, here $\mathrm{c}$ is not a arbitrary constant, ' $\mathrm{c}$ ' is a fixed constant. Hence solving eq. (iv) will give a differential equation of second degree.

$\begin{aligned}& \Rightarrow\left|\begin{array}{ccc}y-c & 1 & x \\
y_1 & 2 & (2 x+1) \\
y_2 & 4 & (4 x+4)
\end{array}\right|=0\left\{\because \text{ dividing by }\left(-e^{2 x}\right)^2\right. \\
& \Rightarrow y_2+(8 x+4) y_1+4(y-c)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 2^{\text{nd }$}$\text{ order diff. Eq. }$
\end{aligned}

Option (d) can be written as

Which follows the standard form of linear differential equation.

$\Rightarrow \quad \cos y=\frac{1}{x^2}-0 \Rightarrow \cos y=\frac{1}{x^2}$

Given,

Here, $p=\sec ^2 x\Rightarrow \quad \int p d p=\int \sec ^2 x d x=\tan xI F=e^{\tan x}$
Multiplying Eq. (i) by $I F$, we get

Integrating both sides, we get

On putting $\tan x=t$,

If $y\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=1\Rightarrow \quad 1=1-1+C e^{-1} \Rightarrow 1=C e^{-1}\therefore \quad C=e$

questions.q:
Assertion (A) Order of the differential equations of a family of circles with constant radius is two.
Reason (R) An algebraic equation having two arbitrary constants is general solution of a second order differential equation.
options: $(\mathrm{A})$ and $(\mathrm{R})$ are true, $(\mathrm{R})$ is the correct explanation to $(A)$
(A) and (R) are false, $(R)$ is not the correct explanation to $(A)$
questions.solution:
Any circle with given radius can be written as, $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=a^2$ where $(h, k)$ be the centre of the circle which is variable. So, in above algebraic equation, there are two arbitrary constant $h$ and $k$. Hence, order of differential equation will be second order.
Hence, assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation to assertion.
