questions.q: If $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$ is a right angled isosceles triangle and $\angle \mathrm{C}=90^{{}^{\circ}}$, then $\mathrm{r}: \mathrm{r}_3=$

$\because A B C$ is isosceles triangle. $\therefore A C=B C$ and $\angle C=90^{{}^{\circ}}$ Let $A C=B C \Rightarrow a=b$
In $\triangle A B C$, $\begin{aligned} & c^2=a^2+b^2=a^2+a^2=2 a^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad c=a \sqrt{2} \end{aligned}$ Now, $\frac{r}{r_3}=\frac{\frac{\Delta}{s}}{\frac{\Delta}{s-c}}=\frac{s-c}{s}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{\frac{a+b+c}{2}-c}{\frac{a+b+c}{2}}=\frac{a+b-c}{a+b+c} \\ & =\frac{a+a-a \sqrt{2}}{a+a+a \sqrt{2}}=\frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{2+\sqrt{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{\sqrt{2}+1} \\ & \Rightarrow r: r_3=(\sqrt{2}-1):(\sqrt{2}+1) . \end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The difference of the slopes of the lines represented by
$\mathrm{y}^2-2 \mathrm{xysec}^2 \alpha+\left(3+\tan ^2 \alpha\right)\left(-1+\tan ^2 \alpha\right) \mathrm{x}^2=0 \text{ is } 4$
Reason (R): The difference of the slopes represented by
$a x^2+2 h x y+b y^2=0 \text{ is } \frac{2 \sqrt{h^2-a b}}{|b|}$
options: Both $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{R}$ are true and $\mathrm{R}$ is the correct explanation of $\mathrm{A}$
Both $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{R}$ are true but $\mathrm{R}$ is not correct explanation of $A$
A is true but $R$ is false
questions.solution:
Since the difference of the slopes of the lines $a x^2+2 h x y+b y^2=0$ is given by $\frac{2 \sqrt{h^2-a b}}{|b|}$ Now the given line is
$y^2-2 x y \sec ^2 \alpha+\left(3+\tan ^2 \alpha\right)\left(-1+\tan ^2 \alpha\right) x^2=0$
So the difference of slope is
$=\frac{2 \sqrt{\left(\sec ^2 \alpha\right)^2+\left(3+\tan ^2 \alpha\right)\left(\tan ^2 \alpha-1\right)}}{1}=2 \sqrt{\sec ^2 \alpha\left(\sec ^2 \alpha+3-\tan ^2 \alpha\right)}=2 \sqrt{4}=4$
So $\mathrm{a}$ is correct option.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The combined equation of the lines passing through the point $(3,4)$ and each making an angle $45^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the line $x+y+1=0$ is
questions.solution:
All the lines passing from pt $(3,4)$ is $(y-4)=m(x-3)$
where $m=$ slope
Slope of given line $x+y+1=0$ is $\frac{3 \pi}{4}$
Hence $m_1=\frac{3 \pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{4}=\pi$ and $m_2=\frac{3 \pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}$ will be the slopes of lines which make $\frac{\pi}{4}$ angle with $x+y+1=0$
When $m=m_1=\pi$ then equation of line is $y-4=0(x-3)\Rightarrow(y-4)=0$
When $m=m_2=\frac{\pi}{2}$ then equation of line is $y-4=\frac{1}{0}(x-3)\Rightarrow(x-3)=0$
Hence combined equation is $\rightarrow(x-3)(y-4)=0\Rightarrow x y-4 x-3 y+12=0$

questions.q: The equal sides of an isosceles triangle are given by equations $7 x-y+3=0$ and $x+y-3=0$. If the slope $m$ of the third side is an integer, then $\mathrm{m}=$
questions.solution:

$=\mathrm{k}(\sin \mathrm{B}+\sin \mathrm{C}) \cdot \operatorname{Sin}\left(\frac{\mathrm{A}}{2}\right)$
$\begin{aligned} & =\mathrm{k}\left[2 \sin \left(\frac{\mathrm{B}+\mathrm{C}}{2}\right) \cdot \cos \left(\frac{\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{C}}{2}\right)\right] \sin \left(\frac{\mathrm{A}}{2}\right) \\ & =\mathrm{k}\left[2 \sin \left(\frac{\pi+\mathrm{A}}{2}\right) \cdot \cos \left(\frac{\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{C}}{2}\right)\right] \sin \left(\frac{\mathrm{A}}{2}\right) \\ & =\mathrm{k}\left[2 \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\mathrm{A}}{2}\right) \cdot \cos \left(\frac{\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{C}}{2}\right)\right] \sin \left(\frac{\mathrm{A}}{2}\right) \\ & =\mathrm{k}\left[2 \sin \left(\frac{\mathrm{A}}{2}\right) \cdot \cos \left(\frac{\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{C}}{2}\right)\right] \sin \left(\frac{\mathrm{A}}{2}\right) \\ & =\mathrm{k} \operatorname{Sin} \mathrm{A} \cdot \cos \left(\frac{\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{C}}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$
$=\mathrm{a} \cos \left(\frac{\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{C}}{2}\right)$

questions.q: The least distance from origin to a point on the line $y = x + 3$ which lies at a distance of $2$ units from $\left(0, 3\right)$ is
questions.solution:
Let the point be& $\left(x, y\right)$~on the line& $y = x + 3$,

Now slope of the line is~$m = 1 ⇒ \theta = 45 °$,

Now given point is at~$2$~unit distance from point& $\left(0, 3\right)$

Now by parametric form we get,

$\dfrac{x - 0}{cos\theta} = \dfrac{y - 3}{sin\theta} = \pm 2$

$⇒ \dfrac{x - 0}{1\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{y - 3}{1\sqrt{2}} = \pm 2$~$\left\{\text{as}\theta = 45 °\right\}$

$⇒ x = \pm \sqrt{2} & y = \pm \sqrt{2} + 3$

Now distance from origin is given by~$D = \sqrt{\left(\pm \sqrt{2} - 0\right)2 + \left(\pm \sqrt{2} + 3 - 0\right)2}$

Taking positive sign we get,~$D = \sqrt{13 + 6\sqrt{2}}$

And taking negative sign we get,~$D = \sqrt{13 - 6\sqrt{2}}$

So least distance is~$D = \sqrt{13 - 6\sqrt{2}}$

questions.q: Starting from the point $A  \left(-3, 4\right)$, a moving object touches $2x + y - 7 = 0$ at $B$ and reaches the point $C  \left(0, 1\right)$. If the object travels along the shortest path, the distance between $A$ and $B$ is
questions.solution:
Given,

Point& $A \left(-3, 4\right)$ and& $C \left(0, 1\right)$ and let moving point be& $B \left(x, y\right)$

Now given equation of line $2x + y = 7 ⇒ y = - 2x + 7 . . . \left(1\right)$

Now finding distance we get, $AB + BC = \sqrt{\left(x + 3\right)2 + \left($ y - 4\right)2}$ + \sqrt{ \left($ x - 0\right)2 + $\left($ y - 1\right)2} . . . $\left(2\right)$

Now substituting the value of $y$ in& (2) we get,

$= \sqrt{\left(x + 3\right)2 + \left(- 2x + 7 - 4\right)2} + \sqrt{\left(x - 0\right)2 + \left(- 2x + 7 - 1\right)2}$

$= \sqrt{x^{2} + 9 + 6x + 4x^{2} + 9 - 12x} + \sqrt{x^{2} + 4x^{3} + 36 - 24x}$

$= \sqrt{5x^{2} - 6x + 18} + \sqrt{5x^{2} - 24x + 36}$

Now let $f\left(x\right) = \sqrt{5x^{2} - 6x + 18} + \sqrt{5x^{2} - 24x + 36}$

Now to get minimum value we will differentiate wrt $x$ we get,

$f^{'}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{10x - 6}{2\sqrt{5x^{2} - 6x + 18}} + \dfrac{10x - 24}{2\sqrt{5x^{2} - 24x + 36}}$

$⇒ f^{'}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{5x - 3}{5x^{2} - 6x + 18} + \dfrac{5x - 12}{5x^{2} - 24x + 36} =0$

$⇒ \dfrac{5x - 3}{5x^{2} - 6x + 18} = \dfrac{12 - 5x}{5x^{2} - 24x + 36}$

Now squaring on bothisdes we get,

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(5x - 3\right)2}{5x^{2} - 6x + 18} = \dfrac{\left(12 - 5x\right)2}{5x^{3} - 24x + 36}$

$⇒ \dfrac{25x^{2} + 9 - 30x}{5x^{2} - 6x + 18} = \dfrac{144 + 25x^{2} - 120x}{5x^{2} - 24x + 36}$

By solving the above equation we get $25x^{2} - 192x + 252 = 0$

As it is a quadratic equation, we get two values of $x$.

So, $x = \dfrac{+ 192 \pm \sqrt{\left(192\right)2 - 4\left(252\right)\left(25\right)}}{2\left(25\right)}$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{192 \pm \sqrt{11664}}{50}$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{192 \pm 108}{50}$

So, $x = \dfrac{192 + 108}{50}\text{or}\dfrac{192 - 108}{50}$

$⇒ x = 6\text{or}\dfrac{42}{25}$

So we will take $x = \dfrac{42}{25}$ as it is a smaller value and& we want minimum distance,

Then by substitute $x$ in the equation we get $y = \dfrac{91}{25}$

So, $B \left(x, y\right) = \left(\dfrac{42}{25}, \dfrac{91}{25}\right)

Now by distance formula we get $AB = $\dfrac{9\sqrt{170}}{25}$

questions.solution:
Given,

$\left[xcos\theta - y\right]\left[\left(cos\theta + tan\alpha\right)x - \left(1 - cos\theta \cdot tan\alpha\right)y\right] = 0$

Now taking line~${L}_{1} \to xcos\theta - y = 0$

And~${L}_{2} \to \left(cos\theta + tan\alpha\right)x - \left(1 - cos\theta \cdot tan\alpha\right)y = 0$

Now slope of line~${L}_{1}$~is& ${m}_{1} = cos\theta$~and slope of line& ${L}_{2}$~is& ${m}_{2} = \dfrac{cos\theta + tan\alpha}{1 - cos\theta . tan\alpha}$

Now we know that angle between two line is given by~$tanϕ = \left|\dfrac{{m}_{2} - {m}_{1}}{1 + {m}_{1}{m}_{2}}\right|$

$⇒ tan\phi = \left|\dfrac{\dfrac{cos\theta + tan\alpha}{1 - cos\theta . tan\alpha} - cos\theta}{1 + \dfrac{cos\theta + tan\alpha}{1 - cos\theta . tan\alpha} \times cos\theta}\right|$

$⇒ tan\phi = \left|\dfrac{cos\theta + tan\alpha - cos\theta + {cos}^{2}\theta . tan\alpha}{1 - cos\theta . tan\alpha + {cos}^{2}\theta + tan\alpha . cos\theta}\right|$

$⇒ tan\phi = \left|\dfrac{tan\alpha\left(1 + {cos}^{2}\theta\right)}{1 + {cos}^{2}\theta}\right|$

$⇒ tan\phi = tan\alpha$

$⇒ \phi = \alpha$

either in first or in third quadrant
questions.solution:
Let the point $P(h, k)$ lie on the line $3 x+5 y=15$
Distance from coordinate axes are equal from $P$.
$\therefore \quad|h|=|k|\Rightarrow \quad h= \pm k$
Point $P$ line of $3 x+5 y=153 h+5 k=15 \Rightarrow 3 h+5 h=15\Rightarrow \quad h=15 / 8 \Rightarrow k=15 / 8$
Put $k=-h$,
$3 h-5 h=15=h=\frac{-15}{2}, k=\frac{15}{2} \left(\frac{15}{8}, \frac{15}{8}\right) lie in first quadrant and \left(\frac{-15}{2}, \frac{15}{2}\right) ie in second quadrant.
\therefore P$ lies in the first or in second quadrant.

questions.q: If one of the lines given by the equation $2 x^2+a x y+3 y^2=0$ coincide with one of those given by the equation $2 x^2+b x y-3 y^2=0$, while the other two lines are perpendicular to each other, then the values of $a$ and $b$ are
questions.solution:
Given, equation of pair of straight line
$2 x^2+a x y+3 y^2=0$
and $2 x^2+b x y-3 y^2=0$
Let the slope of line $m$ and $m_1$ of the equation
$2 x^2+a x y+3 y^2=0\therefore \quad m+m_1=\frac{-a}{3}$ and $m m_1=\frac{2}{3}$
Slope of the other line is $m$ and $m_2$.
Then, $m+m_2=\frac{b}{3}$ and $m m_2=-2 / 3$
Given, $\quad m_1 m_2=-1$...(i)
$\therefore \quad \frac{m m_1}{m m_2}=-1\Rightarrow \quad m_1=-m_2\Rightarrow \quad m_1+m_2=0$...(ii)
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$m_1=1$ and $m_2=-1\therefore \quad m=2 / 3m+m_1=-a / 3\Rightarrow \quad \frac{2}{3}+1=-a / 3 \Rightarrow a=-5$
and $m+m_2=b / 3\Rightarrow \quad \frac{2}{3}-1=b / 3 \Rightarrow b=-1\therefore \quad a=-5$ and $b=-1$

( y-2)=m(x-1) \text{$ and $} m & =\tan \theta\\

questions.solution:

Given, $\theta=45^{{}^{\circ}}$, then $x=\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $y=\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}$
Putting value of $x and y$ in Eq. (i), we get $\begin{aligned}& 3\left(\frac{X}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{Y}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2+3\left(\frac{X}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{Y}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 \\
& +2\left(\frac{X}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{Y}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{X}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{Y}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=2 \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{3}{2}( X-Y)^2+\frac{3}{2}( X+Y)^2+\left( X^2-Y²\right)=2 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{3}{2}\left[2 X²+2 Y²\right]+X²-Y²=2 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 3 X²+3 Y²+X²-Y²=2 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 4 X²+2 Y²=2 \\
& \text{$ or $}\\
& 2 X²+Y²=1 \\
&
\end{aligned}$\therefore$ Transformed equation is 2 x^2+y^2=1$

questions.q: A point moves so that the sum of its distances from $( ae, 0 )$ and $( - ae, 0 )$ is $2a$, then the equaton to its locus where $b^{2} = a^{2}  \left(1 - e^{2}\right)& is$
questions.solution:
Suppose that the co-ordinates of the moving point be $\left(x, y\right),$then from the given condition

$\sqrt{\left[{\left(x - ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right]} + \sqrt{\left[{\left(x + ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right]} = 2a . . . . . \left(1\right)$

Now

$\left[{\left(x - ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right] - \left[{\left(x + ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right] = - 4aex . . . . \left(2\right)$

$\left[∵ {\left(a - b\right)}^{2} - {\left(a + b\right)}^{2} = - 4ab\right]$

On dividing $\left(2\right)$by $\left(1\right)$, we get

$\dfrac{\left[{\left(x - ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right] - \left[{\left(x + ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right]}{\sqrt{\left[{\left(x - ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right]} + \sqrt{\left[{\left(x + ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right]}} = \dfrac{- 4aex}{2a}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{\left[\sqrt{{\left(x - ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}}\right]}^{2} - {\left[\sqrt{{\left(x + ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}}\right]}^{2}}{\sqrt{\left[{\left(x - ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right]} + \sqrt{\left[{\left(x + ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right]}} = - 2ex$

$⇒ \sqrt{\left[{\left(x - ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right]} - \sqrt{\left[{\left(x + ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right]} = - 2ex . . . . . . \left(3\right)$

Adding $\left(1\right)$and $\left(3\right)$ we get

$2\sqrt{\left[{\left(x - ae\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right]} = 2\left(a - ex\right) .$

Squaring on both sides, we get

${x}^{2} - 2aex + {a}^{2}{e}^{2} + {y}^{2} = {a}^{2} - 2aex + {e}^{2}{x}^{2}$

 $⇒ {x}^{2}\left(1 - {e}^{2}\right) + {y}^{2} = {a}^{2}\left(1 - {e}^{2}\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}\left(1 - {e}^{2}\right)} = 1$

$∴ \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1$

Let $ABCD$ be a square where A ≡ $\left(1, 3\right)$ & $C ≡ \left(7, 5\right).

when $m = - \dfrac{1}{2}$

questions.q: The distance of the point $\left(1, 2\right)$ from the line $x + y + 5 = 0$ measured along the line parallel to $3x - y = 7$& is equal to
questions.solution:
Let the equation of the line parallel to $3x - y = 7$~be $3x - y = \lambda$.

Since, it passes through $\left(1, 2\right)$, this point will satisfy the equation~$3x - y = \lambda$.

$∴ 3 - 2 = \lambda$

$⇒ \lambda = 1$

So, the line is $3x - y = 1$.

Now,~$\left(x + y + 5\right) + \left(3x - y\right) = 0 + 1 ⇒ 4x = - 4 ⇒ x = - 1$.

Putting in~$x + y + 5 = 0,$~we get

$y = - x - 5 = 1 - 5 = - 4$

So, the point of intersection of~$x + y + 5 = 0$~and $3x - y = 1$~is $\left(- 1, - 4\right)$.

The required distance is the distance between~$\left(1, 2\right) and \left(- 1, - 4\right).

By distance formula,

the required distance~$= \sqrt{$\left\{1 - \left(- 1\right)$\right\}2 + $\left\{2 - \left(- 4\right)\right\}2}= \sqrt{\left(2\right)2 + \left(6\right)2} = \sqrt{4 + 36} = \sqrt{40}$.

Equation of line passing through $\left(2{cos}^{3}\theta, 2{sin}^{3}\theta\right)$& perpendicular to line $\left(1\right)$ is$

$y - 2{sin}^{3}\theta = $\dfrac{- sin\theta}{cos\theta}\left(x - 2{cos}^{3}\theta\right)

$⇒ ycos\theta - 2{sin}^{3}\theta . cos\theta = - xsin\theta + 2{cos}^{3}\theta . sin\theta$

$⇒ xsin\theta + ycos\theta = 2{cos}^{3}\theta . sin\theta + 2{sin}^{3}\theta . cos\theta$

$⇒ xsin\theta + ycos\theta = 2sin\theta . cos\theta $\left({cos}^{2}\theta + {sin}^{2}\theta\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{xsin\theta}{sin\theta . cos\theta} + \dfrac{ycos\theta}{sin\thetacos\theta} =2$

$∴ xsec\theta + ycosec\theta = 2$

questions.solution:

questions.q: A line has slope $m$ and $y$-intercept 4. The distance between the origin and the line is equal to
questions.solution:
Given, the& line with slope& $m$~and& $y$~intercept& $4$.

As we know~by the slope-intercept form of a line, a line with a slope& $m$~and& $y$~intercept& $c$, the equation of the line is~$y = mx + c$.

$⇒$The equation of the line is $y = mx + 4$.

Also, the~distance between a point& $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)$~and a line& $ax + by + c = 0$~is given by& $\left|\dfrac{a{x}_{1} + b{y}_{1} + c}{a^{2} + b^{2}}\right|$~units.

$∴$~The& distance between origin and the line& $y = mx + 4$~$= \dfrac{4}{1 + m^{2}}$.

questions.q: The equation of the base of an equilateral triangle is $x + y = 2$ and one vertex is $( 2, - 1 )$, then the length of the side of the triangle is
questions.solution:
Let,& $∆ ABC,$~be the triangle, with side& $BC$~as& $x + y = 2,$~and vertex& $A$~as& $\left(2, - 1\right) .

The length$ of perpendicular from the point~$\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)$~to the line& $ax + by + c = 0$~is& $\left|a{x}_{1} + b{y}_{1} + c\right|\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}} .

Hence,$ the length of altitude~AM = $\left|\dfrac{2 - 1 - 2}{{1}^{2} + {1}^{2}}\right|$

$⇒ AM = \dfrac{1}{2} .

We know that,$ in an equilateral triangle, altitude, median, angle bisector all are same.

Hence,~AM$~is also the median, thus& $MC = $\dfrac{1}{2}$BC = $\dfrac{1}{2}$AC .

Now, in~$∆ AMC,$~by Pythagoras theorem& $AC^{2} = AM^{2} + MC^{2}$

$⇒ AC^{2} = AM^{2} + \dfrac{1}{4}AC^{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{3}{4}AC^{2} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)2$

$⇒ \dfrac{3}{4}AC^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ AC = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}} .

Thus, the $side of the equilateral triangle is~\sqrt{$\dfrac{2}{3}}$.

$⇒ \dfrac{a\left({cos}^{2}\theta - {sin}^{2}\theta\right)\left({cos}^{2}\theta + {sin}^{2}\theta\right)}{sin\thetacos\theta} = - k$

Using~${cos}^{2}\theta + {sin}^{2}\theta = 1, {cos}^{2}\theta - {sin}^{2}\theta = cos2\theta,$

questions.q: If the orthocenter of the triangle formed by the lines $2x + 3y - 1 = 0, x + 2y + 1 = 0$ and $ax + by - 1 = 0$ lies at origin, then $\dfrac{1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{b} =$
questions.solution:
We have triangle $∆ ABC$

$AB: 2x + 3y - 1 = 0 . . . \left(1\right)$

Slope ${m}_{1} = - \dfrac{2}{3}$

$BC: x + 2y + 1 = 0 . . . \left(2\right)$

Slope ${m}_{2} = - \dfrac{1}{2}$

$CA: ax + by - 1 = 0 . . . \left(3\right)$

Slope ${m}_{3} = - \dfrac{a}{b}$

We know, the orthocenter of a triangle is the point of intersection of altitudes passing through the vertices of the triangle.

Here we have altitudes $AD, BEandCF$

So, the family of line passing through the vertex $B$,

is, $\left(2x + 3y - 1\right) + \lambda\left(x + 2y + 1\right) = 0 . . . \left(4\right)$

As, the orthocentre is origin,

Substituting $\left(x = 0andy = 0\right)$ in $\left(4\right)$, we get $\lambda = 1$,

So, the equation of altitude $BE$ is $3x + 5y = 0 . . . \left(5\right)$

Slope ${m}_{BE} = - \dfrac{3}{5}$

As, $BE ⊥ AC$

So, the product of slopes of $BE$ and side $AC = - 1$

$⇒ \left(- \dfrac{a}{b}\right) \times \left(- \dfrac{3}{5}\right) = - 1 ⇒ 3a = - 5b . . . \left(6\right)$

And, the family of lines passing through the vertex $A$ is, 

$\left(2x + 3y - 1\right) + \mu\left(ax + by - 1\right) = 0 . . . \left(7\right)$

As, the orthocentre is origin,

Substituting $\left(x = 0andy = 0\right)$ in $\left(7\right)$, we get, $\mu = - 1$

So, the equation of altitude $AD$ is $\left(2 - a\right)x + \left(3 - b\right)y = 0 . . . \left(8\right)$

As, $AD$ $⊥$side $BC$.

So, product of their slopes$= - 1$

$\left(- \dfrac{2 - a}{3 - b}\right) \times \left(- \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = - 1 ⇒ \dfrac{2 - a}{2\left(3 - b\right)} = - 1 ⇒ a + 2b = 8 . . . \left(9\right)$

Solving equations $\left(6\right)$ and $\left(9\right)$, we get

$a = - 40andb = - 24$.

Hence, $\dfrac{1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{b} = - \dfrac{1}{40} + \dfrac{1}{24} = \dfrac{1}{60}$

questions.solution:
The given line is& $ax + by + c = 0$.~

Since& $a, b$~and& $c$~are three consecutive odd integers, so they are in arithmetic progression,

$⇒ b - a = c - b$

$⇒ c = 2b - a$

Hence, the equation of line is~$ax + by + 2b - a = 0$

$⇒ a\left(x - 1\right) + b\left(y + 2\right) = 0$.

Now, the is given that the line always pass through point~$\left(\alpha, \beta\right)$

$⇒ a\left(\alpha - 1\right) + b\left(\beta + 2\right) = 0$

This is only possible when,~$\left(\alpha - 1\right) = 0$~and& $\left(\beta + 2\right) = 0$

$⇒ \alpha = 1$~and& $\beta = - 2$

$⇒ {α}^{2} + {β}^{2} = {1}^{2} + \left(- 2\right)2 = 5$

(i), we have C_1+C_2=-\frac{2 f}{b} \text{ and }$ m_1 C_2+m_2 C_1=$\frac{2 g}{b}$ and $C_1 C_2=\frac{c}{b} and m_1 m_2=\frac{9}{b} \begin{aligned}& \therefore\left| C_1-C_2\right|=\sqrt{\frac{4 f^2}{b^2}-\frac{4 c}{b}}=2 \sqrt{\frac{f^2-b c}{b^2}}=\frac{2}{|b|} \sqrt{f^2-b c}\\
& \text{ and }\left| C_2 m_1-C_1 m_2\right|=\sqrt{\frac{4 g^2}{b^2}-4 \frac{a c}{b^2}}=\frac{2}{|b|} \sqrt{g^2-a c}
\end{aligned}$ Therefore from Eq. (ii), we have $\begin{aligned}& -\frac{2 f}{b} \times \frac{2}{|b|} \sqrt{f^2-b c}=\frac{2 g}{b} \times \frac{2}{|b|} \sqrt{g^2-a c}\\
\Rightarrow & f²\left( f^2-b c\right)=g²\left( g^2-a c\right)\text{ (on squaring both sides) }\\
\Rightarrow & f⁴-g⁴=c\left( b f²-a g²\right)
\end{aligned}
$

$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of possible straight lines passing through the point $(2,3)$, while forming a triangle with coordinate axes enclosing an area 12 sq. units is
questions.solution:
Let the equation of line forming a triangle having area $12 \mathrm{sq}$. units is

$\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=$1

So,

|a b|=24

$\because$ Line (i) passes through point $(2,3)$, so

$\frac{2}{a}+\frac{3}{b}=$1

from Eqs. (ii) and (iii), we get

|2 b+3 a|=24

If $a$ and $b$ are positive, then

$\begin{array}{rlrl}$& & a b=24 $\text{ and }$3 a+2 b=24 \\
\Rightarrow & a$\left(\frac{24-3 a}{2}\right)=$24 \\
\Rightarrow & 3 a²-24 a+48=0 \\
& \because $\text{ Discriminant }=$24^2-4 $\times$3 $\times$48=0 \\
\therefore & a=4 $\text{ and }$b=6
\end{array}

If $a$ is positive and $b$ is negative then $a b=-24$ and $3 a+2 b=24$.

\Rightarrow \quad 2$\left(\frac{24-3 a}{2}\right)=-$24 \Rightarrow 3 a²-24 a-48=0

$\because$ Discriminant $=24^2+4 \times 3 \times 48 \gt 0$
$\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore \quad$a=$\frac{24 \pm \sqrt{2 \times 24^2}}{6}=$4+4 $\sqrt{2} \quad \because$a>0 \\
$\text{ and } \quad$b=6-6 $\sqrt{2}
\end{array}$If $a$ is negative and $b$ is positive, then $a b=-24$ and $3 a+2 b=24$
\Rightarrow \quad a=4-4 $\sqrt{2} \text{ and }$b=6+6 $\sqrt{2}$And at the last it is not possible that $a$ and $b$ both are negative.
So, 3 triangles are possible.

questions.q: The equation of the line through the point $(-1,3)$ in symmetrical form, when the angle made by the line with the positive direction of $X$-axis is $120^{{}^{\circ}}$, is given by
questions.solution:

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The equation of the circle circumscribing the triangle formed by the straight lines \(x+y=6\). \(2 x+y=4\) and \(x+2 y=5\) is given by
questions.solution:
Equation of circle circumscribing the triangle formed by the straight lines, \(x+y=6,2 x+y=4\) and \(x+2 y=5\) is
$\begin{aligned}& (x+y-6)(2 x+y-4)+\lambda(2 x+y-4)(x+2 y-5) \\
& +\mu(x+2 y-5)(x+y-6)=0
\end{aligned}$\(\because\)$ For $a circle the coefficients of terms \(x²\) and \(y²\) must be equal and non-zero and coefficient of \(x y\) must be zero.
\(\therefore\) Coefficient of \(x²=\) coefficient of \(y²\)
\(\Rightarrow 2+2 \lambda+\mu=1+2 \lambda+2 \mu \Rightarrow \mu=1\)
and coefficient of \(x y=0\)
\(\Rightarrow 1+2+4 \lambda+\lambda+\mu+2 \mu=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=-6 / 5 \text{. }\)
So, equation of required circle is$\begin{array}{ll}
( x+y-6)(2 x+y-4)-\frac{6}{5}(2$ x+y-4)(x+2 y-5)+(x+2 y-5)(x+y-6)=0 \\
\Rightarrow 5(x+y-6)(3 x+3 y-9)-6(2 x+y-4)(x+2 y-5)=0 \\
\Rightarrow 5(x+y-6)(x+y-3)-2(2 x+y-4)(x+2 y-5)=0
\end{array}$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow& 5 \left(x^2+x y-3 x+x y+y²-3 y-6 x-6 y+18\right) \\
& -2\left(2 x²+4 x y-10 x+x y+2 y²-5 y-4 x\right. \\
\Rightarrow & x²+y²-45 x-45 y+90+28 x+26 y-40=0 \\
\Rightarrow & x²+y²-17 x-19 y+50=0
\end{aligned}\)
Hence, option (b) is correct.$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: In quadrilateral \(A B C D, \mathbf{A B}=\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{B C}=\mathbf{b}\), \(\mathbf{A D}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}\) if \(M\) is the midpoint of \(B C\) and \(N\) is a point on \(D M\) such that \(D N=\left(\frac{4}{5}\right) D M\), then \(5 \mathbf{A N}=\)
questions.solution:
It is given that for a quadrilateral \(A B C D\),
\(\mathbf{A B}=\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{B C}=\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{A D}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}\)
\(\therefore\) According to the question, \(\mathbf{B M}=\frac{\mathbf{b}}{2}\) and
\(\begin{aligned}
& \frac{D N}{N M}=\frac{4}{1} \quad\left\{\because D N=\left(\frac{4}{5}\right) D M \text{ given }\right\} \\
& \therefore \quad \mathbf{A N}-\mathbf{A D}=\frac{4}{1}(\mathbf{A M}-\mathbf{A N}) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 5 \mathrm{AN}=4 \mathbf{A M}+\mathbf{A D}=4\left(\mathbf{a}+\frac{\mathbf{b}}{2}\right)+(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\
& =4 \mathbf{a}+2 \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}=3(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})=3 \mathbf{A C} \\
\end{aligned}\)
Hence, option (c) is correct.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The equation of the line through the point \((2,3)\) such that its \(x\)-intercept is twice its \(y\)-intecept is..........

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the length of the intercept made on the line \(y=a x\) by the lines \(y=2\) and \(y=6\) is less than 5
questions.solution:
The point of intersection of lines \(y=a x\) and \(y=2\) is \(A\left(\frac{2}{a}, 2\right)\) and of the lines \(y=a x\) and \(y=6\) is \(B\left(\frac{6}{a}, 6\right)\), so

& A B=\sqrt{\left(\frac{6}{a}-\frac{2}{a}\right)^2+(6-2)^2}  < 5  \quad \text{(given)} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{16}{a^2}+16 < 25 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad a^2 > \frac{16}{9} \Rightarrow a \in\left(-\infty,-\frac{4}{3}\right) \cup\left(\frac{4}{3}, \infty\right) \\
\end{aligned}\)
(given)
Hence, option (d) is correct.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If \(3 a+5 b+6 c=0\) then the family of lines \(a x+b y+c=0\) pass through the fixed point
questions.solution:
Given equation of family of lines
\(\begin{aligned}
& a x+b y+c=0 \\
& \because \quad 3 a+5 b+6 c=0, \text{ so }a x+b y-\frac{3 a+5 b}{6}=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 3 a(2 x-1)+b(6 y-5)=0
\end{aligned}\)
So, the family of lines passes through the fixed point \ $\left(\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{5}{6}\right)$.
Hence, option (d) is correct.

questions.q: Find the equation of the right bisector of the line segment joining the points \((3,4)\) and \((-1,2)\).
questions.solution:
The right angle bisector of the line segment joining points \(A(3,4)\) and \(B(-1,2)\) passes through the mid-point of \(A\) and \(B\) perpendicular to line segment \(A B\).
Now, the mid-point of \(A(3,4)\) and \(B(-1,2)\) is
\(M\left(\frac{3-1}{2}, \frac{4+2}{2}\right)=M(1,3)\)
and slope of right angle bisector is \(=-\frac{3-(-1)}{4-2}=-2\)
\(\therefore\) Equation of required right angle bisector is
\begin{aligned} y-3 & =-2(x-1) \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2 x+y & =5 $\text{$ or } 2 x+y-5=0
\end{aligned}
Hence, option (a) is correct.

questions.q: The equation of the line through the intersection of \(3 x-4 y+1\) and \(5 x+y-1=0\) which cuts off equal intercepts on the axes is given by
questions.solution:
Equation of family of lines passes through the intersection of lines \(3 x-4 y+1=0\) and \(5 x+y-1=0\) is

questions.q: Maximum area of the rectangle that can be formed with the fixed perimeter ' \(p\) ' \($\mathrm{cm}$\)
questions.solution:
Let length of adjacent sides of rectangle is \(x $\mathrm{~cm}$ and \(y $\mathrm{~cm}$ so perimeter of rectangle is \(p=2(x+y) $\mathrm{cm}$ and the area \(A=x y $\mathrm{~cm}^$2\)

questions.q: If the lines \(3 x+y-2=0, p x+2 y-3=0\) and \(2 x-y-3=0\) are concurrent, then \(p=\)

\(3 x+y-2=0, p x+2 y-3=0\) and \(2 x-y-3=0\)
are concurrent, so
\(\begin{array}{lll} \left|\begin{array}{rrr}3 \text{ and } 1 \text{ and } -2 \\
p \text{ and } 2 \text{ and } -3 \\
2 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } -3

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The locus of a point \(P\) such that \(P A+P B=4\) where \(A(2,3,4), B(-2,3,4)\) is
questions.solution:
Given points are \(A(2,3,4)\) and \(B(-2,3,4)\) and \(A B=4\).
Now let point \(P(x, y, z)\), such that \(P A+P B=4=A B\) means point \(P\) is collinear with points \(A\) and \(B\) and lies between them, so
$\begin{array}{ll}& \frac{x-2}{2+2}=\frac{y-3}{3-3}=\frac{z-4}{4-4}\\
\Rightarrow & y-3=0=z-4 \\
\text{or }& (y-3)^2+(z-4)^2=0 \\
\Rightarrow & y²+z²-6 y-8 z+25=0

Hence, option (c) is correct.

Hence, option (a) is correct.$

questions.solution:

+17(x-2)-7(y-3)-11=0 \\

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: A straight line \(L_1\) passing through \(A(3,1)\) meets the coordinate axes at \(P\) and \(Q\) such that its distance from the origin \(O\) is maximum. Then area of \(\triangle O P Q\) is sq. units

\(A=(3,1)\) Let slope of line be \(m\) $\begin{array}{ll} \therefore \quad& y-y_1=m\left(x-x_1\right)\quad \text{ [be the required line] }\\ & y-1=m(x-3) \end{array}$\) $\begin{aligned}& y-1=m x-3 m \\ & m x-y+(1-3 m)=0 \quad \ldots (i) \end{aligned}$ \)
The greatest distance of line from origin passes through \(A(3,1)\) is perpendicular to the given line. \(\therefore \quad O A \perp P Q\) Slope of \(O A \times\) Slope of \$(\mathrm{PQ}=-$1\) \$(\frac{1}{3} \timesm=-$1 \Rightarrow m=-3\) Put, \(m=-3\) in Eq. (i), $\begin{aligned} -3 x-y+(1-3)(-3) & =0 \\ -3 x-y+(10) & =0 \\ 3 x+y+10 & =0 \end{aligned}$ \) \(\therefore\) Area of \(\triangle P O $Q=\frac{1}{2}\left|\frac{c^2}{a b}\right|=\frac{1}{2}\left|\frac{100}{3 \times 1}\right|=\frac{50}{3} \mathrm{sq}$\) units. Hence, option (c) is correct.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If a diagonal of a square is along the line \(8 x-15 y=0\) and one of its vertices is \((1,2)\), then the equations of the sides of the square passing through this vertex are
questions.solution:
Equation of line passes through point \((1,2)\) and inclined with an angle \(45^{{}^{\circ}}\) with respect to line \(8 x-15 y=0\), because sides of a square inclined with diagonal at \(45^{{}^{\circ}}\), is

Let the point \(P\) on the straight line \(x+y=4\), so

questions.solution:
Given equation is
\begin{aligned}& & 4 x²+9 y²-8 x+36 y+4 & =0 \\
\Rightarrow & & 4(x-1)^2+9(y+2)^2 & =36 \\
\Rightarrow & & $\frac{(x-1)^2}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^2}{4}$& =1
\end{aligned}
If we shift the origin to \((l,-2)\), the equation reduce to \(\frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1\) and it is free from \(x\) and \(y\) terms.

questions.q: Given that lines \(L_1: y=m_a x, L_2: y=m_b x\) and \(L_3: y=m_c x\) make equal intercepts on the line \(x+y=1\), then
questions.solution:
Since, the point of intersecting of given lines \(L_1: y=m_a x, L_2: y=m_b x\) and \(L_3: y=m_c x\) with line \(x+y=1\) are
$\begin{aligned}
& A\left(\frac{1}{1+m_a}, \frac{m a}{1+m_a}\right), B\left(\frac{1}{1+m_b}, \frac{m_b}{1+m_b}\right) \text{$ and $} \\
& C\left(\frac{1}{1+m_c}, \frac{m_c}{1+m_c}\right) \text{ respectively. }
\end{aligned}\)
It is given that,
\(A B=B C \Rightarrow A B^2=B C^2\)
\(\begin{gathered}
\Rightarrow\left(\frac{1}{1+m_a}-\frac{1}{1+m_b}\right)^2+\left(\frac{m_a}{1+m_a}-\frac{m_b}{1+m_b}\right)^2 \\
=\left(\frac{1}{1+m_b}-\frac{1}{1+m_c}\right)^2+\left(\frac{m_b}{1+m_b}-\frac{m_c}{1+m_c}\right)^2 \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\left(m_b-m_a\right)^2}{\left(1+m_a\right)^2\left(1+m_b\right)^2}+\frac{\left(m_a-m_b\right)^2}{\left(1+m_a\right)^2\left(1+m_b\right)^2} \\
=\frac{\left(m_c-m_b\right)^2}{\left(1+m_b\right)^2\left(1+m_c\right)^2}+\frac{\left(m_b-m_c\right)^2}{\left(1+m_b\right)^2\left(1+m_c\right)^2} \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2 \frac{\left(m_a-m_b\right)^2}{\left(1+m_a\right)^2\left(1+m_b\right)^2}=2 \frac{\left(m_b-m_c\right)^2}{\left(1+m_b\right)^2\left(1+m_c\right)^2} \\
\Rightarrow \quad\left(m_a-m_b\right)\left(1+m_c\right)=\left(m_b-m_c\right)\left(1+m_a\right) \\
\Rightarrow \quad\left[\left(1+m_a\right)-\left(1+m_b\right)\right]\left(1+m_c\right) =\left[\left(1+m_b\right)-\left(1+m_c\right)\right]\left(1+m_a\right) \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2\left(1+m_a\right)\left(1+m_c\right)=\left(1+m_b\right)\left(1+m_c+1+m_a\right) \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2\left(1+m_a\right)\left(1+m_c\right)=\left(1+m_b\right)\left(2+m_a+m_c\right)
\end{gathered}\)$

Centroid is given by

So, \(x=\frac{1+a \cos t+b \sin t}{3}\)

\(\Rightarrow(3 x-1)=a \cos t+b \sin t\)...(i)

 $\begin{aligned}& 9 x²-6 x+1+9 y²=a²+b² \\

After rotation of coordinate axes about the origin in the positive direction through on angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}$, the new coordinates are \((X, Y)\) have relation with older coordinates \((x, y)\) is

\(\begin{aligned}
& $25 $\left(\frac{X-Y}{\sqrt{2}}\rright)^$2+9 $\left(\frac{X+Y}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2=$225 \\

& \Rightarrow 17 X²+17 Y²-16 X Y=225
\end{aligned}\)
On comparing, we get
$(\begin{aligned}$& \alpha=\gamma=17, \beta=-16 $\text{$ and } \delta=225 \\
& \$therefore(\alpha+\beta+\$gamma-\sqrt{\delta})^$2$\\

& =3^2=9
\end{aligned}\)
Hence, option (2) is correct.

\(A(2,3,5)\) and \(D\left(\frac{\alpha+7}{2},4, \frac{3+\beta}{2}\right)\) is
\(\left(\frac{\alpha+3}{2},1, \frac{\beta-7}{2}\right)\).
\(\because\) The line segment \(A D\) is equally inclined with the co-ordinate axes, so
$\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{\alpha+3}{2}= 1=\frac{\beta-7}{2}$\\
& \Rightarrow \quad \alpha=-1 $\text{$ and } \beta=9 \\
& \therefore$\cos ^{-1}\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right)=\cos ^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{9}\right)\end{aligned}$
Hence, option (1) is correct.

questions.q: If the system of linear equations given by $x + y + z = 3, 2x + 2y - z = 3, x + y - z = 1$ is consistent and if~$\left({x}_{0}, {y}_{0}, {z}_{0}\right)$ is a solution, then $2{x}_{0} + 2{y}_{0} + {z}_{0} =$
questions.solution:
Given,

$x + y + z = 3... \left(i\right)

$2x + 2y - z = 3... $\left(ii\right)$

$x + y - z = 1... \left(iii\right)

Adding, we get

$x + y = 2... $\left(iv\right)$

Substituting this value of $\left(x + y\right)$ in& $\left(i\right)$, we get

$z = 1$

Now, if $\left({x}_{0}, {y}_{0}, {z}_{0}\right)$ is the solution then ${x}_{0} + {y}_{0} = 2 & {z}_{0} = 1$.

Then,

$2{x}_{0} + 2{y}_{0} + {z}_{0} = 2\left({x}_{0} + {y}_{0}\right) + {z}_{0}

$= 2 \times$2 + 1 = 5$.

questions.q: Let $A, B$ and $C$ be three points in a plane. The locus of a point $P$ moving such that $PA^{2} + PB^{2} = 2PC^{2}$ is a
questions.solution:
We have $A, B$ and $C$ be three points in a plane.

Let

$A ≡ \left(0, 1\right), B ≡ \left(1, 0\right) \text{ and } C ≡ \left(- 1, 0\right)$

Let $P\left(x, y\right)$ be any variable point. Then we have

$P{A}^{2} + P{B}^{2} = 2P{C}^{2}$

$⇒ {\left[\sqrt{{\left(x - 0\right)}^{2} + {\left(y - 1\right)}^{2}}\right]}^{2} + {\left[\sqrt{{\left(x - 1\right)}^{2} + {\left(y - 0\right)}^{2}}\right]}^{2} = 2{\left[\sqrt{{\left(x + 1\right)}^{2} + {\left(y - 0\right)}^{2}}\right]}^{2}$

$⇒ {x}^{2} + {\left(y - 1\right)}^{2} + {\left(x - 1\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2} = 2\left\{{\left(x + 1\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right\}$

$⇒ 6x + 2y = 0$

It is a linear equation. Hence, locus of point $P\left(x, y\right)$ is a straight line.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: When the coordinate axes are rotated by an angle $\tan^{-1} \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right) about the origin, then the equation $ x^{2} + y^{2} = 9$ is transformed to the equation$
questions.solution:
Let& $\theta$ be& the angle of rotation, then& $\theta = {tan}^{- 1} \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right).

Now, new coordinate axes are

$ X = xcos$\theta -$ ysin$\theta

$ Y = xsin$\theta +$ ycos$\theta

Then,

$ X = xcos$\left$\{{tan}^{- 1}$\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\right$\} - ysin$\left$\{{tan}^{- 1}$\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\right$\}$

$Y = xsin$\left$\{{tan}^{- 1}$\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\right$\} + ycos$\left$\{{tan}^{- 1} $\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\right\}$

Or

$X = x\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right) - y\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)$

$Y = x \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) +y \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)

On solving, we get

$x = $\dfrac{4X + 3Y}{5}

$ y = $\dfrac{4Y - 3X}{5}

Now, putting these values in $ x^{2} + y^{2} = 9$, we get

\dfrac{\left(4X + 3Y\right)2}{25} + \dfrac{\left(4Y - 3X\right)2}{25} =9$

or $X^{2} + Y^{2} = 9$

questions.q: Let& $a, b$ and $c$ be distinct and none of them is equal to $1$. If the lines $x + ay + a = 0 bx + y + b = 0$ and $cx + cy + 1 = 0$ are concurrent, then the value of $\dfrac{a}{a - 1} + \dfrac{b}{b - 1} + \dfrac{c}{c - 1}$ is
questions.solution:
We know that, three lines

${a}_{1}x + {b}_{1}y + {c}_{1} = 0$

${a}_{2}x + {b}_{2}y + {c}_{2} = 0$

${a}_{3}x + {b}_{3}y + {c}_{3} = 0$

are concurrent if

$\left|\begin{cases}{a}_{1} & {b}_{1} & {c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{2} \\ {a}_{3} & {b}_{3} & {c}_{3}\end{cases}\right| = 0$

Therefore, given lines are concurrent if

$\left|\begin{cases}1 & a & a \\ b & 1 & b \\ c & c & 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

Expanding along ${R}_{1}$, we have

$1\left(1 - bc\right) - a \left(b - bc\right) + a \left($ bc - c\right) = 0$

or $ab + bc + ca = 1 + 2abc . . . $\left($ i\right)$

Now,

\dfrac{a}{a - 1} + \dfrac{b}{b - 1} + \dfrac{c}{c - 1}$

$= \dfrac{a\left(b - 1\right)\left(c - 1\right) + b\left(a - 1\right)\left(c - 1\right) + c\left(a - 1\right)\left(b - 1\right)}{\left(a - 1\right)\left(b - 1\right)\left(c - 1\right)}$

$= \dfrac{3abc + \left(a + b + c\right) - 2\left(ab + bc + ca\right)}{1 - \left(a + b + c\right) + \left($ ab + bc + ca\right) - abc}$

Substituting the value of $ab + bc + ca$ from& \left($ i\right)$, we get

\dfrac{3abc + \left(a + b + c\right) - 2 - 4abc}{1 - \left(a + b + c\right) + 1 + 2abc - abc}$

$= \dfrac{- abc + \left(a + b + c\right) - 2}{2 - \left(a + b + c\right) + abc}$

$= - \left$\${\dfrac{abc - \left(a + b + c\right) + 2}{abc - \left(a + b + c\right) + 2}\right\}

$= - 1$

questions.q: If $ad - bc \ne 0,$ then the area (in sq. units) of the parallelogram formed by the lines $ax + by + 2 = 0, ax + by + 5 = 0, cx + dy + 3 = 0$ and $cx + dy + 7 = 0$ is
questions.solution:
Given:

$\left\{\begin{array}{ll}ax + by + 2 = 0 . . . \left(i\right) \\ ax + by + 5 = 0 . . . . \left(ii\right)\end{array} \to \text{Parallel lines}\right$

$\left\{\begin{array}{ll}cx + dy + 3 = 0 . . . . \left(iii\right) \\ cx + dy + 7 = 0 . . . . \left(iv\right)\end{array} \to \text{Parallel lines}\right$

Opposite sides are parallel in parallelogram.

Let ${d}_{1}$ be the distance between $\left(i\right) \text{ and } \left(ii\right)$, then

${d}_{1} = \dfrac{5 - 2}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}}$

Let ${d}_{2}$ be the distance between $\left(iii\right) \text{ and } \left(iv\right)$, then

${d}_{2} = \dfrac{7 - 3}{\sqrt{{c}^{2} + {d}^{2}}} = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{{c}^{2} + {d}^{2}}}$

Area of parallelogram$= \left(\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{{c}^{2} + {d}^{2}}}\right)$

                                   $= \dfrac{12}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}\sqrt{{c}^{2} + {d}^{2}}}$

questions.q: The circumcentre of the triangle with vertices at $( - 2, 3 ) , ( 1, - 2 )$and $(2,1)$ is
questions.solution:
Circumcentre of the triangle is equidistant from the vertices of the triangle. Let& $O \left(x, y\right)$ be the& circumcentre& of the triangle.

Now,

$OA = \sqrt{ \left(x + 2\right)2 + \left(y - 3\right)2}$$ . . . $\left(i\right)$

$OC = \sqrt{ \left(x - 2\right)2 + \left(y - 1\right)2$}$$ . . . \left(iii\right)$

$OA = OB = OC$

Equating $\left($ i\right) & $\left($ ii\right)$, we get

\sqrt{\left(x + 2\right)2 + \left(y - 3\right)2} = \sqrt{\left(x - 1\right)2 + \left(y + 2\right)2}$

$⇒ \left($ x + 2\right)2 + $\left($ y - 3\right)2 = $\left($ x - 1\right)2 + $\left($ y + 2\right)2$

3x - 5y + 4 = 0 . . . \left($ iv\right)$

Equating \left(ii\right) & \left($ iii\right)$, we get

\sqrt{\left(x - 1\right)2 + \left(y + 2\right)2} = \sqrt{\left(x - 2\right)2 + \left(y - 1\right)2}

$⇒ $\left($ x - 1\right)2 + $\left($ y + 2\right)2 = $\left(x - 2\right)2 + \left(y - 1\right)2$

$x + 3y = 0 . . . \left(v\right)$

On solving $\left($ iv\right) & $\left(v\right)$, we get

$\left($ x, y\right) ≡ $\left(\dfrac{- 6}{7}, \dfrac{2}{7}\right)$

questions.q: The product of lengths of the perpendiculars drawn from the point $( - 1, 5 )$ to the pair of lines $2x^{2} - xy - 3y^{2} + 6x + y + 4 = 0$ is
questions.solution:
Given:

$2x^{2} - xy - 3y^{2} + 6x + y + 4 = 0$

First, we will find the separate equations.

$2x^{2} - xy - 3y^{2} = 0$

$⇒ 2x^{2} - xy + 2xy - 2xy - 3y^{2} = 0$

$⇒ \left(x + y\right)\left(2x - 3y\right) = 0$

Now, $m & l$ be the constants term in the above equations.

$x + y + m = 0$

$2x - 3y + l = 0$

Then,

$2x^{2} - xy - 3y^{2} + 6x + y + 4 = \left(x + y + m\right)\left(2x - 3y + l\right)$

On comparing the coefficients, we get

$lx + 2mx = 6x$

$⇒ l + 2m = 6 . . . \left( i\right)

$ly - 3my = y$

$⇒ l - 3m = 1 . . . $\left( ii\right)$

Solving $\left(i\right) & \left( ii\right), we get

$m = 1 & l = 4$

So, we have the separate equations for lines are

$x + y + 1 = 0 . . . $\left(iii\right)$

$2x - 3y + 4 = 0 . . . \left( iv\right)

Now, we need$ to calculatePM & PN$.

$PM = $\left|-1 \times1 + 5 \times1 + 1\right|\sqrt{{1}^{2} + {1}^{2}} = \dfrac{5}{2}

$ PN = $\left|2 \times \left(-1\right) + \left(-3\right)\times \left(5\right) + 4\right|\sqrt{{2}^{2} + \left(- 3\right)2} = \dfrac{13}{13}

Now,

$ PM \timesPN = $\left(\dfrac{5}{2} \times \dfrac{13}{13}\right)$

& & & & & & & & $= \dfrac{65}{26}.

$

questions.solution:
Let the equation of line passing through origin is $y=m x$ which cut the parallel lines $x-y+10=0 and x-y+20=0$ at points $A and B$ respectively. Then, co-ordinates of points $A and B$ are,

$\begin{gathered}$y=m x $\text{$ and }x-y+10=0 \\
x-m x=-10 \\
x=$\frac{-10}{1-m}=\frac{10}{m-1} \text{$ and }y=$\frac{10 m}{m-1}$\\
\therefore A$\left(\frac{10}{m-1}, \frac{10 m}{m-1}\right)
\end{gathered}$So,

$\begin{aligned}$O A & =$\sqrt{\frac{100}{(m-1)^2}+\frac{100 m^2}{(m-1)^2}}$\\
& =$\sqrt{\frac{100\left(1+m^2\right)}{(m-1)^2}}=\frac{10 \sqrt{\left(1+m^2\right)}}{m-1}
\end{aligned}$Similarly, coordinate of point $B$ is
$\therefore$
B$\left(\frac{20}{m-1}, \frac{20 m}{m-1}\right)$Then, $O B=\sqrt{\frac{400}{(m-1)^2}+\frac{400 m^2}{(m-1)^2}}=\frac{20 \sqrt{1+m^2}}{(m-1)}$
Let point $P(h, k)$ lies on the line $y=m x$
So,

k=m h \Rightarrow m=$\frac{k}{h}$and $\quad O P=\sqrt{h^2+k^2}$
Now, $O A, O P, O B$ in H.P.
So, $\frac{1}{O A}, \frac{1}{O P}, \frac{1}{O B}$ in AP.
Hence, $\quad \frac{1}{O P}=\frac{1}{O A}+\frac{1}{O B}\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{2}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2}}=\frac{m-1}{10 \sqrt{1+m^2}}+\frac{m-1}{20 \sqrt{1+m^2}}$\\
& $\frac{2}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2}}=\frac{m-1}{10 \sqrt{1+m^2}}\left[$1+$\frac{1}{2}\right]
\end{aligned}$Putting the value of $m$, we get

$\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{2}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2}}=\frac{\left(\frac{k}{h}-1\right)}{10 \cdot \sqrt{1+\frac{k^2}{h^2}}} \cdot \frac{3}{2}$\\
\Rightarrow \quad $\frac{2}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2}}$& =$\frac{3(k-h) / h}{20 \frac{\sqrt{h^2+k^2}}{h}}$\\
\Rightarrow \quad $\frac{2}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2}}=$& $\frac{3(k-h)}{20 \sqrt{h^2+k^2}}$\\
\Rightarrow \quad 3(k-h) & =40 \Rightarrow 3 h-3 k+40=0
\end{aligned}

Hence, locus of the point is

3 x-3 y+40=0 .

questions.solution:
Given equations are
$\begin{aligned}
& x+a y+a=0 \\
& b x+y+b=0 \text{$ and $} c x+c y+1=0
\end{aligned}$
The above three lines are concurrent, so
$\begin{aligned}
& \left|\begin{array}{lll}
1 & a & a \\
b & 1 & b \\
c & c & 1
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
\Rightarrow & 1(1-b c)-a(b-b c)+a(b c-c)=0 \\
\Rightarrow & 1-b c-a b+a b c+a b c-a c=0 \\
\Rightarrow & 1+2 a b c=a b+b c+a c \\
\text{ Now, } \frac{a}{a-1}+\frac{b}{b-1}+\frac{c}{c-1} & (a-1)(b-1)(c-1) \\
= & \frac{a(b-1)(c-1)+b(a-1)(c-1)+c(a-1)(b-1)}{a c-a b-a c+b+a b c} \\
= & \frac{a b c-a b-a c+a+a b c-a b-b c+b c+c}{a b c+a+b+c-a b-b c-a c-1} \\
= & \frac{3 a b c-2(a b+b c+a c)+a+b+c}{a b c+a+b+c-(a b+b c+a c)-1} \\
= & \frac{3 a b c-2(1+2 a b c)+a+b+c}{a b c+a+b+c-(1+2 a b c)-1} \\
= & \frac{3 a b c-2-4 a b c+a+b+c}{a b c+a+b+c-1-2 a b c-1} \\
= & \frac{-a b c+a+b+c-2}{-a b c+a+b+c-2}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If the portion of a line intercepted between the coordinates axes is divided by the point $(2,-1)$ in the ratio of $3: 2$, then the equation of that line is
questions.solution:
Let the equation of the line be

$\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=1$ The line meets the coordinate axes at A(a, 0) and B(0, b) respectively. The coordinate of the point which divides the line joining A(a, 0) and B(0, b)$ in the ratio 3: 2$ are

$\left(\frac{3 \times 0+2 \times a}{3+2}, \frac{3 \times b+2 \times 0}{3+2}\right) \Rightarrow \left(\frac{2 a}{5}, \frac{3 b}{5}\right)If is given that,$ the point(2,-1)$ divides the A B$ in the ratio $3: 2$.

\therefore $\frac{2 a}{5}=2 \text{$ and } $\frac{3 b}{5}=$-1 \Rightarrow a=5 $\text{$ and }}b=$\frac{-5}{3}$ Hence, the required equation of the required line is

$\begin{array}{rlrl}& & \frac{x}{5}$+$\frac{y}{\frac{-5}{3}$}& =1 \\
\Rightarrow & $\frac{x}{5}-\frac{3 y}{5}& =1 \\
\Rightarrow & x-3 y & =5 \\
\Rightarrow & x-3 y-5 & =0
\end{array} $

questions.q: The equation of the line passing through the point of intersection of the lines $2 x+y-4=0, x-3 y+5=0$ and lying at a distance of $\sqrt{5} units from the origin, is$
questions.solution:
The equation of a line passing through the
in ter section of 2x + y − 4 = 0 and x − 3y + 5 = 0 is
(2x + y − 4) + λ(x − 3y + 5) = 0 …(i)
⇒ x(2 + λ) + y(1 − 3λ) + 5λ − 4 = 0
This is at a distance of $\sqrt{5}$ units from the origin.
$\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore & \left|\frac{5 \lambda-4}{\sqrt{(2+\lambda)^2+(1-3 \lambda)^2}}\right|=\sqrt{5} \\
\Rightarrow & \frac{(5 \lambda-4)^2}{4+\lambda^2+4 \lambda+1+9 \lambda^2-6 \lambda}=5 \\
\Rightarrow & \frac{(5 \lambda-4)^2}{10 \lambda^2-2 \lambda+5}=5 \\
\Rightarrow & 25 \lambda^2+16-40 \lambda=50 \lambda^2-10 \lambda+25 \\
\Rightarrow & 25 \lambda^2+30 \lambda+9=0
\end{array}
By solving, we get $\lambda=-$\frac{3}{5}
Putting the value of $\lambda=-$\frac{3}{5} in Eq. (i), we get \begin{array}{rrrl}
\Rightarrow (2 x+y-4)-\frac{3}{5}($ x-3 y+5) =0 \\
\Rightarrow 10 x+5 y-20-3 x+9 y-15 =0 \\
\Rightarrow 7 x+14 y-35 =0 \\
\Rightarrow x+2 y-5 =0
\end{array}

questions.solution:
Let these three lines be $L_1, L_2$ and $L_3\begin{aligned}
& L_1=x+2 a y+a=0 \\
& L_2=x+3 b y+b=0 \\
& L_3=x+2 c y+c=0
\end{aligned}$
If $L_1, L_2$ and $L_3$ are concurrent, then
$\left|\begin{array}{lll}
1 & 2 a & a \\
1 & 3 b & b \\
1 & 4 c & c
\end{array}\right|=0$
Applying $R_1 \rightarrow R_1-R_2, R_2 \rightarrow R_2-R_3$,
$\begin{aligned}
& \left|\begin{array}{ccc}
0 & 2 a-3 b & a-b \\
0 & 3 b-4 c & b-c \\
1 & 4 c & c
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 1[(2 a-3 b)(b-c)-(3 b-4 c)(a-b)]=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad(2 a-3 b)(b-c)=(3 b-4 c)(a-b) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 2 a b-2 c a-3 b^2+3 b c=3 a b-3 b^2-4 c a+4 b c \\
& \Rightarrow \quad a b+b c=2 c a \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{c}=\frac{2}{b}
\end{aligned}$
Hence, $a, b$ and $c$ are in Harmonic progression.

questions.q: The co-ordinate axes are rotated through an angle $135^{{}^{\circ}}$. If the co-ordinates of a point $P$ in the new system are known to be $(4,-3)$, then the co-ordinates of $P$ in the original system are
questions.solution:
Let $\left(x_1, y_1\right)$ be the co-ordinate of new system, then
$x_1=x \cos \theta+y \sin \thetay_1=-x \sin \theta+y \cos \theta$
Given that $\left(x_1, y_1\right)=(4,-3)$ and $\theta=135^{{}^{\circ}}4=x \cos 135^{{}^{\circ}}+y \sin 135^{{}^{\circ}}\Rightarrow \quad 4=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}\ldots(\mathrm{i})-3=-x \sin 135^{{}^{\circ}}+y \cos 135^{{}^{\circ}}\Rightarrow \quad-3=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}\ldots(\mathrm{ii})$
On adding Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$1=-\frac{2 x}{\sqrt{2}}\Rightarrow \quad x=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
On subtracting Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$7=\frac{2 y}{\sqrt{2}}\Rightarrow \quad y=\frac{7}{\sqrt{2}}$
Thus $(x, y)= \left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{7}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$

From Eq. (ii),

On solving Eqs. (iii) and (iv), we get
$x=-8, y=-10$
Now, $P A^2=(-8-1)^2+(-10-3)^2=81+169=250P A=\sqrt{250}=5 \sqrt{10}$

questions.q: If the direction cosines of two lines are given by $l+m+n=0$ and $m n-2 l m-2 n l=0$, then the acute angle between those lines is
questions.solution:
$l+m+n=0 \Rightarrow l=-m-n \qquad$ ...(i)
$\begin{aligned}
& \text{$ and $} m n-2 l m-2 n l=0 \\
& \Rightarrow m n+2(m+n) m+2(m+n) n=0 \\
& \Rightarrow(2 m+n)(m+2 n)=0 \Rightarrow n=-2 m \text{ or } m=-2 n \\
& \Rightarrow l=m \text{ or } l=n
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Direction ratios of lines are $(1,1,-2) and (1,-2,1)$, then angle between them is given by
$\cos \theta=\left|\frac{1-2-2}{\sqrt{6} \sqrt{6}}\right|=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$

questions.solution:
(2,-1, $\sqrt{\lambda}) are the direction ratios perpendicular to the plane. $(1,2,2)$ is the direction ratio of the line. Then, \vec{l}=\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+2 \hat{k}$ and $\vec{p}=2 \hat{i}-\hat{j}+\sqrt{\lambda} \hat{k}$
Since, $\sin \theta=\frac{\vec{l} \cdot \vec{p}}{|\vec{l}| \cdot|\vec{p}|}=\frac{2-2+2 \sqrt{\lambda}}{3 \times \sqrt{5+\lambda}}\Rightarrow \sin \theta=\frac{2 \sqrt{\lambda}}{3 \sqrt{5+\lambda}}=\frac{2}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{5+\lambda}} \Rightarrow \sin \theta=\frac{2}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{5+\lambda}}\Rightarrow \frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3} \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{5+\lambda}} \Rightarrow 5+\lambda=4 \lambda \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{5}{3}$.

questions.q: If $l, m, n$ are the direction cosines of a line that is perpendicular to the lines having the direction ratios $1,2,-1$ and $1,-2,1$ then $(l+m+n)^2=$
questions.solution:
$(l, m, n)$ are direction cosine of a line that is perpendicular to the lines having direction ratios $(1,2,-1)$ and $(1,-2,1)\therefore l+2 m-n=0$...(i)
$l-2 m+n=0$...(ii)
Adding (i) and (ii), $2 l=0 \Rightarrow l=0$
From (i), $2 m-n=0 \Rightarrow 2 m=n$
Also, $l^2+m^2+n^2=1 \Rightarrow m^2+4 m^2=1 \Rightarrow m^2=\frac{1}{5}$
Now, $(l+m+n)^2=l^2+m^2+n^2+2(l m+m n+l n)=1+2(m n)=1+4 m^2=\frac{9}{5}$

Now, $($\alpha+\beta+\gamma)2=\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2=\frac{4}{2}=2$

\Rightarrow & \vec{r} \cdot[\hat{i}(1+3 \lambda)+\hat{j}(-2+\lambda)+\hat{k}(3-2 \lambda)]=5+7 \lambda
\end{aligned}$$ 
...(iii)

  $$\begin{aligned} \text{ but given that } \vec{r}=(2 \hat{i}-3 \hat{j}+\hat{k}) \\
& \Rightarrow 2(1+3 \lambda)+(-3)(-2+\lambda)+(1)(3-2 \lambda)=5+7 \lambda \\

putting \lambda=1$ in equation (iii), we get

questions.solution:
Step-1 Using mid point concept:
Given that the equation of the plane is $a x+b y+c z+d=0$ and the line passed the plane having the coordinates as $P(4,-3,1) and Q(2,3,-5)$.
Let $M(x, y, z)$ be the mid-point of the line passing through the plane. Using the mid-point formula find the coordinate of $M(x, y, z)$.
$x=\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow x=\frac{4+2}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow x=\frac{6}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow x=3\end{aligned}$ And $\begin{aligned} y & =\frac{y_1+y_2}{2} \\ \Rightarrow y & =\frac{-3+3}{2} \\ \Rightarrow y & =\frac{0}{2} \\ \Rightarrow y & =0\end{aligned}
And
\begin{aligned} z & =\frac{z_1+z_2}{2} \\ \Rightarrow z & =\frac{1-5}{2} \\ \Rightarrow z & =\frac{-4}{2} \\ \Rightarrow z & =-2\end{aligned}$
Therefore, the mid-point $M(x, y, z)$ is obtained as $(3,0,-2)$.
Step-2 : Normal vector to the plane:
The normal of the plane $P Q$ is determined as, $P Q=-2 i+6 j-6 k$
[where coefficient of $i=2-4$, coefficient of $j=3-(-3)$, coefficient of $k=-5-1$]
Then the value of $a$ is $-2, b$ is 6 and $c$ is -6 .
Now the equation of plane is $-2 x+6 y-6 z+d=0$
Using the mid-point coordinate $(3,0,-2)$ finding the value of $d$.
$-2(3)+6(0)-6(-2)+d=0\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & & -6+0+12+d & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & & 6+d & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & & d & =-6\end{aligned}$
Therefore, the equation of the plane is $-2 x+6 y-6 z+-6=0$.
$\Rightarrow x-3 y+3 z+3=0 \quad$ [equation is of the form ax + by $+\mathbf{c z}+\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{0}]$
Now substitute the values of $a$ as $1, b$ as $-3, c$ as 3 and $d$ as 3 in
$\begin{aligned}& \left(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2\right) . \\&a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2=(1)^2+(-3)^2+(3)^2+(3)^2\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & =1+9+9+9 \\ & =28\end{aligned}$
Therefore, the minimum value of $\left(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2\right)$ is 28

$y -$coordinate $= - 2$ (z$ coordinate of $P$)

So by perpendicular distance formula we get,

$\left|\dfrac{d}{{1}^{2} + {2}^{2} + {2}^{2}}\right| = \dfrac{1}{3} ⇒ d = 1$

We get,~$p = 2, q = 2 & r = - 1$

So, the value of~$\sqrt{p^{2} + q^{2} + r^{2}} = \sqrt{{2}^{2} + {2}^{2} + {1}^{2}} = \sqrt{9} = 3$

questions.q: The $x$-intercept of a plane $\pi$ passing through the point $\left(1, 1, 1\right)$ is $\dfrac{5}{2}$ and the perpendicular distance from the origin to the plane $\pi$ is $\dfrac{5}{7}$. If the $y$-intercept of the plane $\pi$ is negative and the $z$-intercept is positive then its $y$-intercept is
questions.solution:
Let the equation of plane be

$\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} + \dfrac{z}{c} = 1$

Now given~$a = \dfrac{5}{2}$

So, equation becomes~$\dfrac{2x}{5} + \dfrac{y}{b} + \dfrac{z}{c} = 1$

Now given plane passes through $\left(1, 1, 1\right)$~

$⇒ \dfrac{2}{5} + \dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c} = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

Now given distance from origin is $\dfrac{5}{7}$

So~ by formula we get,& $\left|\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{4}{25} + \dfrac{1}{b2} + \dfrac{1}{c2}}\right| = \dfrac{5}{7}$

$⇒ \left|\sqrt{\dfrac{4}{25} + \left(\dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c}\right)2 - \dfrac{2}{bc}}\right| = \dfrac{7}{5}$

Now using value of~$\dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c} = \dfrac{3}{5}$~we get,

$⇒ bc = - \dfrac{25}{18} . . . \left(1\right)

&~\dfrac{1}{b} + \dfrac{1}{c} = \dfrac{3}{5}⇒ \dfrac{b + c}{bc} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

$⇒ b + c = - \dfrac{5}{6}$ . . .$\left(2\right)$

Now equation (1) & (2) we get,~

$⇒ b - \dfrac{25}{18b} = \dfrac{- 5}{6}$

$⇒ 18b^{2} + 15b - 25 = 0$

$⇒ \left(6b - 5\right)\left(3b + 5\right) = 0$

$⇒ b = \dfrac{5}{6}$ or $- \dfrac{5}{3}$

So $b = - \dfrac{5}{3}$ {as given $y$ intercept is negative}

Since, we know that the equation of plane passing through a point $\left(x_1, y_1, z_1\right)$ is
$A\left(x-x_1\right)+B\left(y-y_1\right)+C\left(z-z_1\right)=0$
Equation of plane passing through $(0,1,2)$ is
$A(x-0)+B(y-1)+C(z-2)=0$  ...(i)

Hence,$A(-1-0)+B(0-1)+C(3-2)=0-A-B+C=0\Rightarrow \quad A+B-C=0$ ...(ii)
If plane (i) is perpendicular to $2 x+3 y+z=5\therefore \quad 2 A+3 B+C=0$ ...(iii)
[by using condition of perpendicularly]
On solving Eqs. (ii) and (iii),
$\frac{A}{1 \cdot 1-3(-1)}=\frac{B}{2(-1)-1 \cdot 1}=\frac{C}{1 \cdot 3-2 \cdot 1}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{A}{4}=\frac{B}{-3}=\frac{C}{1}$
Using these proportional values of $A, B, C$ in Eq. (i),
$4(x-0)+(-3)(y-1)+(z-2)=0\Rightarrow 4 x-3 y+z+1=0$

and~line& ${L}_{2}$~passes through& $2\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - 3\overset{^}{k}$~and parallel to& $\overset{^}{i} - 2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$.

Then,~${a}_{1} = 2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{k}$,~${b}_{1} = 3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}$~and& ${a}_{2} = 2\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - 3\overset{^}{k}$,~${b}_{2} = \overset{^}{i} - 2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$

Shortest distance between lines is given by,~$d = \left(\overset{→}{b}1 \times \overset{→}{b}2\right) \cdot \left(\overset{→}{a}2 - \overset{→}{a}1\right)\left|\overset{→}{b}1 \times \overset{→}{b}2\right|$.

Now,~$\left(\overset{→}{b}1 \times \overset{→}{b}2\right) = \left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 3 & - 1 & 2 \\ 1 & - 2 & 1\end{cases}\right| = 3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} - 5\overset{^}{k}$

$⇒ \left|\overset{→}{b}1 \times \overset{→}{b}2\right| = \sqrt{{3}^{2} + \left(- 1\right)2 + \left(- 5\right)2} = \sqrt{35}$

And,~$\left(\overset{→}{a}2 - \overset{→}{a}1\right) = \overset{^}{j} - 2\overset{^}{k}$

Putting these values, we get~$d = \dfrac{\left(3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} - 5\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \left(\overset{^}{j} - 2\overset{^}{k}\right)}{35} = \dfrac{- 1 + 10}{35} = \dfrac{9}{35}$

questions.solution:
Given points$A ( - 1, 2, - 3 ) , B ( 5, 0, - 6 ) , C ( 0, 4, - 1 )$

Let, the vector $AD$is the internal bisector of $∠ BAC$, point $D$ lie on the side& $BC$.

Now, $AB = \sqrt{\left(- 1 - 5\right)2 + {2}^{2} + \left(- 3 + 6\right)2} = \sqrt{36 + 4 + 9} = 7$

and, $AC = \sqrt{\left(- 1 - 0\right)2 + \left(2 - 4\right)2 + \left(- 3 + 1\right)2} = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$

We know that, the bisector of angle $∠ BAC$, divides the side $BC$ in ratio& $AB: AC$, i.e. $7: 3$

So, the coordinate of $D$ is& $\left(\dfrac{3 \times 5 + 7 \times 0}{3 + 7}, \dfrac{3 \times 0 + 7 \times 4}{3 + 7}, \dfrac{3 \times \left(- 6\right) + 7 \times \left(-1\right)}{3 + 7}\right) = \left(\dfrac{3}{2}, \dfrac{14}{5}, - \dfrac{5}{2}\right)

Hence,$ the vector\overset{→}{AD} =$\dfrac{5}{2}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{4}{5}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{1}{2}\overset{^}{k}

So,$ the $direction cosines are \dfrac{\dfrac{5}{2}}{\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)2}, \dfrac{\dfrac{4}{5}}{\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)2}$' $\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}}{\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)2}

$ i . e . $\dfrac{25}{714}, \dfrac{8}{714}, \dfrac{5}{714}$

questions.q: If the projections of the line segment $\overset{→}{AB}$ on $XY, YZ$ and $ZX$ planes are $\sqrt{15}, \sqrt{46},$7$ respectively, then the projection of \overset{→}{AB}$ on $y -$axis is
questions.solution:
Let, the vector $\overset{→}{AB} = l\overset{^}{i} + m\overset{^}{j} + n\overset{^}{k}$

Projection on $XY$ plane is& \sqrt{l^{2} + m^{2}} = \sqrt{15} ⇒ l^{2} + m^{2} = 15... $\left(1\right)$

Projection on $YZ$ plane is \sqrt{m^{2} + n^{2}} = \sqrt{46}$⇒ m^{2} + n^{2} = 46... \left(2\right)

Projection on $ZX$ plane is& \sqrt{n^{2} + l^{2}} =7 ⇒ n^{2} + l^{2} = 49... \left(3\right)

Subtracting equation \left(2\right) from& equation& \left(3\right),

\left(l^{2} + n^{2}\right)- \left(n^{2} + m^{2}\right)$ =49 - 46 = 3 ⇒ l^{2} - m^{2} = 3 ⇒ $\left(l + m\right)\left(l - m\right)$ = 3$

$⇒ l + m = 3 and l - m = 1$

So, $l = 2, m = 1$
Hence, the projection of $\overset{→}{AB}$ on $y$-axis is $m = 1$

$

questions.q: Find the equation of the plane passing through the point $( 2, 1, 3 )$ and perpendicular to the planes $x - 2y + 2z + 3 = 0$ and $3x - 2y + 4z - 4 = 0.$
questions.solution:
We can conclude, the normal& to the plane ${S}_{1}$

i.e. $x - 2y + 2z + 3 = 0$ is& (say) $\overset{→}{r1} = \overset{^}{i} - 2\overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}$
and the normal to the plane ${S}_{2}$

i.e. $3x - 2y + 4z - 4 = 0$ is (say) $\overset{→}{r2} = 3\overset{^}{i} - 2\overset{^}{j} + 4\overset{^}{k}$
So, the normal to the plane ${S}_{3}$ (which is perpendicular to the plane ${S}_{1} and {S}_{2}$)

is $\overset{→}{r3} = \left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 1 & - 2 & 2 \\ 3 & - 2 & 4\end{cases}\right| = - 4\overset{^}{i} + 2\overset{^}{j} + 4\overset{^}{k}$

So, the equation of plane ${S}_{3}$ is

$- 4x + 2y + 4z + c = 0... \left(1\right)$

As, it is passing through the point $\left(2, 1, 3\right)$

So, substituting in equation $\left(1\right)$, we get,

$- 4 \times2 + 2 \times1 + 4 \times3 + c = 0 ⇒ - 8 + 2 + 12 + c = 0 ⇒ c = - 6$

Hence, the equation of the plane ${S}_{3}$ is

$- 4x + 2y + 4z - 6 = 0 or 2x - y - 2z + 3 = 0$

questions.q: The harmonic conjugate of $(2,3,4)$ with respect to the points $(3,-2,2)$ and $(6,-17,-4)$ is
questions.solution:
Let $A=(3,-2,2) \begin{aligned}$& B=(6,-17,-4) \\
& P=(2,3,4)
\end{aligned}

Let $P$ divides $A B$ in the ratio of $m: n$.

$\begin{gathered}$P=$\left[\frac{m x_2+n x_1}{m+n}, \frac{m y_2+n y_1}{m+n}, \frac{m z_2+n z_1}{m+n}\right]$\\
(2,3,4)=$\left[\frac{m(6)+n(3)}{m+n}, \frac{m(-17)+n(-2)}{m+n},\right.$\\
(2,3,4)=$\left[\frac{6 m(-4)+n(2)}{m+n}\right]$\\
$\frac{6 m+3 n}{m+n}=$2 \\
6 m+3 n=2 m+2 n \\
4 m=-n \\
$\frac{m}{n}=-\frac{1}{4}$\\
m: n=-1: 4
\end{gathered}

We know that,
If point $P$ divides a line segment in the ratio of $m: n$, then its harmonic conjugate will divide same segment in the ratio of $-m: n\therefore$ Required ratio $=-m: n=1: 4\therefore$ Required harmonic conjugate

$\begin{aligned}$& =$\left(\frac{m x_2+n x_1}{m+n}, \frac{m y_2+n y_1}{m+n}, \frac{m z_2+n z_1}{m+n}\right)$\\
& =$\left(\frac{1(6)+4(3)}{1+4}, \frac{1(-17)+4(-2)}{1+4}, \frac{1(-4)+4(2)}{1+4}\right)$\\
& =$\left(\frac{18}{5}, \frac{-25}{5}, \frac{4}{5}\right)=\left(\frac{18}{5},-$5, $\frac{4}{5}\right)
\end{aligned}$Hence option (4) is correct.

questions.q: The equation of the locus of a point \(P(x, y, z)\) such that it's distance from the \(X\)-axis is equal to its distance from the plane \(x+z=1\) is
questions.solution:
As it is given that the distance of a point \(P(x, y, z)\) from the \(X\)-axis is equal to its distance from the plane \(x+z=1\), so
\begin{aligned}& $\sqrt{(x-x)^2+(y-0)^2+(z-0)^2}=\frac{|x+z-1|}{\sqrt{1^2+1^2}}$\\
\Rightarrow & $2\left(y^2+z²\right)=x²+z²+1+2 x z-2 x-2 z \\
\Rightarrow & x²-2 y²-z²+2 x z-2 x-2 z+1=0
\end{aligned}\)
Hence, option (a) is correct.$

questions.q: Angle between the lines of intersection of the planes \(x-y=0,2 x+y+z=0\) and \(2 x-z=0, x+y-3 z=0\) is
questions.solution:
Let the direction cosines of line of intersection of the planes \(x-y=0\) and \(2 x+y+z=0\) are \(a_1, b_1, c_1\) so
\(a_1-b_1=0\)
and \(2 a_1+b_1+c_1=0\)
By cross-multiplication method, we have
\($\frac{a_1}{-1-0}=\frac{-b_1}{1-0}=\frac{c_1}{1+2} \Rightarrow \frac{a_1}{1}=\frac{b_1}{1}=\frac{c_1}{-3}$
Similarly, let the direction cosines of line of intersection of the planes \(2 x-z=0\) and
$\begin{aligned}$x+y-3 z & =0 $\text{ are }$a_2, b_2, c_2 $\text{ so, }$\\
2 a_2-b_2 & =0 \\
a_2+b_2-3 c_2 & =0
\end{aligned}\)
By cross-multiplication method, we have
\($\frac{a_2}{3-0}=\frac{-b_2}{-6-0}=\frac{c_2}{2+1} \Rightarrow \frac{a_2}{1}=\frac{b_2}{2}=\frac{c_2}{1}$
So angle ' \($\theta$ ' between lines having directions cosines \(a_1, b_1, c_1\) and \(a_2, b_2, c_2\) respectively. is
$\begin{aligned}\theta$& =\cos ^{-1}$\left(\frac{   \left|$a_1 a_2+b_1 b_2+c_1 c_2\right|}{\sqrt{a_1^2+b_1^2+c_1^2} \sqrt{a_2^2+b_2^2+c_2^2}}\right)$\\
& =\cos $^{-1} $\left(\frac{1+2-3}{\sqrt{1+1+9} \sqrt{1+4+1}}\right)\\
& =$\cos ^{-1}$(0)=90^{{}^{\circ}}
\end{aligned}\)
Hence, option (d) is correct.$

questions.solution:
A vector which is coplanar to the vectors $2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}\)$ and $\(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}\) is
\(\mathbf{a}(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})+\mathbf{b}(\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})\)
\((2 a+b) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+(a-b) \hat{\mathbf{j}}+(a+b) \hat{\mathbf{k}}\) ...(i)
Eq. (i) is orthogonal to \(3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+6 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\)
\begin{aligned}& 3(2 a+b)+2(a-b)+6(a+b) =0 \\
& 14 a+7 b =0 \\
& 2 a+b =0
\end{aligned}\)
Required unit vector,
\begin{aligned}& = \pm \frac{(2 a+b) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+(a-b) \hat{\mathbf{j}}+(a+b) \hat{\mathbf{k}}}{\sqrt{(2 a+b)^2+(a-b)^2+(a+b)^2}}\\
& = \pm \frac{3 a \hat{\mathbf{j}}-a \hat{\mathbf{k}}}{\sqrt{(3 a)^2+a^2}}= \pm \frac{3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}}{\sqrt{10}}
\end{aligned}$
Hence, option (b) is correct.

questions.q: \(\mathbf{A B}=\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{A C}=\mathbf{b}\) are the sides of \(\mathbf{a} \triangle A B C . P\) is a point on \(\mathbf{A B}\) and \(Q\) is a point on \(\mathbf{B C}\) such that \($\frac{A P}{P B}=\frac{1}{2}$\) and \($\frac{B Q}{Q C}=\frac{1}{2}$\). If the point of intersection of \(\mathbf{A Q}\) and \(\mathbf{C P}\) is \(D\) and the area of \(\triangle B C D\) is 7 square units, then the area of the \(\triangle A B C\) (in the same sq units) is
questions.solution:
According to given informations,
$\mathbf{A P}=\frac{\mathbf{a}}{3} \text{ and } \mathbf{A Q}=\frac{2 \mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}}{3}\)
Let \(D\) divides the line \(\mathbf{A Q}\) in ratio \(\lambda: 1\) and \(\mathbf{C P}\) in \(\mu: 1\).
So, \(\quad=\frac{\lambda(2 \mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})}{3(\lambda+1)}=\frac{\mu \frac{\mathbf{a}}{3}+\mathbf{b}}{\mu+1}\)
On comparing
\begin{array}{rlrl}& & \frac{\mu}{3(\mu+1)}& =\frac{2 \lambda}{3(\lambda+1)} \text{ and } \frac{1}{\mu+1}=\frac{\lambda}{3(\lambda+1)}\\
\Rightarrow & \frac{\mu}{3(\mu+1)}& =\frac{2}{\mu+1} \Rightarrow \mu=6 \\
\text{So, }& \frac{1}{7}& =\frac{\lambda}{3(\lambda+1)} \Rightarrow3 \lambda+3=7 \lambda \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{3}{4}\\
\Rightarrow & & \text{ AD }& =\frac{2 a+\mathbf{b}}{7}
\end{array}$
So, $\frac{1}{7}=\frac{\lambda}{3(\lambda+1)} \Rightarrow3 \lambda+3=7 \lambda \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{3}{4}\)
\(\Rightarrow \quad \mathbf{A D}=\frac{2 \mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}}{7}\)
Now area of \(\triangle B C D=\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{B C} \times \mathbf{B D}|\)
\begin{aligned}& =\frac{1}{2}\left|(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \times\left(\frac{\mathbf{b}-5 \mathbf{a}}{7}\right)\right|\\
& =\frac{1}{14}|(-\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a})-(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})|\\
& =\frac{4}{14}|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|=7 \text{ (given) }
\end{aligned}$
\(\Rightarrow \quad $\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|=\frac{49}{4}$\)
\(\Rightarrow\) Area of \(\triangle A B $C=\frac{49}{4}$\)
Hence, option (a) is correct.

\(=\hat{\mathbf{i}}(2-1)-\hat{\mathbf{j}}(2-1)+\hat{\mathbf{k}}(\mathrm{l}-1)=\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}\)
So, unit vector perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) is
\(= \pm \frac{\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}}{\sqrt{2}}\)
Now the magnitude of the projection of \(\pm \frac{\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}}{\sqrt{2}}\) on \(\mathbf{c}\) is
\(\begin{aligned}
& =\left| \pm\left(\frac{\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \cdot \frac{(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{k}})}{\sqrt{4+9+16}}\right|\\
 \text{ and }  =\left|\frac{2-3}{\sqrt{2} \sqrt{29}}\right|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{58}}
\end{aligned}\)
Hence, option (c) is correct.

Equation of lines is passing through \((1,-1,1)\) and having DC's is \((2,3,1)\)

Given line is $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac{z-1}{4}=\lambda$ So, $(x, y, z)$ is $(2 \lambda+1,3 \lambda-1,4 \lambda+1)$ and this point is lies on given line. questions.q: Let $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ be unit vectors with $\theta$ as the acute angle between them. If $\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|=\sin \lambda \theta$, then $4 \lambda^2=$
questions.solution:
It is given, that $\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}|=\sin (\lambda \theta)$ On squaring both sides, we get $\begin{aligned}& \Rightarrow|\mathbf{a}|^2+|\mathbf{b}|^2-2|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}| \cos \theta=4 \sin ^2(\lambda \theta)\\
& \Rightarrow 1+1-2 \cos \theta=4 \sin ^2(\lambda \theta)\\
& \Rightarrow 2(1-\cos \theta)=4 \sin ^2(\lambda \theta) \Rightarrow4 \sin ^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)=4 \sin ^2(\lambda \theta)\\
& \Rightarrow \quad \ lambda=\frac{1}{2} \quad\left[\because(1-\cos \theta)=2 \sin ^2 \frac{\theta}{2}\right]\\
& \therefore \quad 4 \lambda^2=4\ left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=1
\end{aligned} Hence, option (b) is correct.$

Hence,

$\alpha + 8\beta + 7\gamma = 0 . . . \left(ii\right)9\alpha + 2\beta + 3\gamma = 0 . . . \left(iii\right)\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 0 . . . \left(iv\right)$

Subtracting $\left(iv\right)$ from $\left(i\right)$, we get

$\alpha = 1$

Putting in $\left(iii\right) \text{ and } \left(iv\right)$, we get

$2\beta + 3\gamma = - 9 . . . \left(v\right)$

$\beta + \gamma = - 1 . . . \left(vi\right)$

On solving, we get $\gamma = - 7 \text{ and } \beta = 6$

Therefore,

${\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2} + {\gamma}^{2} = 86$

questions.solution:
We know that, if a line makes an angle& $\alpha, \beta & \gamma$~with positive direction of& $X - \text{axis}, Y - \text{axis} & Z - \text{axis}$~then

${cos}^{2}\alpha + {cos}^{2}\beta + {cos}^{2}\gamma = 1 . . \left(i\right)

Now, given angles are~$\alpha = {tan}^{- $1}\sqrt{$7}$~and& $\beta = {tan}^{- 1} $\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{3}}\right)$.

Then,~

$cos\left({tan}^{- 1}\left(\sqrt{7}\right)\right) = cos\left({cos}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)\right) = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$

$cos\left({tan}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)\right) = cos\left({cos}^{- 1} \left(\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)\right) = \dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{2}}

Therefore, from~\left(i\right), we get

$⇒ $\left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)$2 + $\left(\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)$2 + {cos}^{2}\gamma =1$

$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{3}{8} + {cos}^{2}\gamma =$1$

$⇒ {cos}^{2}\gamma =1 - $\dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ {cos}^{2}\gamma = $\dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ cos\gamma = \pm $\dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ \gamma = $\dfrac{π}{4}\text{or}\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

questions.q: A plane passes through the point $( 3, 5, 7 )$. If the direction ratios of its normal are equal to the intercepts made by the plane $x + 3y + 2z = 9$& with the coordinate axes, then the equation of that plane is
questions.solution:
Given:

$x + 3y + 2z = 9$

$⇒ \dfrac{x}{9} + \dfrac{y}{3} + z\left(\dfrac{9}{2}\right) = 1$

Comparing with the standard form $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} + \dfrac{z}{c} = 1$, we get

$a = 9 \to \left($x - $\text{intercept}\right)

$ b = 3 \to $\left($ y - $\text{intercept}\right)

$ c = $\left(\dfrac{9}{2}\right) \to\left(z - \text{intercept}\right)$

So, the normal vector for the required plane is $\overset{→}{n} = 9\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{9}{2}\overset{^}{k}$

$\overset{→}{a} = 3\overset{^}{i} + 5\overset{^}{j} + 7\overset{^}{k}$

Equation of required plane,

$⇒ \overset{→}{r} \cdot \overset{→}{n} = \overset{→}{a} \cdot \overset{→}{n}$

$⇒ \overset{→}{r} \cdot \left(9\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{9}{2}\overset{^}{k}\right) = \left(3\overset{^}{i} + 5\overset{^}{j} + 7\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \left(9\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{9}{2}\overset{^}{k}\right)

$⇒ \overset{→}{r} $\cdot \left(9\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{9}{2}\overset{^}{k}\right) =27 + 15 + \dfrac{63}{2}

$⇒ $\left($ x\overset{^}{i} + y\overset{^}{j} + z\overset{^}{k}\right)$\cdot \left(9\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{9}{2}\overset{^}{k}\right) =42 + \dfrac{63}{2}

$⇒ 9x + 3y + $\dfrac{9}{2}$ z = $\dfrac{147}{2}

$⇒ 3x + y + $\dfrac{3}{2}$ z = $\dfrac{49}{2}

$⇒ 6x + 2y + 3z = 49$.

$

If $\mathbf{n}=2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$,

Plane passing through the line of intersection of planes $\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n}=1$ and $\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{m}=-4\mathbf{r} \cdot(\mathbf{n}+\lambda \mathbf{m})=1-4 \lambda($ where $\lambda$ is a scalar quantities)

This plane is $\perp$ to the plane $\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{1}=-8$
So,

$\begin{gathered}
(\mathbf{n}+\lambda \mathbf{m}) \cdot \mathbf{l}=0 \\
\mathbf{n} $\cdot $\mathbf{1}+$\lambda $\mathbf{m}$ \cdot $\mathbf{1}= 0
\end{gathered}

\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{k}}) $\cdot(2 \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}-\hat{$\mathbf{j}$} & +\hat{$\mathbf{k}$}) \\
& +\lambda(\hat{$\mathbf{i}$}-\hat{$\mathbf{j}$}) $\cdot(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})=0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad(4+3+4)+\lambda(2+1) & =0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad & \lambda=\frac{-11}{3} .
\end{aligned}$ So, required plane is,

$\begin{gathered}
\mathbf{r} \cdot\left[2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{k}} \frac{-11}{3}(\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}})\right]=1-4\left(\frac{-11}{3}\right)$\\
\Rightarrow \quad $\mathbf{r} \cdot\left(\frac{-5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}}{3}+\frac{2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}}{3}+4 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\right)=\frac{47}{3}$\\
(x \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+y \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}+z \hat{$\mathbf{k}$}) $\cdot(-5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+12 \hat{\mathbf{k}})=47 \\
\quad[\mathbf{r}=x \hat{\mathbf{i}}+y \hat{\mathbf{j}}+z \hat{\mathbf{k}}] \\

$

questions.q: If $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ are vectors of equal magnitude such that $(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})=\alpha,(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c})=\beta,(\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{a})=\gamma$, then the minimum value of $\cos \alpha+\cos \beta+\cos \gamma$ is
questions.solution:
We have, $\cos \alpha=\frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|}, \cos \beta=\frac{\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c}}{|\mathbf{b}||\mathbf{c}|}$ and $\cos \gamma=\frac{\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{c}||\mathbf{a}|}$ Also, it is given that $|\mathbf{a}|=|\mathbf{b}|=|\mathbf{c}|=\lambda$ (say), where $\lambda > 0$. Then, $\cos \alpha=\frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\lambda^2} ; \cos \beta=\frac{\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c}}{\lambda^2}$ and $\cos \gamma=\frac{\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a}}{\lambda^2}\Rightarrow \cos \alpha+\cos \beta+\cos \gamma=\frac{1}{\lambda^2}$
We know that, \begin{aligned}$& |\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}|^2=(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}) \cdot(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c})\\ = & {\left[|\mathbf{a}|^2+|\mathbf{b}|^2+|\mathbf{c}|^2+2(\mathbf{a} $\cdot $\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{b}$ \cdot $\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{c}$ \cdot $\mathbf{a}$)\right]$} \\ \Rightarrow & {\left[\lambda^2+\lambda^2+\lambda^2+2(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c}+\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a})\right] \geq0 } \\ & \quad\left[\because|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}|^2 \geq 0\right] \\ \Rightarrow & 2(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c}+\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a}) \geq-3 \lambda^2 \end{aligned} $\\ Now, from $Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get \begin{aligned} \cos\alpha+\cos \beta+\cos \gamma$& \geq $\frac{1}{\lambda^2}\left(-\frac{3}{2}$ \lambda^2\right)$ \\ & =-\frac{3}{2}$\end{aligned}Thus, the $minimum value of \cos \alpha+\cos \beta+\cos \gamma$ is $-\frac{3}{2}$.

questions.solution:
Normal of the plane $P_1$ determined by the vectors $\hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ and $3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$,
$$
\mathrm{n}_1=[(\hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}) \times(3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}})]=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
0 & 1 & -1 \\
0 & 3 & -2
\end{array}\right|=\hat{\mathbf{i}}
$$
Normal of the plane $P_2$ determined by the vectors $2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{n}_2=[(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}) \times(\hat{\mathbf{i}}-3 \hat{\mathbf{j}})] \\
& =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
2 & 3 & 0 \\
1 & -3 & 0
\end{array}\right|=\hat{\mathbf{i}}(0)-\hat{\mathbf{j}}(0)+\hat{\mathbf{k}}(-6-3)=-9 \hat{\mathbf{k}}
\end{aligned}
$$
Since, $a$ is parallel to the line of intersection of planes $P_1$ and $P_2$.
$$
a= \pm\left(n_1 \times n_2\right) \quad= \pm\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -9
\end{array}\right|= \pm 9 \hat{\mathbf{j}}
$$
Now, angle $\theta$ between $9 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ is
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \cos \theta= \pm\left(\frac{9}{9 \sqrt{3}}\right)= \pm\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \\
\therefore \quad & \theta=\cos \left( \pm \frac{}{\sqrt{ }}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Equation of plane is given by

\Rightarrow & r(2 \hat{i}+\hat{k})-5=0 \\
\Rightarrow & r(2 \hat{i}+\hat{k})=5
\end{array}
Now, equation of plane in cartesian form
\begin{aligned}
& (x \hat{i}+y \hat{j}+z \hat{k}) \cdot(2 \hat{j}+\hat{k})=5 \\
& \therefore \quad 2 x+z=5
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $M_1, M_2, M_3$ and $M_4$, are respectively the magnitudes of the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1=2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}, \mathbf{a}_2=-3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$, $\mathbf{a}_3=-\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}, \mathbf{a}_4=-\hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}$, then the correct order of $M_1, M_2, M_3$ and $M_4$ is
questions.solution:
Given that, $a_1=2 \hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}\begin{aligned}
& a_2=3 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}-4 \hat{k} \\
& a_3=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\
& a_4=-\hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+\hat{k}
\end{aligned}$
As $M_1, M_2, M_3 and M_4$ are the magnitudes of the vectors $\mathrm{a}_1, \mathrm{a}_2, \mathrm{a}_3$ and $\mathrm{a}_4$ respectively.
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad M_1=\left|\mathrm{a}_1\right| \\
& =\sqrt{(2)^2+(-1)^2+(1)^2} \\
& =\sqrt{4+1+1}=\sqrt{6} \\
& M_2=\left|\mathrm{a}_2\right| \\
& =\sqrt{(3)^2+(-4)^2+(-4)^2} \\
& =\sqrt{9+16+16}=\sqrt{41} \\
& M_3=\left|\mathrm{a}_3\right| \\
& =\sqrt{(-1)^2+(1)^2+(-1)^2} \\
& =\sqrt{1+1+1}=\sqrt{3} \\
& M_4=\left|\mathrm{a}_4\right|
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& =\sqrt{(-1)^2+(3)^2+(-1)^2} \\
& =\sqrt{1+9+1}=\sqrt{11}
\end{aligned}$
Hence, the correct order of magnitudes
$M_3 \lt  M_1 \lt  M_4 \lt  M_2$

 \begin{aligned}& {\left[\left(\mathbf{a}_2-\mathbf{a}_1\right) \mathbf{b}_1 \mathbf{b}_2\right]=\left(\mathbf{a}_2-\mathbf{a}_1\right)\cdot\left(\mathbf{b}_1 \times \mathbf{b}_2\right)} \\

& =160-68=92

Shortest distance

 \begin{aligned}& =\frac{\left[\left(\mathbf{a}_2-\mathbf{a}_1\right)\cdot\left(\mathbf{b}_1 \times \mathbf{b}_2\right)\right]}{\left|\mathbf{b}_1 \times \mathbf{b}_2\right|}\\

questions.q: If the direction ratio of two lines are given by $3 l m-4 l n+m n=0$ and $l+2 m+3 n=0$, then the angle between the lines, is :
questions.solution:
We have,
$3 l m-4 l n+m n=0\ldots$ (i)
and $l+2 m+3 n=0\ldots$ (ii)
From Eq. (ii), $l=-(2 m+3 n)$ Using in Eq. (i), we get
$-3(2 m+3 n) m+4(2 m+3 n) n+m n=0\Rightarrow \quad-6 m^2-9 m n+8 m n+12 n^2+m n=0\Rightarrow \quad-6 m^2+12 n^2=0$
Now, $m^2=2 n^2 \Rightarrow m= \pm \sqrt{2} n$
Now, $\quad m=\sqrt{2} n\Rightarrow \quad l=-(2 \sqrt{2} n+3 n)=-(2 \sqrt{2}+3) n\therefore l: m: n=-(3+2 \sqrt{2}) n: \sqrt{2} n: n=-(3+2 \sqrt{2}): \sqrt{2}: 1$
Also, $\quad m=-\sqrt{2} n \Rightarrow l=-(-2 \sqrt{2}+3) nl: m: n=-(3-2 \sqrt{2}) n:-\sqrt{2} n: n=-(3-2 \sqrt{2}):-\sqrt{2}: 1$
If $\theta$ is the angle between the lines, then
$\cos \theta=\frac{l_1 l_2+m_1 m_2+n_1 n_2}{\sqrt{l_1^2+m_1^2+n_1^2} \sqrt{l_2^2+m_2^2+n_2^2}}=\frac{(3+2 \sqrt{2})(3-2 \sqrt{2})+(\sqrt{2})(-\sqrt{2})+1.1}{\sqrt{(3+2 \sqrt{2})^2+(\sqrt{2})^2+1^2}{\sqrt{(3-2 \sqrt{2})^2+(-\sqrt{2})^2+1^2}}}=\frac{9-8-2+1}{\sqrt{9+8+12 \sqrt{2}+2+1} \sqrt{9+8-12 \sqrt{2}+2+1}}=0\Rightarrow \cos \theta=0 \Rightarrow \cos \theta=\cos \frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$

questions.q: If $\cos \alpha+4 \cos \beta+9 \cos \gamma=0$ and $\sin \alpha+4 \sin \beta+9 \sin \gamma=0$, then $81 \cos (2 \gamma-2 \alpha)-16 \cos (2 \beta-2 \alpha)=$
questions.solution:
From given equations
$4 \cos \beta=-(\cos \alpha+9 \cos \gamma)$ ...(i)
$4 \sin \beta=-(\sin \alpha+9 \sin \gamma)$ ...(ii)
Squaring both sides and adding equations (i) and (ii)
$\begin{aligned}
& 16\left(\cos ^2 \beta+\sin ^2 \beta\right)=\left(\cos ^2 \alpha+\sin ^2 \alpha\right)+81\left(\cos ^2 \gamma+\sin ^2 \gamma\right) \\
& +18(\cos \alpha \cdot \cos \gamma+\sin \alpha \sin \gamma) \\
& 16=1+81+18 \cos (\gamma-\alpha) \Rightarrow 9 \cos (\gamma-\alpha)=-33 \\
& \Rightarrow(-33)^2=81 \cos ^2(\gamma-\alpha)
\end{aligned}\Rightarrow 1089=81 \frac{[1+\cos (2 \gamma-2 \alpha]}{2}\Rightarrow 81 \cos (2 \gamma-2 \alpha)=2097$ ...(iii)
From given equations
$9 \cos \gamma=-(\cos \alpha+4 \cos \beta)$ ...(iv)
$9 \sin \gamma=-(\sin \alpha+4 \sin \beta)$ ...(v)
Squaring both sides and adding equations (iv) and (v)
$\begin{aligned}
& 81\left(\cos ^2 \gamma+\sin ^2 \gamma\right)=\left(\cos ^2 \alpha+\sin ^2 \alpha\right)+16 \\
& \quad \quad\left(\cos ^2 \beta+\sin ^2 \beta\right)+8(\cos \alpha \cdot \cos \beta+\sin \alpha \sin \beta) \\
& \Rightarrow 81=1+16+8 \cos (\beta-\alpha) \Rightarrow \cos (\beta-\alpha)=8 \\
& \therefore \cos (2 \beta-2 \alpha)=2 \cos ^2(\beta-\alpha)-1=127 \\
& \text{ Now, } 81 \cos (2 \gamma-2 \alpha)-16 \cos (2 \beta-2 \alpha) \\
& =2097-2032=65=64+1 \\
& =8 \cos (\beta-\alpha)+1
\end{aligned}$

Also $|x|+|y|=1\Rightarrow x+y=1, \quad x-y=1x+y=-1, \quad x-y=-1$

We get $\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{-1}{2}\right)$ or $\left(-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\cos A+\cos B+\cos C=0=\sin A+\sin B+\sin C$, then $\cos (A-B)=$
questions.solution:
Given
$\cos A+\cos B+\cos C=0=\sin A+\sin B+\sin C$ ...(i)
Now $\cos A+\cos B+\cos C=0$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow 2 \cos \left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right) \cos \left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)+\cos C=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 2 \cos \left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right) \cdot \cos \left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)=-\cos C
\end{aligned}
$$
$\Rightarrow \quad \cos \left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right)=\frac{-\cos C}{2 \cos \left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)}$ ...(ii)
Again now $\sin A+\sin B+\sin C=0$ (given)
$$
\Rightarrow \quad 2 \sin \left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right) \cdot \cos \left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right)+\sin C=0
$$
$\Rightarrow \quad \cos \left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right)=-\frac{\sin C}{2 \sin \left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)}$ ...(iii)
From (ii) and (iii), we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \frac{-\cos C}{2 \cos \left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)}=-\frac{\sin C}{2 \sin \left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)} \\
& \Rightarrow \tan C=\tan \left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right) \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{C}=\frac{A+B}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$
putting $\mathrm{C}=\frac{A+B}{2}$ in equation (ii), we get
$$
\Rightarrow \cos \left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right)=\frac{-\cos \left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)}{2 \cos \left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)}
$$
$$
\Rightarrow \cos \left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right)=-\frac{1}{2}
$$
we know that
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \cos (A-B)=2 \cdot \cos ^2\left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right)-1 \\
& =2 \cdot\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2-1=-\frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$
